citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

derivations.claim: The rightmost factor is stacked lowest, so the factors from bottom to top are $\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1}$. Starting from the bottom positions, the component-position sequence after successive crossings is $(1,2,3)$, $(1,3,2)$, $(3,1,2)$, $(3,2,1)$, $(2,3,1)$, $(2,1,3)$, $(1,2,3)$. The six crossing-label pairs and signs in that order are respectively $(2,3,+1)$, $(1,3,-1)$, $(1,2,+1)$, $(2,3,-1)$, $(1,3,+1)$, and $(1,2,-1)$, as determined by the signed generators in the braid word and [F1]. Thus the closure returns each label to its own endpoint, and each component pair crosses twice with opposite signs. By [F4] each pairwise linking number is half the signed mixed-crossing sum, hence is zero.

At crossing 1, component 2 passes under component 3, so its meridian becomes $B=x_3^{-1}x_2x_3$. At crossing 2, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the longitude factor $x_1^{-1}$. At crossing 3, component 1 passes under component 2, so its meridian becomes $C=B^{-1}x_1B$. At crossing 5, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the factor $C$. The other crossings do not put component 3 under. Hence $\lambda_3=x_1^{-1}C=x_1^{-1}B^{-1}x_1B$.

In $R_2$, $E(B)\equiv1+X_2\pmod{\mathfrak m^2}$, so
$$E(C)=E(B)^{-1}(1+X_1)E(B)=1+X_1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$
Since $E(x_1^{-1})=1-X_1+X_1^2$, multiplication gives
$$E(\lambda_3)=E(x_1^{-1})E(C)=1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$
Under [A1], the $X_1X_2$ coefficient is $+1$, so [F3] gives $\mu_{\tau_B}(1,2,3)=1$.

The computed longitude has zero degree-one term, as required by the chosen untwisted based peripheral system. Closing the endpoints along crossing-free arcs adds no undercrossing factor, and component 3 has self-writhe zero, so the same word is its based closed-link preferred longitude by [F2]. Every proper length-two subsequence in $\Delta_{123}^b$ is a pairwise linking number, so step 1.1 makes $\Delta_{123}^b=0$. Thus the same coefficient gives the closed-link residue candidate $1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

derivations.claim: The rightmost factor is stacked lowest, so the factors from bottom to top are $\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1}$. Starting from the bottom positions, the component-position sequence after successive crossings is $(1,2,3)$, $(1,3,2)$, $(3,1,2)$, $(3,2,1)$, $(2,3,1)$, $(2,1,3)$, $(1,2,3)$. The six crossing-label pairs and signs in that order are respectively $(2,3,+1)$, $(1,3,-1)$, $(1,2,+1)$, $(2,3,-1)$, $(1,3,+1)$, and $(1,2,-1)$, as determined by the signed generators in the braid word and [F1]. Thus the closure returns each label to its own endpoint, and each component pair crosses twice with opposite signs. By [F4] each pairwise linking number is half the signed mixed-crossing sum, hence is zero.

At crossing 1, component 2 passes under component 3, so its meridian becomes $B=x_3^{-1}x_2x_3$. At crossing 2, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the longitude factor $x_1^{-1}$. At crossing 3, component 1 passes under component 2, so its meridian becomes $C=B^{-1}x_1B$. At crossing 5, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the factor $C$. The other crossings do not put component 3 under. Hence $\lambda_3=x_1^{-1}C=x_1^{-1}B^{-1}x_1B$.

In $R_2$, $E(B)\equiv1+X_2\pmod{\mathfrak m^2}$, so $$E(C)=E(B)^{-1}(1+X_1)E(B)=1+X_1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$ Since $E(x_1^{-1})=1-X_1+X_1^2$, multiplication gives $$E(\lambda_3)=E(x_1^{-1})E(C)=1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$ Under [A1], the $X_1X_2$ coefficient is $+1$, so [F3] gives $\mu_{\tau_B}(1,2,3)=1$.

The computed longitude has zero degree-one term, as required by the chosen untwisted based peripheral system. Closing the endpoints along crossing-free arcs adds no undercrossing factor, and component 3 has self-writhe zero, so the same word is its based closed-link preferred longitude by [F2]. Every proper length-two subsequence in $\Delta_{123}^b$ is a pairwise linking number, so step 1.1 makes $\Delta_{123}^b=0$. Thus the same coefficient gives the closed-link residue candidate $1$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, hence Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected domain with smooth boundary, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite. Let $F:\overline\Omega\to\overline\Omega$ be a diffeomorphism smooth through the boundary, with smooth inverse and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=\operatorname{id}$. For $x=F(y)$, put $J_F(y)=|\det DF(y)|$ and define

$$ (F_*\gamma)(x)=\frac{DF(y)\,\gamma(y)\,DF(y)^T}{J_F(y)},\qquad y=F^{-1}(x). $$

Then $F_*\gamma$ is a smooth uniformly positive-definite matrix conductivity and its weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map equals that of $\gamma$. Explicitly, for every pair of boundary trace-data classes $f,h\in\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$,

$$\langle\Lambda_{F_*\gamma}f,h\rangle=\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle,$$

where each map is the weak energy form $\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, $u_{\gamma,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$, and $V_h$ is any $H^1$ representative of $h$.

The same gauge invariance has a Riemannian form. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary, $g$ a smooth Riemannian metric, $\Gamma\subseteq\partial M$ relatively open, and $\Phi:M\to M$ a smooth diffeomorphism with $\Phi|_\Gamma=\operatorname{id}$. Define $(\Phi^*g)_p(v,w):=g_{\Phi(p)}(D\Phi_pv,D\Phi_pw)$. The cotangent inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_g$ is induced by $g^{-1}$, and in coordinates $dV_g=\sqrt{\det(g_{ij})}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. A smooth function $u$ is $g$-harmonic when $\int_M\langle du,d\psi\rangle_g\,dV_g=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$. Then $u\circ\Phi$ is $\Phi^*g$-harmonic; for any two smooth $g$-harmonic functions $u,v$,

$$\int_M\langle d(u\circ\Phi),d(v\circ\Phi)\rangle_{\Phi^*g}\,dV_{\Phi^*g}=\int_M\langle du,dv\rangle_g\,dV_g.$$

If the boundary traces of $u,v$ are supported in $\Gamma$, then composition by $\Phi$ leaves both traces fixed, so the local energy measurement of every such smooth harmonic pair is unchanged. In particular, if for each $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ the Dirichlet solutions for $g$ and $\Phi^*g$ with trace $f$ are unique and smooth, then the corresponding local energy DN maps agree.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. Under the trace-quotient isomorphism and the local boundedness result, this form gives the usual weak map into the dual $H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ with the scalar convention.

derivations.claim: Write $R_\varepsilon(r)=r(1+\varepsilon(1-r^2))$ for $0\le r\le1$. Then $R_\varepsilon(0)=0$, $R_\varepsilon(1)=1$, and $R_\varepsilon'(r)=1+\varepsilon-3\varepsilon r^2\ge1-2\varepsilon>0$. Thus $R_\varepsilon$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[0,1]$ to itself; $F_\varepsilon$ preserves each radial ray, is bijective on the ball, and fixes the boundary pointwise.

At the origin $DF_\varepsilon(0)=(1+\varepsilon)I_n$ and $J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^n>0$. At $r>0$ the radial derivative is $R_\varepsilon'(r)>0$ and each tangential eigenvalue is $R_\varepsilon(r)/r=1+\varepsilon(1-r^2)>0$. By continuity, $R_\varepsilon'$ stays positive on $[0,1+\delta]$ for some $\delta>0$. The same radial formula extends $F_\varepsilon$ to a smooth diffeomorphism from the ball of radius $1+\delta$ onto its image, which contains a neighborhood of $\overline{B^n}$; its inverse is smooth there. Thus the inverse is smooth through the boundary and the differential is nonsingular on the closed ball.

Since $F_\varepsilon(0)=0$, the pushforward formula in [F1] gives $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon(0)=DF_\varepsilon(0)DF_\varepsilon(0)^T/J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^{2-n}I_n$. Because $n\ge3$ and $\varepsilon>0$, this differs from $I_n$, so the pushed-forward conductivity is nontrivial.

The hypotheses of [F1] hold for $\gamma=I_n$ and $F_\varepsilon$, so $\Lambda_{\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon}=\Lambda_{I_n}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, hence Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected domain with smooth boundary, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite. Let $F:\overline\Omega\to\overline\Omega$ be a diffeomorphism smooth through the boundary, with smooth inverse and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=\operatorname{id}$. For $x=F(y)$, put $J_F(y)=|\det DF(y)|$ and define

$$ (F_*\gamma)(x)=\frac{DF(y)\,\gamma(y)\,DF(y)^T}{J_F(y)},\qquad y=F^{-1}(x). $$

Then $F_*\gamma$ is a smooth uniformly positive-definite matrix conductivity and its weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map equals that of $\gamma$. Explicitly, for every pair of boundary trace-data classes $f,h\in\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$,

$$\langle\Lambda_{F_*\gamma}f,h\rangle=\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle,$$

where each map is the weak energy form $\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, $u_{\gamma,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$, and $V_h$ is any $H^1$ representative of $h$.

The same gauge invariance has a Riemannian form. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary, $g$ a smooth Riemannian metric, $\Gamma\subseteq\partial M$ relatively open, and $\Phi:M\to M$ a smooth diffeomorphism with $\Phi|_\Gamma=\operatorname{id}$. Define $(\Phi^*g)_p(v,w):=g_{\Phi(p)}(D\Phi_pv,D\Phi_pw)$. The cotangent inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_g$ is induced by $g^{-1}$, and in coordinates $dV_g=\sqrt{\det(g_{ij})}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. A smooth function $u$ is $g$-harmonic when $\int_M\langle du,d\psi\rangle_g\,dV_g=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$. Then $u\circ\Phi$ is $\Phi^*g$-harmonic; for any two smooth $g$-harmonic functions $u,v$,

$$\int_M\langle d(u\circ\Phi),d(v\circ\Phi)\rangle_{\Phi^*g}\,dV_{\Phi^*g}=\int_M\langle du,dv\rangle_g\,dV_g.$$

If the boundary traces of $u,v$ are supported in $\Gamma$, then composition by $\Phi$ leaves both traces fixed, so the local energy measurement of every such smooth harmonic pair is unchanged. In particular, if for each $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ the Dirichlet solutions for $g$ and $\Phi^*g$ with trace $f$ are unique and smooth, then the corresponding local energy DN maps agree.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. derivations.claim: Write $R_\varepsilon(r)=r(1+\varepsilon(1-r^2))$ for $0\le r\le1$. Then $R_\varepsilon(0)=0$, $R_\varepsilon(1)=1$, and $R_\varepsilon'(r)=1+\varepsilon-3\varepsilon r^2\ge1-2\varepsilon>0$. Thus $R_\varepsilon$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[0,1]$ to itself; $F_\varepsilon$ preserves each radial ray, is bijective on the ball, and fixes the boundary pointwise.

At the origin $DF_\varepsilon(0)=(1+\varepsilon)I_n$ and $J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^n>0$. At $r>0$ the radial derivative is $R_\varepsilon'(r)>0$ and each tangential eigenvalue is $R_\varepsilon(r)/r=1+\varepsilon(1-r^2)>0$. By continuity, $R_\varepsilon'$ stays positive on $[0,1+\delta]$ for some $\delta>0$. The same radial formula extends $F_\varepsilon$ to a smooth diffeomorphism from the ball of radius $1+\delta$ onto its image, which contains a neighborhood of $\overline{B^n}$; its inverse is smooth there. Thus the inverse is smooth through the boundary and the differential is nonsingular on the closed ball.

Since $F_\varepsilon(0)=0$, the pushforward formula in [F1] gives $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon(0)=DF_\varepsilon(0)DF_\varepsilon(0)^T/J_{F_\varepsilon}(0)=(1+\varepsilon)^{2-n}I_n$. Because $n\ge3$ and $\varepsilon>0$, this differs from $I_n$, so the pushed-forward conductivity is nontrivial.

Fix a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ and a bounded measurable functional
$f:E\to\mathbb R$, with $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|<\infty$. All
target laws below are probability measures on this same space. If a model or
discretization originally uses another state space, specify its measurable
embedding into $E$ and compare its pushforward law; no identification of
different state spaces is implicit. A **posterior law** here is the probability
law for the unknown at the specified computation stage, conditional on the same
fixed observed data. For a probability law $\mu$, write
$\mu(f):=\int_E f\,d\mu$.

Name the successive posterior laws as follows: $\mu_\star$ is the intended
target; $\mu_{\rm model}$ is the posterior under the selected statistical or
physical model; $\mu_{\rm solver}$ is the posterior after replacing the exact
forward or PDE solution by the declared numerical solver output; and
$\mu_{\rm disc}$ is the posterior after the declared finite-dimensional
discretization. These labels refer to the exact adjacent laws recorded for the
computation, even when two stages happen to agree.

Let $K$ be the implemented probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$. An
**invariant law** $\pi_K$ for $K$ is a probability measure satisfying
$$\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi_K(dx)=\pi_K(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal E).$$
Choose and report which invariant law is used if $K$ has more than one. If no
invariant law has been established, the invariant-kernel and burn-in terms
below are unavailable; they are not set to zero. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a
time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative to its
natural filtration, with initial probability law $\lambda$. For burn-in length
$b\ge0$ and retained sample size $N\ge1$, set
$$\bar f_{b,N}:=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N f(X_{b+j}),$$
and let $\mathbb E_\lambda$ denote expectation under this initial law and the
chain's transition randomness.

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability

With the likelihoods stated in the Example, the exact prior-times-likelihood product is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2}$. $$ (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2-(u+2)^2/2}=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-(u+1)^2-1};$$
its normalizing integral is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-1}\sqrt\pi=e^{-1}/\sqrt2$, and its normalized density is $\pi^{-1/2}e^{-(u+1)^2}=N(-1,1/2)$ by [F2].

The exact density is symmetric about zero, so its mass on $(-\infty,0]$ is $1/2$. The standard normal density is positive and symmetric, so $\Phi_0(\sqrt2)>\Phi_0(0)=1/2$.

In the error ledger set $\mu_\star=\mu_{\rm model}=\Pi$ and $\mu_{\rm solver}=\mu_{\rm disc}=\widetilde\Pi$; then the solver-stage term is $\delta_{\rm solver}=\Phi_0(\sqrt2)-1/2$ and the model and discretization terms vanish. Since $\|f\|_\infty=1$, [F3] also gives $\delta_{\rm solver}\le2\|\Pi-\widetilde\Pi\|_{\rm TV}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on all boundary data, then every inward boundary-normal derivative agrees:
$$\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_1|_{\partial\Omega} =\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_2|_{\partial\Omega} \qquad(k=0,1,2,\ldots),$$
where $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ in a boundary normal collar.

derivations.claim: For every integer $m\geq0$, differentiation gives $\frac{d^m}{dt^m}e^{-1/t}=P_m(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ on $t>0$ for a polynomial $P_m$, by induction on $m$. For every polynomial $P$, $P(s)e^{-s}\to0$ as $s\to\infty$; for each power $s^N$, this follows from $e^s\geq s^{N+1}/(N+1)!$. Thus every right derivative tends to zero at $t=0$, so extension by zero to $t\leq0$ is smooth and flat there. Composition with $t=1-4|x|^2$ proves $\psi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$, with compact support in $\overline{B(0,1/2)}$. It is nonzero at $x=0$, and $\|\psi\|_\infty<\infty$.

The bound $|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty<1$ gives $\gamma_2(x)\geq1-|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty>0$, so [F1] applies. Since $\psi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\partial\Omega$, $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ agree on that neighborhood and all their boundary derivatives agree. At the origin, $\gamma_2(0)-\gamma_1(0)=\epsilon e^{-1}\ne0$. Thus identical boundary jets do not force interior equality.

$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: For $d_1$, $A_1CA_1^T=9$ and $\Gamma_1=1$, so [F1] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_1)=\frac12\log(1+9)=\frac12\log 10$. For $d_2$, $A_2CA_2^T=1$ and $\Gamma_2=1$, so [F1] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_2)=\frac12\log(1+1)=\frac12\log 2$.
The costs are equal and $10>2>0$, so strict increase of the logarithm [F2] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_1)>\operatorname{EIG}(d_2)$. Thus $d_1$ is the unique maximizer among the two candidates.

$$ \operatorname{supp}(\mu_X)=m+\operatorname{Ran}(C). $$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be random elements of a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
on a common probability space, and let $h:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable.
Suppose $Y_n:=h(X_n)$ is a strictly stationary real process in the sense of
[[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]], and suppose
$0<\sigma_h^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_0)<\infty$ using
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For $k\ge1$, put

$$\rho_h(k):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)}{\sigma_h^2}.$$

If $\sum_{k\ge1}|\rho_h(k)|<\infty$ and
$\tau_h:=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_h(k)>0$, define the theoretical
**functional-specific effective sample size** for an integer $n\ge1$ draws by
$\operatorname{ESS}_h(n):=n/\tau_h$. Here $Y_n$ is the scalar
functional whose Monte Carlo average is being assessed. When a central limit
theorem for that average has asymptotic variance
$\sigma_h^2\tau_h$, this definition is the iid sample size with the same
asymptotic variance. It does not assert that such a central limit theorem holds.
If the covariance series is not absolutely summable or $\tau_h\le0$, this
definition does not assign a finite positive effective sample size.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability
measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
$|f|\le M$ for some $0\le M<\infty$. Use the library convention
$$\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|.$$
Then
$$|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}.$$

For the complete posterior computation error budget defined above, the
pathwise total error satisfies
$$|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f.$$
This is a telescoping bound; it does not estimate any component.

Separately, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with transition kernel $K$, invariant law $\pi_K$, and initial law
$X_0\sim\pi_K$, and use the same bounded functional $f$. Put
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))\qquad(k\ge0).$$
If $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|<\infty$, then for every burn-in $b\ge0$ and
sample size $N\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[|\bar f_{b,N}-\pi_K(f)|^2\right]=\frac{1}{N^2}\left[N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k\right]\le\frac{\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|}{N}.$$
The sample bound assumes stationarity; for a nonstationary start, the budget
keeps $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$ as a separate burn-in term.
This finite-$N$ variance bound is not a central limit theorem or a confidence
interval.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: For either singleton $\{x\}$, $\pi K_\varepsilon(\{x\})=\tfrac12(1-\varepsilon)+\tfrac12\varepsilon=\tfrac12=\pi(\{x\})$; additivity gives $\pi K_\varepsilon=\pi$ by [F2]. The rows are probability measures by [F1].

Since $X_0\sim\pi$ and $\pi$ is invariant by step 1.1, [A1] permits the invariant-initial-law result [F4], which makes the chain strictly stationary. Its one-time law is symmetric, so $\mathbb E X_j=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=1$.

Put $\lambda=1-2\varepsilon=49/50$. By [F3], $\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=\lambda X_n$. Hence $\mathbb E[X_0X_{k+1}]=\lambda\mathbb E[X_0X_k]$ and $\mathbb E[X_0X_0]=1$, so induction gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,X_k)=\lambda^k$ and $\rho_f(k)=\lambda^k$.

The autocorrelations are absolutely summable because $0<\lambda<1$, with $\sum_{k\ge1}\lambda^k=\lambda/(1-\lambda)=49$. Thus $\tau_f=1+2\cdot49=99>0$, and [F5] gives $\operatorname{ESS}_f(10{,}000)=10{,}000/99$. The covariance bound [F6] applies, but neither it nor the ESS definition supplies a CLT.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain whose Euclidean metric is isometric to the product metric $dx_1^2\oplus g_0$ on a compact subdomain of $\mathbb R\times D^\circ$, where $(D,g_0)$ is a compact connected simple Riemannian surface with smooth boundary. Let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical scalar conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on every boundary datum, then $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ in $\overline\Omega$.

This classifies the configuration as outside the theorem's scope and asserts no uniqueness or nonuniqueness conclusion.

Assume AC. Let $\mu\sim N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ with $\tau_0^2>0$, and, conditional
on $\mu$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be IID $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known
$\sigma^2>0$ and $n\ge1$. The sampling data use the Borel sigma-algebra on
$\mathbb R^n$ with $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. For every
$y_{1:n}\in\mathbb R^n$, define
$$V_n=(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1},\qquad \mu_n=V_n\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} +\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i.$$
The evidence is finite and positive, and the posterior is $N(\mu_n,V_n)$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of Standard normal and normal laws has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$, let
$D\subseteq H$ be Borel with $\mu_0(D)=1$, and let
$\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be Borel. Assume the evidence
$$
Z:=\int_D e^{-\Phi_D(u)}\,\mu_0(du)
$$
satisfies $0<Z<\infty$. Extend the potential to all of $H$ by setting
$\bar\Phi(u)=\Phi_D(u)$ for $u\in D$ and $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$ for
$u\notin D$, and define the target probability
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For a scale $\beta\in[0,1]$,
write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. At state $u\in H$, draw $\xi\sim\mu_0$
independently and propose $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$. Set the acceptance probability
to $0$ if either $\bar\Phi(u)$ or $\bar\Phi(v)$ is $+\infty$, and otherwise set
$$
\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp(\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v))\}.
$$
Draw an independent uniform random variable on $[0,1]$ and move to $v$ if it
is at most $\alpha(u,v)$; otherwise remain at $u$. The resulting one-step
transition rule is the prior-preserving Crank–Nicolson, or pCN, rule
$P_\beta$. States with infinite potential are absorbing under this total
definition; they have $\mu$-measure zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the inputs of the prior-preserving
Crank–Nicolson algorithm: a separable real Hilbert space $H$, centered Borel
Gaussian reference probability $\mu_0$, full-mass Borel domain $D$, Borel
potential $\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, positive finite evidence $Z$, and
scale $\beta\in[0,1]$. Let $\mu$ be the normalized target on $H$ obtained by
extending $\Phi_D$ by $+\infty$ off $D$, and let $P_\beta$ be the algorithm's
accept-reject transition. Then $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$:
its joint flow
$$\Lambda_\beta(C):=\int_H P_\beta(u,C_u)\,\mu(du),\qquad C_u:=\{v\in H:(u,v)\in C\},$$
is unchanged by $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$ for every Borel
$C\subseteq H\times H$. Consequently, $\mu$ is invariant:
$$\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal B(H)).$$
This conclusion gives invariance only; it does not assert uniqueness,
convergence, mixing, an effective-sample-size bound, mesh-independent cost,
or correctness of an approximate forward solver.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] with $\mu_0=0$, $\tau_0^2=1$, $\sigma^2=1$, $n=1$, and $y=0$. The posterior variance is $(1+1)^{-1}=1/2$, and its mean is $(1+1)^{-1}(0+0)=0$. The evidence is finite and positive, so the posterior is the proper law $N(0,1/2)$.

By [F2], the likelihood density at $y=0$ is
$(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$. Its constant factor cancels when the likelihood is normalized against the prior, so the potential $\Phi(u)=u^2/2$ gives exactly the posterior from step 1.1. It is finite on $D=H=\mathbb R$, and the pCN target assumptions are satisfied.

For the proposal in [F3],
$$\Phi(u)-\Phi(v)=\frac{u^2-v^2}{2},$$
so the stated acceptance probability is precisely the algorithm's pCN acceptance rule for this target.

Step 1.1 identifies the normalized target, and step 2.1 identifies the kernel as the pCN accept-reject kernel for that target. Applying [F4] proves that $N(0,1/2)$ is invariant for every $\beta\in[0,1]$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.
