The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Every $u\in X$ is integrable on compact subsets by Cauchy–Schwarz. Define its extended distributional total variation by
$$TV_2(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\ \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2),\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}|\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$
where $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^2)$ denotes smooth compactly supported vector fields, $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm, and $\operatorname{div}\varphi=\partial_1\varphi_1+\partial_2\varphi_2$. This definition treats $L^2$ functions as almost-everywhere classes and does not require $u\in L^1(\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, or let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Set $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ for a measure space $(\Sigma,\mu)$, using the real integral inner products; under Countable Choice these are real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $A^*:Y\to X$ be its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$. Define $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ as follows. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, take $R(u)=TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$, the supremum of $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ over smooth compactly supported vector fields of Euclidean norm at most one. For bounded $\Omega$, either take Neumann TV, $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ when $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise, or Dirichlet TV, $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ when the zero extension $\widetilde u$ belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $+\infty$ otherwise. Thus the bounded-domain choices count, respectively, only the interior derivative or also the jump of the zero extension across the boundary. In the full-space case finite $R$ does not require global $L^1$ integrability.

Identify each $q\in X$ with the continuous linear functional $h\mapsto\langle q,h\rangle_X$ by the real Hilbert-space Riesz representation. For exact data $f=Au^\dagger$, a **minimum-TV exact solution** is a point $u^\dagger\in X$ satisfying $Au^\dagger=f$ and $R(u^\dagger)\le R(u)$ for every $u\in X$ with $Au=f$. A vector $p^\dagger\in Y$ is a **dual source certificate** for $u^\dagger$ if $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$, where $\partial R$ is the convex subdifferential on the real Banach space $X$. The **TV source condition** at $u^\dagger$ is that such a certificate exists; it does not assert uniqueness of the truth or of the certificate. For a chosen certificate, the associated Bregman distance is

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger):=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle A^*p^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X,$$

for $u\in\operatorname{dom}R$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$, with functions identified when they agree almost everywhere. For full-space TV, use $u$ itself. For a bounded-domain Dirichlet or Neumann problem, use the zero extension $\widetilde u$ only to define the geometric level sets; this does not change the selected regularizer, and for each nonzero level the resulting set lies inside $\Omega$. For $t>0$, the positive $t$-level class is the measurable-set class of $E_t^+(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)>t\}$; for $t<0$, the negative $t$-level class is the class of $E_t^-(u):=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:u(x)<t\}$. These classes do not depend on the representative of $u$. For any measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, its density-one representative is

$$E^{(1)}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|E\cap B(x,r)|}{|B(x,r)|}=1\right\}.$$

This representative depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $E$. The canonical level set $U_u^{(t)}$ is $(E_t^+(u))^{(1)}$ when $t>0$ and $(E_t^-(u))^{(1)}$ when $t<0$. Its canonical boundary is the ordinary topological boundary $\partial U_u^{(t)}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. For two nonempty boundary sets, use the usual extended Hausdorff distance induced by Euclidean distance; set $d_H(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$ and $d_H(E,F)=+\infty$ if exactly one set is empty. Hausdorff convergence uses this convention and is invariant under changes to a function on a null set.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero

$L^2$ norm.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link with $r\ge1$ components, and let $X_L=S^3\setminus L$ be its open complement. For each component choose a smooth fibrewise norm on its normal plane bundle $\nu(K_i)$ and a tubular map $\Phi_i$ from an open neighborhood of the zero section, fixing the zero section, together with a radius $\epsilon_i>0$ whose closed disk subbundle lies in that neighborhood. Require the resulting closed tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$ to be pairwise disjoint, and put $N(L)=\bigcup_{i=1}^rN(K_i)$ and $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(L)$, the resulting compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary. The tube choices are part of the input. Choose a basepoint $b\in E_L\subset X_L$. Orient each normal disk so that the positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the fixed orientation of $S^3$. A **positive meridian** $\mu_i$ of $K_i$ is the oriented boundary of the radius-$\epsilon_i$ normal disk in one fibre of $\nu(K_i)$; the curve lies on $\partial E_L$ and is disjoint from every component of $L$; its spanning normal disk meets $K_i$ transversely once with positive sign and misses every other component. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ and identifies the classes of $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ with its standard basis. Write $G=\pi_1(X_L,b)$ and let $\phi:G\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ be the first Hurewicz homomorphism, equivalently abelianization. The subgroup $\ker\phi$ is normal. The connected covering $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ classified by $\ker\phi$ is the **maximal abelian cover**; it is regular and its deck group is identified with $G/\ker\phi\cong H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. Put $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)]\cong\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, where $t_i$ is the deck transformation corresponding to $[\mu_i]$. The isomorphism sends each variable to its group-ring basis element; monomials $t_1^{n_1}\cdots t_r^{n_r}$ correspond bijectively to the basis elements indexed by $n_1[\mu_1]+\cdots+n_r[\mu_r]$. Define the absolute multivariable Alexander module by

$$A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z),$$

as a left $\Lambda_r$-module under the deck action. “Absolute” means this is ordinary homology of the covering space, not relative homology with respect to a fibre over the basepoint.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every integer $r\ge1$, the commutative ring
$$
\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]
$$
is Noetherian and a unique factorisation domain. Its units are exactly the elements $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $L$ be a nonempty oriented $r$-component link with $r\ge1$ and maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$ over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$

derivations.claim: Every point of $S^3\setminus H$ has $z\ne0$ and $w\ne0$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto(z/|z|,w/|w|,|z|)$ has inverse $(u,v,s)\mapsto(su,\sqrt{1-s^2}v)$, so the open complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and a compact exterior is $T^2\times I$. The two phase loops are positive meridians of the two coordinate-circle components, hence form the basis of $\pi_1(E_H)=H_1(E_H;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$. By [F3], the maximal abelian cover is the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$, whose first homology vanishes. The compact-exterior/open-complement identification [F7] therefore gives $A_H=0$.

By [F1], the two positive meridians form the coordinate basis; the coordinate-sum definition [F2] therefore sends both to $1$, so its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(1,-1)$. Quotienting the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$ by this rank-one translation subgroup gives $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$. Its first homology is $\mathbb Z$ generated by the circle. Every deck transformation is represented by a translation, and the path of translations from the identity to that translation is a homotopy, so $t$ acts as $1$. Thus the cyclic module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)\ne0$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$ because $A_H=0$.

Each piece is a solid-torus unknot exterior with the interior of one disjoint standard ball removed. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link with $r\ge1$ components, and let $X_L=S^3\setminus L$ be its open complement. For each component choose a smooth fibrewise norm on its normal plane bundle $\nu(K_i)$ and a tubular map $\Phi_i$ from an open neighborhood of the zero section, fixing the zero section, together with a radius $\epsilon_i>0$ whose closed disk subbundle lies in that neighborhood. Require the resulting closed tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$ to be pairwise disjoint, and put $N(L)=\bigcup_{i=1}^rN(K_i)$ and $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(L)$, the resulting compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary. The tube choices are part of the input. Choose a basepoint $b\in E_L\subset X_L$. Orient each normal disk so that the positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the fixed orientation of $S^3$. A **positive meridian** $\mu_i$ of $K_i$ is the oriented boundary of the radius-$\epsilon_i$ normal disk in one fibre of $\nu(K_i)$; the curve lies on $\partial E_L$ and is disjoint from every component of $L$; its spanning normal disk meets $K_i$ transversely once with positive sign and misses every other component. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ and identifies the classes of $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ with its standard basis. Write $G=\pi_1(X_L,b)$ and let $\phi:G\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ be the first Hurewicz homomorphism, equivalently abelianization. The subgroup $\ker\phi$ is normal. The connected covering $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ classified by $\ker\phi$ is the **maximal abelian cover**; it is regular and its deck group is identified with $G/\ker\phi\cong H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. Put $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)]\cong\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, where $t_i$ is the deck transformation corresponding to $[\mu_i]$. The isomorphism sends each variable to its group-ring basis element; monomials $t_1^{n_1}\cdots t_r^{n_r}$ correspond bijectively to the basis elements indexed by $n_1[\mu_1]+\cdots+n_r[\mu_r]$. Define the absolute multivariable Alexander module by

$$A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z),$$

as a left $\Lambda_r$-module under the deck action. “Absolute” means this is ordinary homology of the covering space, not relative homology with respect to a fibre over the basepoint.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every integer $r\ge1$, the commutative ring
$$
\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]
$$
is Noetherian and a unique factorisation domain. Its units are exactly the elements $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $L$ be a nonempty oriented $r$-component link with $r\ge1$ and maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$ over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$

$$
Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, $H:Y\times I\to B$ a homotopy, and $\widetilde H_0:Y\to E$ a lift of $H(-,0)$. There is a unique lift $\widetilde H:Y\times I\to E$ of $H$ extending $\widetilde H_0$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$

citations.quote:
Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. Let $F$ be a compact connected oriented Seifert surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,w,z)$ be an admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram representing $(K,F)$. The associated one-pointed hat chain complex $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is the finite-dimensional chain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from the minus complex by setting its basepoint variable to zero; its differential counts index-one disks with zero multiplicity at $w$. Assume for this specified data that the differential is nonincreasing in the Alexander filtration, that the absolute Alexander formula below takes integer values, and that $H(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))\cong\mathbb F_2$. Give a generator $\mathbf x$ its absolute Alexander filtration
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field assigned to $\mathbf x$ by the pointed Morse construction, with its prescribed boundary data near the two basepoints; $c_1$ is the first Chern class of the oriented plane field perpendicular to that vector field. To form the zero-framed surgery, remove a tubular neighborhood of $K$ and glue in a solid torus whose meridian is the longitude induced by $F$. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by deleting a boundary collar of $F$ and capping its longitude by the meridian disk of that solid torus. This is the standard integer normalization, with the one-generator diagram of the standard unknot at filtration zero. The subcomplex $F_s\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is spanned by generators of Alexander filtration at most $s$.

More generally, a finite integer-filtered chain complex is a finite-dimensional chain complex $C$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with subcomplexes $F_sC$ such that $F_sC=0$ for all sufficiently small integers $s$ and $F_sC=C$ for all sufficiently large integers $s$. If $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$, define
$$\tau(C):=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z:\operatorname{im}(H(F_sC)\longrightarrow H(C))\ne0\}.$$
For the fixed diagram and surface above, write $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)=\tau(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H),F_*\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))$. Once diagram and surface independence is proved, their common value is the knot invariant $\tau(K)$. Until that comparison is proved, $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)$ denotes only the value for the specified data.

For the standard oriented unknot $U$ and its standard genus-zero one-pointed Heegaard diagram, the normalized Alexander-filtered hat complex has total homology $\mathbb F_2$ generated at filtration level $0$. Consequently the diagramwise threshold is $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(U)=0$.

Take the grid on $\mathbb R^2/(5\mathbb Z)^2$ with marks $O_r=(r+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ and $X_r=((r+2)\bmod5+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ for $0\le r<5$. Let $C$ have the $120$ grid states as its $\mathbb F_2$-basis, Maslov grading $M_{\mathbb O}$ and Alexander filtration $A_G$. Its differential counts empty directed torus rectangles avoiding every $O$ but allowing $X$; equivalently, it is the full filtered minus matrix with all five variables set to zero. Then $C$ is a filtered chain complex and is filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving Maslov grading, to $S\otimes V^{\otimes4}$. Here $S$ has basis $a,b,c$ at respective $(M,A)$ values $(0,-1),(1,0),(2,1)$ with $\partial c=b$ and other differential zero, and $V$ has zero differential and basis at $(M,A)=(0,0),(-1,-1)$.

In particular, $H(C)$ has rank $16$. Its homology classes in Maslov degree $-k$, $0\le k\le4$, have multiplicity $\binom4k$ and first appear in Alexander filtration $-1-k$. This is a calculation of the specified grid matrix; no knot type or normalized analytic knot Floer identification is asserted.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $F$ be a compact connected oriented surface embedded in $S^3$ with boundary $K$ and minimum possible genus; write $g(K)=\operatorname{genus}(F)$. Let $G$ be any toroidal grid diagram for $K$ with grid number $n$. Let $C^-_{\mathrm{grid}}(G)$ be the full filtered minus complex produced by the grid-complex algorithm, and let $C^-_U(G)$ denote this same complex regarded over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by letting $U$ act as one chosen $U_i$, with the other variables retained independently. For an admissible $2n$-pointed Heegaard diagram $\mathcal H$ compatible with $(K,F)$, define $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ by the same restriction to a single variable action. Write $CFK^-(K)$ for the full filtered complex of an admissible doubly-pointed diagram. The ordinary fully collapsed quotient, obtained instead by setting all $U_i=U$, has type $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$; the restriction of scalars $C^-_U$ has type $CFK^-(K)$.

For the absolute Alexander normalization, let $\mathcal H_1$ be an admissible doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram for $(K,F)$. For a generator $\mathbf x$ of $\mathcal H_1$, set
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure assigned to this generator by the pointed Heegaard construction: it is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field obtained from the gradient trajectories through $\mathbf x$ and the chosen basepoint pair, after extending the field across small balls around the critical points. Its first Chern class is that of the oriented plane field orthogonal to this vector field. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by removing a tubular neighborhood $N(K)$ from $F$ and capping the resulting longitude with the meridian disk of the solid torus attached in zero-framed surgery on $K$. Let $\widehat{HFK}(K)$ be the homology of the Alexander-associated-graded complex obtained from the doubly-pointed complex $C^-_U(\mathcal H_1)$ by quotienting by its sole variable $U$, with this $A_F$ normalization.

Then $C^-_U(G)$ and $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ are filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving relative Maslov grading and the $A_F$ filtration, and their Alexander-associated-graded minus complexes are chain homotopy equivalent. For any two grids of $K$, the resulting normalized filtered complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent. If $\widetilde{GH}(G)$ denotes the homology of the tilde grid complex over $\mathbb F_2$, then
$$\widetilde{GH}(G)\cong\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)},$$
where $V$ is the two-dimensional bigraded vector space with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C(K)=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be its normalized bifiltered complex over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$. The complex of the reverse mirror $-K$ is filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to the dual complex $C(K)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]}(C(K),\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}])$, with dual differential $d\phi(x)=\phi(\partial x)$ and dual basis elements at negated bifiltration coordinates. There is also a Maslov-graded filtered-chain-homotopy equivalence from $C(K)$ to the complex obtained by exchanging the algebraic and Alexander filtrations. These are distinct symmetries: duality negates both filtration coordinates, while conjugation exchanges them.

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied regular admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram and normalized finite filtered hat complex $C_K$ whose total homology is $\mathbb F_2$. Let $K^\dagger$ be its reverse mirror under the fixed orientation-reversing reflection convention, with the reflected Seifert surface and reflected regular diagram. For a finite filtered complex $C$, define its dual complex $C^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2}(C,\mathbb F_2)$ with transposed differential and filtration
$$F_sC^\vee=\{\lambda\in C^\vee:\lambda(F_{-s-1}C)=0\}.$$
Then the reflected diagram's normalized filtered hat complex is filtered chain isomorphic to $C_K^\vee$. In particular, its total homology is $\mathbb F_2$ and
$$\tau_{\mathcal H^\dagger,F^\dagger}(K^\dagger)=-\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a connected compact oriented disk-and-band surface $F$ is built from $s$ disjoint disks by attaching $c$ rectangular bands along boundary intervals and has one boundary component, then $\chi(F)=s-c$ and $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. In particular, if the Seifert algorithm on an oriented knot diagram $D$ has $s$ Seifert circles and $c$ crossings, its output surface has genus $(1-s+c)/2$ and the knot genus satisfies $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. This is an upper bound from one spanning surface, not a minimality assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $S$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface properly embedded in $S^3\times[0,1]$, with product collars and oriented boundary $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$ for smooth oriented knots $K_0,K_1$. Let $g$ be the genus of $S$, and use the standard absolute Alexander normalization for the endpoint knot Floer complexes. Then
$$|\tau(K_1)-\tau(K_0)|\le g.$$
In particular, a smooth concordance annulus gives equal tau values, and a genus-$g$ surface from a knot to the unknot gives the four-ball genus estimate.

derivations.claim: The finite grid in [F3] is an actual negative trefoil diagram. Subtract $1/2$ from the marking coordinates for this projection description. Its row segments are $[0,2]$ in row $0$, $[1,3]$ in row $1$, $[2,4]$ in row $2$, $[0,3]$ in row $3$, and $[1,4]$ in row $4$, with the orientations $O\to X$. Vertical segments run $X\to O$ and pass over. The only interior crossings are $(2,1),(3,2),(1,3)$. Following the single component $O_0\to O_2\to O_4\to O_1\to O_3\to O_0$ encounters them as $A_{\rm over},B_{\rm under},C_{\rm over},A_{\rm under},B_{\rm over},C_{\rm under}$. The first two crossings have upward over-strand and rightward under-strand; the third has downward over-strand and leftward under-strand. Thus all have the same negative sign. Smoothing the degree-two grid corners gives the standard alternating three-crossing negative trefoil projection: each successive over-under pair forms one of the three braid crossings, and its two exterior connecting arcs give the closure. This is the closure of $\sigma_1^{-3}$, with the displayed cyclic traversal fixing its orientation. Reflection gives the positive trefoil convention of the Example. This finite knot admission uses the actual segments, not a deduction of knot type from a Floer polynomial.

By [F3, F4], the normalized all-variable-zero complex of this negative trefoil is filtered equivalent to both $S_-\otimes V^{\otimes4}$ and $\widehat{CFK}(T^\dagger)\otimes V^{\otimes4}$. Total homology in Maslov degree zero is one-dimensional in both tensor products: every non-top $V$ factor lowers Maslov degree, whereas $H(\widehat{CFK})$ is supported in degree zero. Its first filtered appearance in the first product is $-1$. In the second product its threshold is the threshold in $\widehat{CFK}$: inclusion into the top $V$ summand and projection onto that summand are filtered maps, with composition identity. Hence $\tau(T^\dagger)=-1$. Duality [F5] gives $\tau(T)=1$, independently of the genus inequality. The unknot value is [F2].

The same finite calculation also identifies the associated-graded generator ranks needed for the full Laurent staircase. Record bigraded ranks by Laurent polynomials in $m,a$. The associated graded of $S_-$ has one generator in each bidegree $(0,-1),(1,0),(2,1)$ and zero differential. Thus the accepted associated-graded comparison gives
$$P_{\widehat{HFK}(T^\dagger)}(m,a)(1+m^{-1}a^{-1})^4=(a^{-1}+m+m^2a)(1+m^{-1}a^{-1})^4.$$
Cancel the nonzero factor in the integral Laurent polynomial domain. Duality gives for the positive trefoil exactly one group in each bidegree $(0,1),(-1,0),(-2,-1)$, and no others, over $\mathbb F_2$. This is a mod-two conclusion; no integral rank formula is inferred.

Reduce the actual finite free Laurent complex at its differential terms preserving both coordinates. Normalize each finite basis vector to first coordinate zero. Such a term has coefficient $1$, preserves Alexander grading, and lowers Maslov grading by one. Elementary cancellation of this unit term is bifiltered: the coefficient and its inverse have zero filtration shift, and the usual finite formulas $d'=d-dh d$, $i'=i-hd i$, $p'=p-pd h$ stay in both filtrations. Maslov homogeneity prevents a second, different $U$ power in the same matrix entry. Consequently no power-series inverse is needed. Each cancellation removes two generators, and finite linear changes within a fixed bidegree and these cancellations leave precisely the three generators represented by the associated-graded homology from step 2.1. This gives an actual bifiltered Laurent equivalent complex with generators $a,b,c$ of the Example, rather than promoting a rank polynomial alone to a filtered equivalence.

The only possible differential entries in that reduced positive-trefoil complex, by Maslov degree and the two filtration inequalities, are
$$\partial a=\alpha b,\quad\partial b=\beta Ua+\gamma c,\quad\partial c=\delta Ub,\qquad \alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb F_2.$$
In its first-coordinate hat specialization the total homology is one-dimensional. If $\alpha=1$, its surviving class would be $c$ at level $-1$, contrary to step 1.2; if $\alpha=\gamma=0$, the hat homology would have rank three. Hence $\alpha=0$, $\gamma=1$. Squaring the differential gives $\delta=0$. In the other coordinate hat specialization the only possible remaining differential is $b\mapsto\beta Ua$; if $\beta=0$, it would have rank-three homology, contrary to conjugation [F5]. Thus $\beta=1$. This proves the displayed full Laurent staircase. Its dual has $\partial a^\vee=Ub^\vee$, $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$; after $U=0$ its hat differential is exactly the displayed reverse-mirror differential.

The oriented smoothing of the positive two-strand three-crossing braid has two circles and three bands. Its surface has genus $(1-2+3)/2=1$. Reflection gives the same for its reverse mirror, and an inward push gives smooth spanning surfaces in the four-ball. Therefore both smooth four-ball genera are at most one. By [F7] every smooth spanning surface has genus at least the absolute value of the independently computed tau invariant, which is one. Thus both genera equal one.

This proves all original Example clauses: the actual admitted finite grid and retained comparison/duality supply the invariant-level thresholds and both normalized filtered models, while Hom’s direct $\mathbb F_2$ genus input supplies the matching smooth lower bound. No integral Floer ranks or merely topological genus conclusion has been substituted.

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere. Let $F$ be a compact connected oriented Seifert surface with boundary $K$, and let $\mathcal H=(\Sigma,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,w,z)$ be an admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram representing $(K,F)$. The associated one-pointed hat chain complex $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is the finite-dimensional chain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ obtained from the minus complex by setting its basepoint variable to zero; its differential counts index-one disks with zero multiplicity at $w$. Assume for this specified data that the differential is nonincreasing in the Alexander filtration, that the absolute Alexander formula below takes integer values, and that $H(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))\cong\mathbb F_2$. Give a generator $\mathbf x$ its absolute Alexander filtration
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field assigned to $\mathbf x$ by the pointed Morse construction, with its prescribed boundary data near the two basepoints; $c_1$ is the first Chern class of the oriented plane field perpendicular to that vector field. To form the zero-framed surgery, remove a tubular neighborhood of $K$ and glue in a solid torus whose meridian is the longitude induced by $F$. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by deleting a boundary collar of $F$ and capping its longitude by the meridian disk of that solid torus. This is the standard integer normalization, with the one-generator diagram of the standard unknot at filtration zero. The subcomplex $F_s\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H)$ is spanned by generators of Alexander filtration at most $s$.

More generally, a finite integer-filtered chain complex is a finite-dimensional chain complex $C$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with subcomplexes $F_sC$ such that $F_sC=0$ for all sufficiently small integers $s$ and $F_sC=C$ for all sufficiently large integers $s$. If $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$, define
$$\tau(C):=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z:\operatorname{im}(H(F_sC)\longrightarrow H(C))\ne0\}.$$
For the fixed diagram and surface above, write $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)=\tau(\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H),F_*\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H))$. Once diagram and surface independence is proved, their common value is the knot invariant $\tau(K)$. Until that comparison is proved, $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K)$ denotes only the value for the specified data.

For the standard oriented unknot $U$ and its standard genus-zero one-pointed Heegaard diagram, the normalized Alexander-filtered hat complex has total homology $\mathbb F_2$ generated at filtration level $0$. Consequently the diagramwise threshold is $\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(U)=0$.

Take the grid on $\mathbb R^2/(5\mathbb Z)^2$ with marks $O_r=(r+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ and $X_r=((r+2)\bmod5+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ for $0\le r<5$. Let $C$ have the $120$ grid states as its $\mathbb F_2$-basis, Maslov grading $M_{\mathbb O}$ and Alexander filtration $A_G$. Its differential counts empty directed torus rectangles avoiding every $O$ but allowing $X$; equivalently, it is the full filtered minus matrix with all five variables set to zero. Then $C$ is a filtered chain complex and is filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving Maslov grading, to $S\otimes V^{\otimes4}$. Here $S$ has basis $a,b,c$ at respective $(M,A)$ values $(0,-1),(1,0),(2,1)$ with $\partial c=b$ and other differential zero, and $V$ has zero differential and basis at $(M,A)=(0,0),(-1,-1)$.

In particular, $H(C)$ has rank $16$. Its homology classes in Maslov degree $-k$, $0\le k\le4$, have multiplicity $\binom4k$ and first appear in Alexander filtration $-1-k$. This is a calculation of the specified grid matrix; no knot type or normalized analytic knot Floer identification is asserted.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $F$ be a compact connected oriented surface embedded in $S^3$ with boundary $K$ and minimum possible genus; write $g(K)=\operatorname{genus}(F)$. Let $G$ be any toroidal grid diagram for $K$ with grid number $n$. Let $C^-_{\mathrm{grid}}(G)$ be the full filtered minus complex produced by the grid-complex algorithm, and let $C^-_U(G)$ denote this same complex regarded over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by letting $U$ act as one chosen $U_i$, with the other variables retained independently. For an admissible $2n$-pointed Heegaard diagram $\mathcal H$ compatible with $(K,F)$, define $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ by the same restriction to a single variable action. Write $CFK^-(K)$ for the full filtered complex of an admissible doubly-pointed diagram. The ordinary fully collapsed quotient, obtained instead by setting all $U_i=U$, has type $CFK^-(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$; the restriction of scalars $C^-_U$ has type $CFK^-(K)$.

For the absolute Alexander normalization, let $\mathcal H_1$ be an admissible doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram for $(K,F)$. For a generator $\mathbf x$ of $\mathcal H_1$, set
$$A_F(\mathbf x)=\frac12\left\langle c_1(\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)),[\widehat F]\right\rangle,$$
where $\mathfrak s_{w,z}(\mathbf x)$ is the relative $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ structure assigned to this generator by the pointed Heegaard construction: it is the homology class of the nowhere-vanishing vector field obtained from the gradient trajectories through $\mathbf x$ and the chosen basepoint pair, after extending the field across small balls around the critical points. Its first Chern class is that of the oriented plane field orthogonal to this vector field. The surface $\widehat F$ is obtained by removing a tubular neighborhood $N(K)$ from $F$ and capping the resulting longitude with the meridian disk of the solid torus attached in zero-framed surgery on $K$. Let $\widehat{HFK}(K)$ be the homology of the Alexander-associated-graded complex obtained from the doubly-pointed complex $C^-_U(\mathcal H_1)$ by quotienting by its sole variable $U$, with this $A_F$ normalization.

Then $C^-_U(G)$ and $C^-_U(\mathcal H)$ are filtered chain homotopy equivalent, preserving relative Maslov grading and the $A_F$ filtration, and their Alexander-associated-graded minus complexes are chain homotopy equivalent. For any two grids of $K$, the resulting normalized filtered complexes are filtered chain homotopy equivalent. If $\widetilde{GH}(G)$ denotes the homology of the tilde grid complex over $\mathbb F_2$, then
$$\widetilde{GH}(G)\cong\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)},$$
where $V$ is the two-dimensional bigraded vector space with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C(K)=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be its normalized bifiltered complex over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$. The complex of the reverse mirror $-K$ is filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to the dual complex $C(K)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]}(C(K),\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}])$, with dual differential $d\phi(x)=\phi(\partial x)$ and dual basis elements at negated bifiltration coordinates. There is also a Maslov-graded filtered-chain-homotopy equivalence from $C(K)$ to the complex obtained by exchanging the algebraic and Alexander filtrations. These are distinct symmetries: duality negates both filtration coordinates, while conjugation exchanges them.

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied regular admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagram and normalized finite filtered hat complex $C_K$ whose total homology is $\mathbb F_2$. Let $K^\dagger$ be its reverse mirror under the fixed orientation-reversing reflection convention, with the reflected Seifert surface and reflected regular diagram. For a finite filtered complex $C$, define its dual complex $C^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F_2}(C,\mathbb F_2)$ with transposed differential and filtration
$$F_sC^\vee=\{\lambda\in C^\vee:\lambda(F_{-s-1}C)=0\}.$$
Then the reflected diagram's normalized filtered hat complex is filtered chain isomorphic to $C_K^\vee$. In particular, its total homology is $\mathbb F_2$ and
$$\tau_{\mathcal H^\dagger,F^\dagger}(K^\dagger)=-\tau_{\mathcal H,F}(K).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If a connected compact oriented disk-and-band surface $F$ is built from $s$ disjoint disks by attaching $c$ rectangular bands along boundary intervals and has one boundary component, then $\chi(F)=s-c$ and $g(F)=(1-s+c)/2$. In particular, if the Seifert algorithm on an oriented knot diagram $D$ has $s$ Seifert circles and $c$ crossings, its output surface has genus $(1-s+c)/2$ and the knot genus satisfies $g(K)\le (1-s+c)/2$. This is an upper bound from one spanning surface, not a minimality assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere and let $B^4$ be the standard four-ball with boundary $S^3$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable smooth properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. Let $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K)$ be the set of genera of connected compact orientable locally flat topologically properly embedded surfaces $F\subset B^4$ with oriented boundary $K$. For each such surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. Define the smooth slice genus and the locally flat topological slice genus by

$$
g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sm}}(K),\qquad g_4^{\mathrm{top}}(K):=\min\mathcal S_{\mathrm{top}}(K).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $S$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface properly embedded in $S^3\times[0,1]$, with product collars and oriented boundary $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$ for smooth oriented knots $K_0,K_1$. Let $g$ be the genus of $S$, and use the standard absolute Alexander normalization for the endpoint knot Floer complexes. Then
$$|\tau(K_1)-\tau(K_0)|\le g.$$
In particular, a smooth concordance annulus gives equal tau values, and a genus-$g$ surface from a knot to the unknot gives the four-ball genus estimate.

derivations.claim: The finite grid in [F3] is an actual negative trefoil diagram. Subtract $1/2$ from the marking coordinates for this projection description. Its row segments are $[0,2]$ in row $0$, $[1,3]$ in row $1$, $[2,4]$ in row $2$, $[0,3]$ in row $3$, and $[1,4]$ in row $4$, with the orientations $O\to X$. Vertical segments run $X\to O$ and pass over. The only interior crossings are $(2,1),(3,2),(1,3)$. Following the single component $O_0\to O_2\to O_4\to O_1\to O_3\to O_0$ encounters them as $A_{\rm over},B_{\rm under},C_{\rm over},A_{\rm under},B_{\rm over},C_{\rm under}$. The first two crossings have upward over-strand and rightward under-strand; the third has downward over-strand and leftward under-strand. Thus all have the same negative sign. Smoothing the degree-two grid corners gives the standard alternating three-crossing negative trefoil projection: each successive over-under pair forms one of the three braid crossings, and its two exterior connecting arcs give the closure. This is the closure of $\sigma_1^{-3}$, with the displayed cyclic traversal fixing its orientation. Reflection gives the positive trefoil convention of the Example. This finite knot admission uses the actual segments, not a deduction of knot type from a Floer polynomial.

By [F3, F4], the normalized all-variable-zero complex of this negative trefoil is filtered equivalent to both $S_-\otimes V^{\otimes4}$ and $\widehat{CFK}(T^\dagger)\otimes V^{\otimes4}$. Total homology in Maslov degree zero is one-dimensional in both tensor products: every non-top $V$ factor lowers Maslov degree, whereas $H(\widehat{CFK})$ is supported in degree zero. Its first filtered appearance in the first product is $-1$. In the second product its threshold is the threshold in $\widehat{CFK}$: inclusion into the top $V$ summand and projection onto that summand are filtered maps, with composition identity. Hence $\tau(T^\dagger)=-1$. Duality [F5] gives $\tau(T)=1$, independently of the genus inequality. The unknot value is [F2].

The same finite calculation also identifies the associated-graded generator ranks needed for the full Laurent staircase. Record bigraded ranks by Laurent polynomials in $m,a$. The associated graded of $S_-$ has one generator in each bidegree $(0,-1),(1,0),(2,1)$ and zero differential. Thus the accepted associated-graded comparison gives $$P_{\widehat{HFK}(T^\dagger)}(m,a)(1+m^{-1}a^{-1})^4=(a^{-1}+m+m^2a)(1+m^{-1}a^{-1})^4.$$ Cancel the nonzero factor in the integral Laurent polynomial domain. Duality gives for the positive trefoil exactly one group in each bidegree $(0,1),(-1,0),(-2,-1)$, and no others, over $\mathbb F_2$. This is a mod-two conclusion; no integral rank formula is inferred.

Reduce the actual finite free Laurent complex at its differential terms preserving both coordinates. Normalize each finite basis vector to first coordinate zero. Such a term has coefficient $1$, preserves Alexander grading, and lowers Maslov grading by one. Elementary cancellation of this unit term is bifiltered: the coefficient and its inverse have zero filtration shift, and the usual finite formulas $d'=d-dh d$, $i'=i-hd i$, $p'=p-pd h$ stay in both filtrations. Maslov homogeneity prevents a second, different $U$ power in the same matrix entry. Consequently no power-series inverse is needed. Each cancellation removes two generators, and finite linear changes within a fixed bidegree and these cancellations leave precisely the three generators represented by the associated-graded homology from step 2.2. This gives an actual bifiltered Laurent equivalent complex with generators $a,b,c$ of the Example, rather than promoting a rank polynomial alone to a filtered equivalence.

The only possible differential entries in that reduced positive-trefoil complex, by Maslov degree and the two filtration inequalities, are $$\partial a=\alpha b,\quad\partial b=\beta Ua+\gamma c,\quad\partial c=\delta Ub,\qquad \alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb F_2.$$ In its first-coordinate hat specialization the total homology is one-dimensional. If $\alpha=1$, its surviving class would be $c$ at level $-1$, contrary to step 2.1; if $\alpha=\gamma=0$, the hat homology would have rank three. Hence $\alpha=0$, $\gamma=1$. Squaring the differential gives $\delta=0$. In the other coordinate hat specialization the only possible remaining differential is $b\mapsto\beta Ua$; if $\beta=0$, it would have rank-three homology, contrary to conjugation [F5]. Thus $\beta=1$. This proves the displayed full Laurent staircase. Its dual has $\partial a^\vee=Ub^\vee$, $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$; after $U=0$ its hat differential is exactly the displayed reverse-mirror differential.

The oriented smoothing of the positive two-strand three-crossing braid has two circles and three bands. Its surface has genus $(1-2+3)/2=1$. Reflection gives the same for its reverse mirror, and an inward push gives smooth spanning surfaces in the four-ball. Therefore both smooth four-ball genera are at most one. By [F7] every smooth spanning surface has genus at least the absolute value of the independently computed tau invariant, which is one. Thus both genera equal one.

This proves all original Example clauses: the actual admitted finite grid and retained comparison/duality supply the invariant-level thresholds and both normalized filtered models, while Hom’s direct $\mathbb F_2$ genus input supplies the matching smooth lower bound. No integral Floer ranks or merely topological genus conclusion has been substituted.

Work over $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ be its finitely generated free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ chain complex with Maslov grading $M$ and bifiltration coordinates $(i,j)$. Multiplication by $U$ lowers each filtration coordinate by one and lowers $M$ by two; the differential lowers $M$ by one and does not increase either filtration. The total homology is $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ with its generator normalized in Maslov grading zero.

For a filtration region $R$, write $C\{R\}$ for the corresponding subquotient of the bifiltered complex; in particular $C\{i=0\}$ is the vertical complex, $C\{j=s\}$ is the horizontal complex at Alexander level $s$, and $C\{i=0,j\le s\}$ is the subcomplex of the vertical complex at levels at most $s$. Define
$$ \tau(C)=\min\{s\in\mathbb Z: H_*(C\{i=0,j\le s\})\longrightarrow H_*(C\{i=0\})\text{ is nonzero} \}. $$
For each integer $s$, let $F_s$ be the homology map induced by the chain map from $C\{i=0\}$ to $C\{\min(i,j-s)=0\}$ obtained by quotienting by $C\{i=0,j<s\}$ and then including the quotient. Let $G_s$ be the homology map from $C\{\max(i,j-s)=0\}$ to $C\{i=0\}$ obtained by quotienting by $C\{i<0,j=s\}$ and then including. The epsilon invariant is
$$ \epsilon(C)=\begin{cases} 1,&F_{\tau(C)}=0,\\ -1,&G_{\tau(C)}=0,\\ 0,&F_{\tau(C)}\ne0\text{ and }G_{\tau(C)}\ne0. \end{cases} $$
Here zero and nonzero refer to the induced homology maps. This definition fixes the sign convention; invariance under stable equivalence is a separate claim.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and $C=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ a finitely generated free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ complex. Choose a finite homogeneous basis $\{x_r\}$, with $M(x_r)$ and Alexander filtration $A(x_r)$. The translate $U^k x_r$ has Maslov grading $M(x_r)-2k$ and filtration coordinates $(i,j)=(-k,A(x_r)-k)$. The total homology is $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$; use the standard normalization in which its Maslov-zero tower generator first appears at algebraic filtration level $i=0$, and denote it by $\xi_K$.

For $t\in[0,2]$ and a nonzero finite chain $z$, define
$$ F_t(U^k x_r)=(1-t/2)(-k)+(t/2)(A(x_r)-k),\qquad F_t(z)=\max\{F_t(U^k x_r):U^k x_r\text{ has nonzero coefficient in }z\}. $$
Let $\mathcal Z_0(C)$ be the set of Maslov-zero cycles representing $\xi_K$. Set
$$ \nu_t(C)=\min_{z\in\mathcal Z_0(C)}F_t(z),\qquad \Upsilon_K(t)=-2\nu_t(C). $$
The minimum is over cycles representing the normalized homology generator, not over individual basis terms. For comparison, let $C^-(K)$ be the $\mathbb F_2[U]$-span of the chosen basis and form its $t$-modified complex over the ring $\mathcal R$ of formal sums $\sum_{\alpha\in S}c_\alpha v^\alpha$ whose support $S\subset[0,\infty)$ is well-ordered (every nonempty subset of $S$ has a least element). The coefficient extension uses $U=v^2$. In the extended Laurent complex, $v$ lowers both filtration coordinates by $1/2$ and Maslov grading by one, so a diagonal $U$-translation lowers the extended $t$-grading by two. On arbitrary homogeneous Laurent terms this grading is $M-t(j-i)$; the formula $M-tA$ below is specified on the chosen generators at $i=0$. A homogeneous generator $x$ has $t$-grading $M(x)-tA(x)$, extended by $\operatorname{gr}_t(v^\alpha x)=\operatorname{gr}_t(x)-\alpha$. If a term $U^k y$ occurs in $\partial x$, its $t$-modified differential coefficient is $v^{\operatorname{gr}_t(y)-\operatorname{gr}_t(x)+1}$; thus for $\partial x=\sum_y c_{xy}U^{(M(y)-M(x)+1)/2}y$, define $\partial_t x=\sum_y c_{xy}v^{\operatorname{gr}_t(y)-\operatorname{gr}_t(x)+1}y$. This differential lowers $t$-grading by one. The comparison between its non-torsion tower grading and the finite cycle minimum is the separate filtered tower-splitting claim.

Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots, and use the epsilon sign convention from the preceding definition. If their knot Floer complexes are stably filtered equivalent, meaning that there are totally acyclic bifiltered complexes $A$ and $B$ with $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A$ filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(J)\oplus B$, then $\epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)$. The acyclic summands here need not be acyclic after taking either associated-graded filtration.

The invariant satisfies $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$, $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$, and the tensor rules
$$ \epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(K),\qquad \epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(J). $$
The converse of $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$ fails: the knot $T_{2,5}\#-T_{4,5}\#T_{2,3;2,5}$ has $\tau=0$ and $\epsilon=1$, where $T_{p,q}$ is the positive $(p,q)$ torus knot and $T_{2,3;2,5}$ is the $(2,5)$ cable of the right-handed trefoil with longitudinal winding two. Epsilon is not an integer-valued homomorphism on the smooth concordance group: the right-handed trefoil has $\epsilon=1$ and its connected sum with itself also has $\epsilon=1$, not $2$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $F$ be a compact connected oriented surface embedded in $S^3$ with boundary $K$ and minimum possible genus; write $g(K)=\operatorname{genus}(F)$. Let $G$ be any toroidal grid diagram for $K$ with grid number $n$. where $V$ is the two-dimensional bigraded vector space with one generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ and one in bidegree $(-1,-1)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold with collared boundary $\partial W=\partial_0W\sqcup\partial_1W$, let $\varphi:S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k}\to\partial_1W$ be an attaching embedding of a $k$-handle and let $\psi:S^k\times D^{n-k-1}\to\partial_1(W\cup_\varphi h^k)$ be an attaching embedding of a $(k+1)$-handle attached after it, where $0\le k\le n-1$. If the attaching sphere of $h^{k+1}$ meets the belt sphere of $h^k$ transversely in exactly one point, then $W\cup_\varphi h^k\cup_\psi h^{k+1}$ is diffeomorphic to $W$ relative to $\partial_0W$. Consequently a geometrically cancelling consecutive pair may be deleted from, or added to, any handle presentation of the same manifold; the diffeomorphism may be taken to act only in a collar of the affected boundary disc and in the two handles, so the attaching data of all later handles are carried along.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude. Call $K$ smoothly slice when it bounds a smooth
properly embedded disk in the standard $B^4$, with a product collar at its
boundary. Then $K$ is smoothly slice if and only if the compact smooth
$4$-manifold $X_0(K)$, formed using that preferred-longitude framing, admits a
smooth codimension-zero embedding into the standard $S^4$.

derivations.claim:
The standard spanning disk for $U$ in $B^4$ is a smooth proper slice disk.
By [F4], its zero-trace embeds smoothly in $S^4$.

Glue the spanning disk for $U$ in the boundary $S^3$ to the core disk of
the attached $2$-handle. Their union is an embedded $S^2$, and its regular
neighborhood is the disk bundle over $S^2$ whose clutching map along the
equator has degree equal to the handle framing. The framing is zero by [F1],
so this clutching map has degree zero. Since $SO(2)\cong S^1$ and a degree-zero
map $S^1\to S^1$ is null-homotopic, the oriented disk bundle is trivial.
Therefore $X_0(U)\cong S^2\times D^2$.

The standard unknotted $S^2$ in $S^4$ has trivial oriented normal bundle:
in the round model one normal vector is radial in $\mathbb R^3$ and the other
is the constant fourth-coordinate vector. Its tubular neighborhood is thus
$S^2\times D^2$, giving the stated embedding of $X_0(U)$.

Each of $B$ and $G$ bounds its chosen normal disk meeting the core $R$
once, so both indicated sublinks are a knot and its meridian. The disks are
disjoint, so $B$ and $G$ have zero linking number. Their framings are zero by
the stated preferred-longitude pushoffs. Thus $(B,G,R)$ satisfies [F2].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Let $V$ be an even-order square matrix with integer entries, of size $n=2g$. A unimodular congruence replaces $V$ by $P^TVP$ for an integer matrix $P$ with determinant $+1$ or $-1$. For $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ as column vectors and $z\in\mathbb Z$, the two elementary enlargements of $V$ are
$$E_0(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_1(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Two even-order integral matrices are **S-equivalent** if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of unimodular congruences, elementary enlargements, and reverse elementary enlargements.

derivations.claim:
If two integral coordinate vectors $x,x'$ represent the same class modulo two, then $x'=x+2y$ for an integral vector $y$, and
$$(x+2y)^TV(x+2y)-x^TVx=2x^TVy+2y^TVx+4y^TVy$$
is even. Thus $x^TVx\pmod2$ is well-defined. Expanding the quadratic expression gives
$$q_F(x+y)-q_F(x)-q_F(y)=x^T(V+V^T)y\pmod2=x^T(V-V^T)y=x\cdot_Fy,$$
where plus and minus agree in $\mathbb F_2$. By [F2], this alternating form is nondegenerate.

In a symplectic basis, every vector is uniquely $x=\sum_i(a_i a_i+b_i b_i)$ with $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb F_2$. The refinement identity gives
$$q_F(x)=\sum_i\bigl(a_iq_F(a_i)+b_iq_F(b_i)+a_ib_i\bigr).$$
Therefore the finite Gauss sum factors as
$$\sum_{x\in H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)}(-1)^{q_F(x)}=\prod_i\sum_{a,b\in\mathbb F_2}(-1)^{a q_F(a_i)+b q_F(b_i)+ab}=2^g(-1)^{\sum_iq_F(a_i)q_F(b_i)}.$$
The left side depends only on $q_F$, not on a basis, so the exponent defining the Arf value is basis-independent.

Under either enlargement in [F3], the new basis vectors $u,v$ have $u\cdot v=1$, $q(u)=z\pmod2$, and $q(v)=0$; moreover $v$ is orthogonal to all old basis vectors because its encircling disk misses them. If $u$ pairs nontrivially with old basis vectors, add a linear combination of the old symplectic basis to $u$ to obtain $u'$ orthogonal to all of them; the nondegenerate old intersection matrix gives the required coefficients, and $u'\cdot v=1$ remains unchanged. The old basis together with $u',v$ is symplectic; its new Arf contribution is $q(u')q(v)=0$, while the old $q$-values are unchanged. More precisely, put $u''=u'+q(u')v$. The refinement identity and $q(v)=0$, $u'\cdot v=1$ give $q(u'')=q(u')+q(u')=0$, while $u''\cdot v=1$ and both $u'',v$ remain orthogonal to the old subspace. Thus the enlarged quadratic space is isometric to the old one orthogonally summed with the hyperbolic plane $q_H(s,t)=st$: on $su''+tv$ the value is $st$. An integral congruence reduces to an invertible mod-two coordinate change and hence an isometry of quadratic spaces. Consequently, the stable isometry class is invariant under congruences, enlargements and their reverses. Here stable isometry means isometry after adjoining finitely many copies of $q_H$ on either side. Thus the Gauss-sum Arf value is unchanged by enlargement or reduction. By the knot-matrix S-equivalence lemma, all spanning surfaces give the same value.
