Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: Choose the norming family from [F3]. Fix $r>0$, $h\in E$, and $n\ge1$. Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Thus $a_n\perp\ker\Sigma_n$, so $a_n\in S_n:=\operatorname{ran}(\Sigma_n)$, the support subspace of $Y_n$.

In the finite-dimensional space $S_n$, the restriction of $Y_n$ is a nondegenerate Gaussian vector. Let $Q_n=[-r,r]^n$ and $D_n=Q_n\cap S_n$, a closed symmetric convex set. Since $a_n\in S_n$, the event $Y_n-a_n\in Q_n$ is the translate by $a_n$ of $D_n$ inside $S_n$. An invertible linear change of coordinates turns the centered law on $S_n$ into a nondegenerate Gaussian law and preserves symmetry and convexity of $D_n$. Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields
$$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$
If $S_n=\{0\}$, then $Y_n=a_n=0$ almost surely and the same inequality is equality.

Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. The sets $A_n(h)$ decrease with $n$, and [F3] gives $\bigcap_n A_n(h)=\{\|W-ih\|_B\le r\}$; likewise $\bigcap_n A_n(0)=\{\|W\|_B\le r\}$. Apply [F5] to both decreasing sequences and pass to their limits in the finite-dimensional inequalities. This proves the stated ball-mass bound.

Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus

then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,

Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. derivations.claim: Choose boundary normal coordinates $(y,x_n)$ near $x_0$, with $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ and inward unit normal $\partial_{x_n}$. The induced metric on the boundary is smooth. Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it.

In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set
$$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$
For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. Choose any positive $\varepsilon_j$ for the finitely many smaller $j$. For each fixed derivative order, the tail then converges uniformly, so $\Phi$ is smooth and has the prescribed jets. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$.

For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives
$$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$
where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and
$L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$.
The phase is common to both conductivities and $p_\gamma=\gamma p_1$ vanishes to infinite order on the boundary by step 1.2. Prescribe $b_{0,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=\chi$ and $b_{-j,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ for $j\geq1$. In boundary normal coordinates the coefficient of the new normal derivative in $L_\gamma b$ is $2i\gamma$, which is nonzero. Therefore the normal derivatives of $b_{0,\gamma}$ can be chosen successively so that $L_\gamma b_{0,\gamma}=0$ to infinite order at the boundary; after choosing $b_{0,\gamma},\ldots,b_{-(j-1),\gamma}$, the same recursion chooses all jets of $b_{-j,\gamma}$ so that $iL_\gamma b_{-j,\gamma}+P_\gamma b_{-(j-1),\gamma}=0$ to infinite order. Realize each sequence by the Borel series in step 1.2 and multiply by a fixed collar cutoff equal to one near the boundary support. Repeat for $\widetilde\gamma$.

Let $b_{\lambda,\gamma}=\sum_{j=0}^K\lambda^{-j}b_{-j,\gamma}$, with the same construction for $\widetilde\gamma$. The order-$\lambda^2$ eikonal term and the order-$\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{1-K}$ transport terms in step 2.1 vanish to infinite order at $x_n=0$. Thus each remaining coefficient is $O(x_n^R)$ for every prescribed integer $R$. On the collar, $|e^{i\lambda\Phi}|\leq e^{-\lambda x_n/2}$. For every fixed $a,R$, direct integration gives
$$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$
Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. The same Gaussian integration shows $\|v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{L^2}=O(\lambda^{-1})$ and bounds its gradient norm above. Thus the $H^1$ norms are bounded above and the residual bounds hold for the arbitrary prescribed $N$.

Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]:
$$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$
If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$.

In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives
$$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$
uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. For each fixed $t$, the rescaled leading term tends to $2t^ke^{-2t}F(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2$. Each displayed remainder has an additional factor $\lambda^{-1}$ after scaling and is dominated by $C\lambda^{-1}(t^k+t^{k+1}+t^{k+2})e^{-t}$, including the phase error $e^{O(t^2/\lambda)}-1=O(t^2/\lambda)$; its integral tends to zero. On the rest of the fixed collar, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$ gives exponential decay $e^{-\lambda x_n}\leq e^{-\sqrt{\lambda}}$; every polynomial prefactor is therefore negligible. The cutoff region away from the collar is also exponentially small. Thus the limit for approximate beams is
$$2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,$$
whose constant is strictly positive.

Taking equal conductivities, $F=1$, and $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_\Omega|\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}|^2dx=c_0\int_{\partial\Omega}|\chi|^2dS>0$. Together with the upper bound in step 2.2 this proves the asserted two-sided $H^1$ norm bound.

The exact corrections satisfy $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$ by step 2.3, while both approximate beams have uniformly bounded $H^1$ norms by step 2.2. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the change in the weighted product integral, after multiplication by $\lambda^k$, by $C\lambda^k\lambda^{-N}$ because $0\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k\leq C$ on the bounded domain. Choose $N>k$. The error tends to zero, so the same limit holds for the exact solutions.

For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives $$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$ where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and $L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$. Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by Lipschitz graph neighborhoods with $\Omega$ on one side of each graph. The zero-extension map is bounded from $BV(\Omega)$ to $BV(\mathbb R^n)$, with support in $\overline\Omega$, and there is a finite $C_\Omega$ such that $$\|\widetilde u\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}+TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)\le C_\Omega\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u;\Omega)\bigr)$$ for every $u\in BV(\Omega)$. For every $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $$\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}\le |h|TV(v;\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be a function.
The **translate** of $f$ by $h$ is the function $\tau_h f$ defined by

$$ (\tau_h f)(x) := f(x-h)\qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

This fixes the sign convention used throughout the page: translating by $h$
shifts the graph of $f$ in the positive $h$-direction.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Set $u:=\gamma-1$ on $\Omega$. Since constants have zero distributional derivative, [F1] gives $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $TV(u;\Omega)=TV(\gamma;\Omega)\le R$, and $\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\le |\Omega|(M+1)$. The smooth bounded domain $\Omega$ is Lipschitz, so [F2] applies.

By the zero-extension part of [F2], $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and
$$TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)\le C_\Omega\bigl(|\Omega|(M+1)+R\bigr)=:V_0.$$
Since $\gamma_e=1+\widetilde u$, [F3] gives $\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_1=\|\widetilde u(\cdot+h)-\widetilde u\|_1\le V_0|h|$. Thus the first inequality holds with $C_1=V_0$.

The bound $m\le\gamma\le M$ inside $\Omega$ and the background value $1$ outside show $|\gamma_e|\le B$ almost everywhere; hence $|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e|\le2B$ almost everywhere. Applying [F3] and step 1.2 yields
$$\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_p^p\le(2B)^{p-1}V_0|h|.$$
Taking $p$-th roots and then the supremum over $|h|\le t$ gives the second inequality with $C_p=((2B)^{p-1}V_0)^{1/p}$. At $t=0$ both sides vanish.

Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be real measurable conductivities with $0<m\le\gamma_j\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Put $\mathcal D=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $E=\mathcal D/\mathbb C\mathbf1$, both with their quotient norms. For $f_j\in\mathcal D$, let $u_j$ be the weak $\gamma_j$-conductivity solution with trace class $f_j$. Then
$$((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(f_2)=\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}\,dx.$$
The exact norm equality
$$\|\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D,\mathcal D^*)}=\|\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(E,E^*)}=:\delta$$
holds, and consequently the integral above has absolute value at most $\delta\|[f_1]\|_E\|[f_2]\|_E$, and at most $\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. Here $[f_j]$ denotes the coset modulo constants; the stars denote continuous conjugate-linear duals.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $s\ge1$, and let $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^d$ be orthonormal. Put $\zeta=s(e_1-ie_2)$ and
$$p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi.$$
Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$, and set
$$\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p_\zeta(\xi)|^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,\qquad \|u\|_{X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$$
For every fixed Schwartz function $\phi$, a constant $C=C(d,\phi)$ independent of $s,e_1,e_2$ satisfies, for all Schwartz $u$,
$$\|\phi u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{X_\zeta^{-1/2}},\qquad \|\phi u\|_{X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
Consequently
$$\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}},\qquad \|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
The norms are finite on Schwartz space; the values of the weights on the measure-zero characteristic sphere do not affect them. All four maps extend continuously to the completions in the respective input norms.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, a ball $B\subset\mathbb R^d$, and $K>0$. Let $\gamma\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$ be real and positive, equal to $1$ outside $B$, and put $a=\nabla\log\gamma$. Suppose
$$\|a\|_\infty+[a]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le K.$$
Define the compactly supported distribution $q$ and its multiplication form by
$$\langle q,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla v+\frac14\int |a|^2v,\qquad \langle m_q u,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla(uv)+\frac14\int |a|^2uv.$$
These pairings are complex bilinear. For the angular Fourier norms with $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$, there are constants $C,s_0\ge1$, depending only on $d,\alpha,B,K$, such that for every null phase $\zeta$ of length $\sqrt2s$ with $s\ge s_0$,
$$\|m_q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\to\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le Cs^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}\le\frac12.$$
There is $r_\zeta\in\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\cap H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$U_\zeta(x)=e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta(x)),\qquad (-\Delta+q)U_\zeta=0,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le2\|q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}.$$
The equation uses the multiplication form above against compactly supported smooth tests. For the phases $\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)$ associated to $k$ and $P\perp k$, if $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}\}$, then for either sign,
$$\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\left(\|q\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{-1/2}}^2+\|r_{\zeta_\pm}\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{1/2}}^2\right)ds\,d\eta\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $k\in\mathbb R^d$, and fix an oriented two-plane $P\perp k$. For a unit vector $\eta\in P$, let $\eta^\perp$ be its positive quarter turn. For $s\ge|k|/2$, put $r(s)=\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}$ and
$$\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)=\pm s\eta+i(k/2\pm r(s)\eta^\perp).$$
These phases are null, have length $\sqrt2s$, and sum to $ik$. Use the unitary angular Fourier convention and the norms $\dot X_\zeta^b,X_\zeta^b$ with inhomogeneous weight $s+|p_\zeta|$, where $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$. For a fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f):=\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)}^{-1/2}}^2\,ds\,d\eta.$$
Here $d\eta$ is arclength, either sign can be used, and the derivative is distributional. For $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C^d)$,
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\|f\|_2^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,\phi$. If $f\in H^1$, also
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le\frac C\lambda\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$
Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$, put $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$, and define $\omega_2(f,h)=\sup_{|y|\le h}\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2$. For $h>0$ one consequently has
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C_\rho\left[\frac{\|f\|_2^2}{\lambda h^2}+\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\omega_2(f,h)^2\right].$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Extend both coefficients by $1$ using [F1], and fix a ball $B$ containing $[0,1]^d$ and a neighborhood of it. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ and $a_j=
abla\log\gamma_j$. These are globally $C^1$ and $C^{0,\alpha}$, respectively, and $a_j$ has support in $\overline{\Omega'}$. Their supremum and Hölder bounds are uniform: the positive lower bound $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ gives $|a_j|\le C_dR/m_*$; on $|x-y|\le1$, expand $
abla\gamma_j(x)/\gamma_j(x)-
abla\gamma_j(y)/\gamma_j(y)$, using the derivative Hölder bound and $|\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(y)|\le\sqrt dR|x-y|$; on larger distances use twice the supremum. Thus [F4] applies uniformly. Let $q_j=	frac12\operatorname{div}a_j+	frac14|a_j|^2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$, with bilinear distribution pairings as in [F4].

The Liouville form identity is $\int
abla v\cdot
abla w+\langle q_j,vwangle=\int\gamma_j
abla(v/g_j)\cdot
abla(w/g_j)$ for $v,w\in H^1$ on a bounded set. Indeed $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ means $\langle q_j,vwangle=-\int
abla g_j\cdot
abla(g_j^{-1}vw)$; expanding this derivative gives the displayed identity term by term. All products are integrable since $g_j,g_j^{-1},
abla g_j$ are bounded and the factors are in $H^1$. The identity extends from smooth factors by local $H^1$ approximation; multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function with bounded derivative is continuous on $H^1$, as follows from the product rule and the same approximation. Since $g_j=1$ near $\partial\Omega$, the trace of $U_j$ equals that of $u_j:=U_j/g_j$. A solution $U_j$ of the Schrödinger form equation therefore gives a weak conductivity solution $u_j$: test the form identity with $w=g_jz$, first for compactly supported tests and then in $H_0^1$ by density. Subtracting the two Schrödinger forms for solutions $U_1,U_2$, or repeating the weak-solution subtraction in [F2], gives $\langle Q,U_1U_2angle=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(\overline{f_2})$. Here $f_j$ is the trace class of $u_j$, and the conjugation converts the sesquilinear DN convention to the bilinear interior form. The compact support of $Q$ makes its whole-space pairing identical to its pairing on $\Omega$. Consequently $|\langle Q,U_1U_2angle|\le\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Use the paired phases $\zeta_\pm=s(\pm\eta)+i(k/2\pm\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}\,\eta^\perp)$ of [F4]. For fixed $s$ their remainders satisfy $\|r_j\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. To verify this last uniform bound, the symbol inequality $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_{\zeta_j}(\xi)|)\le Cs$ follows by splitting $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. Apply the negative cutoff bound in [F3] to $\operatorname{div}a_j$ and $|a_j|^2$ as in [F4] to obtain $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. The two positive cutoff bounds then give $\|r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le C$ and $\|\nabla r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le Cs$. Multiplication by $g_j^{-1}e^{x\cdot\zeta_j}$ yields $\|u_j\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le Ce^{Cs}s$. Thus step 2.1 bounds the exact interior product by $C\delta e^{Cs}s^2$.

Fix a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\phi=1$ near $\overline{\Omega'}$. We first prove the modulated cutoff bound used for each linear remainder term. Let $u$ be Schwartz and write the Fourier convolution for $\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u$ with $h=\xi-\eta-k$. The symbol comparison and characteristic-sphere estimate proved in [F3] give, uniformly in the center $y$, $\int\langle\xi-y\rangle^{-L}(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})\,d\xi\le C_L$ for sufficiently large $L$, and $s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^2$, where $D_\zeta$ is distance to the characteristic sphere of $p_\zeta$. Since $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})$, these estimates imply
 $\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta-k)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C\langle k\rangle^2$.
Indeed, after substituting $h=\xi-\eta-k$, the integrand is bounded by $C|\widehat\phi(h)|\langle k+h\rangle^2(1+D_\zeta(\eta+k+h)^{-1})$; use $\langle k+h\rangle^2\le C\langle k\rangle^2\langle h\rangle^2$, the rapid decay of $\widehat\phi$, and the uniform-center estimate. The same weighted Schur argument as in [F3] gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|u\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Applying the dual argument of [F3] to $\overline\phi e^{-ik\cdot x}$ yields $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, and hence also the same bound with the homogeneous positive-half norm on the left. Density in the weighted Fourier completions follows by truncating away from the characteristic sphere, as in [F3]. Since $2\le N=d+10$, this proves the modulation estimate used below with the stated exponent. Because $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$.

Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. For each linear or quadratic product, integral Cauchy–Schwarz and [F4] bound its average by $C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$, where $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. The same bound applies when the potential $q_j$ and remainder $r_l$ have different indices, because [F4] holds for either coefficient and either phase. Absorbing the fixed Fourier normalization gives $|\widehat Q(k)|\le C\delta e^{C\lambda}\lambda^2+C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$ whenever $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\langle k\rangle\}$. Replacing $k$ by $-k$ if needed accounts for the negative-sign Fourier convention.

Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For $t\ge1$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $Ct^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|$. The high-frequency contribution of the zero-order field is at most $Ct^{-1}$. For the divergence field $f=a_1-a_2$, split $f=\rho_h*f+(f-\rho_h*f)$ with a fixed nonnegative unit-mass mollifier. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$.

Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. Substituting step 5.1 in step 6.1 therefore gives $\mathcal Q\le C[\delta e^{D t^A}+t^{-\beta}]$ for a fixed $D>0$, after absorbing the polynomial factor $t^{d/2}\lambda^2$ into the exponential. For sufficiently small $0<\delta<t_0$, take $t=(\log(1/\delta)/(2D))^{1/A}\ge1$. The first term becomes $\sqrt\delta$, and the second is $C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\beta/A}$. The former is bounded by a constant times the latter, since $e^{-x/2}x^{\beta/A}$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $\mathcal Q\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\rho}$ with $\rho=\beta/A>0$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $
abla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $
abla\log H\cdot
abla w$. Test this identity with $w$ to obtain $\int H|
abla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hwangle$. The test is legitimate by $H^1$ approximation, since $Q$ is an $L^2$ field plus a divergence of an $L^2$ field and $Hw\in H_0^1(B)$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle Q,Hwangle|\le\mathcal Q\|Hw\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^d)}\le C\mathcal Q\|w\|_{H^1(B)}$. Since $H\ge m_*>0$, Poincaré in [F5] implies $\|w\|_{H^1(B)}\le C\mathcal Q$; if this norm is zero the estimate is immediate, otherwise divide the resulting quadratic inequality by it. Finally the mean value theorem on the bounded interval of possible $\log g_j$ gives $|\gamma_1-\gamma_2|=|e^{2\log g_1}-e^{2\log g_2}|\le2\max\{M,1\}|w|$. Thus $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\mathcal Q$. In particular $\delta=0$ forces equality of the coefficients.

Combine steps 7.1–8.1 for $0\le\delta<t_0$, reducing $t_0$ below $1/2$ if necessary. For $\delta\ge t_0$, use $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$ and enlarge $C$ to at least $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$. This is precisely the saturated modulus in the statement. Every bound used only the fixed class parameters, the geometry and $d,\alpha$, and the zero-data case was proved in step 8.1.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

Let $d\ge3$ and let $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ for the domain, collar, ellipticity bounds and exponent $0<\alpha<1$ defining that class. Extend $\gamma$ by $1$ outside $\Omega$, using its continuous representative on $\overline\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$, $\gamma_e-1$ has support contained in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and
$$\min\{m,1\}\le\gamma_e\le M,\qquad \sup_{\mathbb R^d}|\gamma_e|\le\max\{R,1\},\qquad \sup_{\mathbb R^d}|\partial_j\gamma_e|\le R,\qquad [\partial_j\gamma_e]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le R.$$
Here the Hölder seminorm is $[f]_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{x\ne y}|f(x)-f(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, and $j=1,\ldots,d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega)$ be a real almost-everywhere class with $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$. Set $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with quotient norm $\|[U]\|_{\mathcal D}:=\inf_{w\in H_0^1(\Omega)}\|U+w\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$, and let $\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$ be its continuous conjugate-linear dual. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, let $u_{\gamma,f}$ be the unique element of the coset $f$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{\nabla z}\,dx=0\qquad(z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)).$$
Define the weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$ by
$$\bigl(\Lambda_\gamma f\bigr)(g):=\int_\Omega\gamma\,\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{\nabla V_g}\,dx,$$
where $V_g$ is any representative of $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$. The trace quotient identification makes $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ the $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data space with its trace quotient norm. Constants lie in the kernel of $\Lambda_\gamma$, and its range functionals annihilate constants; hence $\Lambda_\gamma$ induces $\dot\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1\to(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*$, the quotient Dirichlet-to-Neumann map used for Calderón stability. Well-posedness, independence from the representative $V_g$, boundedness and the induced quotient map are established by the well-posedness result cited below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $0<m\le M<\infty$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere. Define $\mathcal D(\Omega):=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ with its quotient norm. For every boundary trace class $f\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u_{\gamma,f}\in f$ such that
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\,
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla z}\,dx=0\qquad	ext{for every }z\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C).$$
For every $g\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the value $\int_\Omega\gamma
abla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\overline{
abla V_g}\,dx$ is independent of the representative $V_g\in g$ and defines a bounded linear map $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal D(\Omega)	o\mathcal D(\Omega)^*$. Constants are in its kernel and its range functionals annihilate constants.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be real measurable conductivities with $0<m\le\gamma_j\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Put $\mathcal D=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $E=\mathcal D/\mathbb C\mathbf1$, both with their quotient norms. For $f_j\in\mathcal D$, let $u_j$ be the weak $\gamma_j$-conductivity solution with trace class $f_j$. Then
$$((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(f_2)=\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}\,dx.$$
The exact norm equality
$$\|\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D,\mathcal D^*)}=\|\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_2}\|_{\mathcal L(E,E^*)}=:\delta$$
holds, and consequently the integral above has absolute value at most $\delta\|[f_1]\|_E\|[f_2]\|_E$, and at most $\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. Here $[f_j]$ denotes the coset modulo constants; the stars denote continuous conjugate-linear duals.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $s\ge1$, and let $e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^d$ be orthonormal. Put $\zeta=s(e_1-ie_2)$ and
$$p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi.$$
Use the unitary angular-frequency Fourier transform $\widehat u(\xi)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$, and set
$$\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p_\zeta(\xi)|^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,\qquad \|u\|_{X_\zeta^b}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)^{2b}|\widehat u(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$$
For every fixed Schwartz function $\phi$, a constant $C=C(d,\phi)$ independent of $s,e_1,e_2$ satisfies, for all Schwartz $u$,
$$\|\phi u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{X_\zeta^{-1/2}},\qquad \|\phi u\|_{X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
Consequently
$$\|\phi u\|_2\le Cs^{-1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}},\qquad \|\nabla(\phi u)\|_2\le Cs^{1/2}\|u\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}.$$
The norms are finite on Schwartz space; the values of the weights on the measure-zero characteristic sphere do not affect them. All four maps extend continuously to the completions in the respective input norms.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, a ball $B\subset\mathbb R^d$, and $K>0$. Let $\gamma\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)$ be real and positive, equal to $1$ outside $B$, and put $a=\nabla\log\gamma$. Suppose
$$\|a\|_\infty+[a]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}\le K.$$
Define the compactly supported distribution $q$ and its multiplication form by
$$\langle q,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla v+\frac14\int |a|^2v,\qquad \langle m_q u,v\rangle=-\frac12\int a\cdot\nabla(uv)+\frac14\int |a|^2uv.$$
These pairings are complex bilinear. For the angular Fourier norms with $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$, there are constants $C,s_0\ge1$, depending only on $d,\alpha,B,K$, such that for every null phase $\zeta$ of length $\sqrt2s$ with $s\ge s_0$,
$$\|m_q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\to\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}\le Cs^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}\le\frac12.$$
There is $r_\zeta\in\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}\cap H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$U_\zeta(x)=e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta(x)),\qquad (-\Delta+q)U_\zeta=0,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le2\|q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}.$$
The equation uses the multiplication form above against compactly supported smooth tests. For the phases $\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)$ associated to $k$ and $P\perp k$, if $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}\}$, then for either sign,
$$\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\left(\|q\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{-1/2}}^2+\|r_{\zeta_\pm}\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{1/2}}^2\right)ds\,d\eta\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $k\in\mathbb R^d$, and fix an oriented two-plane $P\perp k$. For a unit vector $\eta\in P$, let $\eta^\perp$ be its positive quarter turn. For $s\ge|k|/2$, put $r(s)=\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}$ and
$$\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)=\pm s\eta+i(k/2\pm r(s)\eta^\perp).$$
These phases are null, have length $\sqrt2s$, and sum to $ik$. Use the unitary angular Fourier convention and the norms $\dot X_\zeta^b,X_\zeta^b$ with inhomogeneous weight $s+|p_\zeta|$, where $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$. For a fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f):=\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)}^{-1/2}}^2\,ds\,d\eta.$$
Here $d\eta$ is arclength, either sign can be used, and the derivative is distributional. For $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C^d)$,
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\|f\|_2^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,\phi$. If $f\in H^1$, also
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le\frac C\lambda\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$
Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$, put $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$, and define $\omega_2(f,h)=\sup_{|y|\le h}\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2$. For $h>0$ one consequently has
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C_\rho\left[\frac{\|f\|_2^2}{\lambda h^2}+\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\omega_2(f,h)^2\right].$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Extend both coefficients by $1$ using [F1], and fix a ball $B$ containing $[0,1]^d$ and a neighborhood of it. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ and $a_j=
abla\log\gamma_j$. These are globally $C^1$ and $C^{0,\alpha}$, respectively, and $a_j$ has support in $\overline{\Omega'}$. Their supremum and Hölder bounds are uniform: the positive lower bound $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ gives $|a_j|\le C_dR/m_*$; on $|x-y|\le1$, expand $
abla\gamma_j(x)/\gamma_j(x)-
abla\gamma_j(y)/\gamma_j(y)$, using the derivative Hölder bound and $|\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(y)|\le\sqrt dR|x-y|$; on larger distances use twice the supremum. Thus [F4] applies uniformly. Let $q_j=	frac12\operatorname{div}a_j+	frac14|a_j|^2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$, with bilinear distribution pairings as in [F4].

The Liouville form identity is $\int
abla v\cdot
abla w+\langle q_j,vwangle=\int\gamma_j
abla(v/g_j)\cdot
abla(w/g_j)$ for $v,w\in H^1$ on a bounded set. Indeed $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ means $\langle q_j,vwangle=-\int
abla g_j\cdot
abla(g_j^{-1}vw)$; expanding this derivative gives the displayed identity term by term. All products are integrable since $g_j,g_j^{-1},
abla g_j$ are bounded and the factors are in $H^1$. The identity extends from smooth factors by local $H^1$ approximation; multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function with bounded derivative is continuous on $H^1$, as follows from the product rule and the same approximation. Since $g_j=1$ near $\partial\Omega$, the trace of $U_j$ equals that of $u_j:=U_j/g_j$. A solution $U_j$ of the Schrödinger form equation therefore gives a weak conductivity solution $u_j$: test the form identity with $w=g_jz$, first for compactly supported tests and then in $H_0^1$ by density. Subtracting the two Schrödinger forms for solutions $U_1,U_2$, or repeating the weak-solution subtraction in [F2], gives $\langle Q,U_1U_2angle=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(\overline{f_2})$. Here $f_j$ is the trace class of $u_j$, and the conjugation converts the sesquilinear DN convention to the bilinear interior form. The compact support of $Q$ makes its whole-space pairing identical to its pairing on $\Omega$. Consequently $|\langle Q,U_1U_2angle|\le\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Use the paired phases $\zeta_\pm=s(\pm\eta)+i(k/2\pm\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}\,\eta^\perp)$ of [F4]. For fixed $s$ their remainders satisfy $\|r_j\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. To verify this last uniform bound, the symbol inequality $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_{\zeta_j}(\xi)|)\le Cs$ follows by splitting $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. Apply the negative cutoff bound in [F3] to $\operatorname{div}a_j$ and $|a_j|^2$ as in [F4] to obtain $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. The two positive cutoff bounds then give $\|r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le C$ and $\|\nabla r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le Cs$. Multiplication by $g_j^{-1}e^{x\cdot\zeta_j}$ yields $\|u_j\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le Ce^{Cs}s$. Thus step 2.1 bounds the exact interior product by $C\delta e^{Cs}s^2$.

Fix a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\phi=1$ near $\overline{\Omega'}$. We first prove the modulated cutoff bound used for each linear remainder term. Let $u$ be Schwartz and write the Fourier convolution for $\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u$ with $h=\xi-\eta-k$. The symbol comparison and characteristic-sphere estimate proved in [F3] give, uniformly in the center $y$, $\int\langle\xi-y\rangle^{-L}(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})\,d\xi\le C_L$ for sufficiently large $L$, and $s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^2$, where $D_\zeta$ is distance to the characteristic sphere of $p_\zeta$. Since $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})$, these estimates imply $\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta-k)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C\langle k\rangle^2$. Indeed, after substituting $h=\xi-\eta-k$, the integrand is bounded by $C|\widehat\phi(h)|\langle k+h\rangle^2(1+D_\zeta(\eta+k+h)^{-1})$; use $\langle k+h\rangle^2\le C\langle k\rangle^2\langle h\rangle^2$, the rapid decay of $\widehat\phi$, and the uniform-center estimate. The same weighted Schur argument as in [F3] gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|u\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Applying the dual argument of [F3] to $\overline\phi e^{-ik\cdot x}$ yields $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, and hence also the same bound with the homogeneous positive-half norm on the left. Density in the weighted Fourier completions follows by truncating away from the characteristic sphere, as in [F3]. Since $2\le N=d+10$, this proves the modulation estimate used below with the stated exponent. Because $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$.

Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. For each linear or quadratic product, integral Cauchy–Schwarz and [F4] bound its average by $C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$, where $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. The same bound applies when the potential $q_j$ and remainder $r_l$ have different indices, because [F4] holds for either coefficient and either phase. Absorbing the fixed Fourier normalization gives $|\widehat Q(k)|\le C\delta e^{C\lambda}\lambda^2+C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$ whenever $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\langle k\rangle\}$. Replacing $k$ by $-k$ if needed accounts for the negative-sign Fourier convention.

Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For $t\ge1$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $Ct^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|$. The high-frequency contribution of the zero-order field is at most $Ct^{-1}$. For the divergence field $f=a_1-a_2$, split $f=\rho_h*f+(f-\rho_h*f)$ with a fixed nonnegative unit-mass mollifier. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$.

Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. Substituting step 5.1 in step 6.1 therefore gives $\mathcal Q\le C[\delta e^{D t^A}+t^{-\beta}]$ for a fixed $D>0$, after absorbing the polynomial factor $t^{d/2}\lambda^2$ into the exponential. For sufficiently small $0<\delta<t_0$, take $t=(\log(1/\delta)/(2D))^{1/A}\ge1$. The first term becomes $\sqrt\delta$, and the second is $C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\beta/A}$. The former is bounded by a constant times the latter, since $e^{-x/2}x^{\beta/A}$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $\mathcal Q\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\rho}$ with $\rho=\beta/A>0$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $
abla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $
abla\log H\cdot
abla w$. Test this identity with $w$ to obtain $\int H|
abla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hwangle$. The test is legitimate by $H^1$ approximation, since $Q$ is an $L^2$ field plus a divergence of an $L^2$ field and $Hw\in H_0^1(B)$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle Q,Hwangle|\le\mathcal Q\|Hw\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^d)}\le C\mathcal Q\|w\|_{H^1(B)}$. Since $H\ge m_*>0$, Poincaré in [F5] implies $\|w\|_{H^1(B)}\le C\mathcal Q$; if this norm is zero the estimate is immediate, otherwise divide the resulting quadratic inequality by it. Finally the mean value theorem on the bounded interval of possible $\log g_j$ gives $|\gamma_1-\gamma_2|=|e^{2\log g_1}-e^{2\log g_2}|\le2\max\{M,1\}|w|$. Thus $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\mathcal Q$. In particular $\delta=0$ forces equality of the coefficients.

Combine steps 7.1–8.1 for $0\le\delta<t_0$, reducing $t_0$ below $1/2$ if necessary. For $\delta\ge t_0$, use $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$ and enlarge $C$ to at least $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$. This is precisely the saturated modulus in the statement. Every bound used only the fixed class parameters, the geometry and $d,\alpha$, and the zero-data case was proved in step 8.1.
