citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

derivations.claim: There is a constant $C_P$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(M)}$ for $w\in H_0^1(M)$. Otherwise choose $w_j\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w_j\|_{L^2}=1$ and $\|\nabla w_j\|_{L^2}\to0$. The sequence is bounded in $H^1$. A finite chart partition and [F2] give an $L^2$-convergent subsequence; a further subsequence converges weakly in the Hilbert space $H^1$, so its limit $w$ belongs to the weakly closed subspace $H_0^1(M)$, has weak gradient zero, and has $L^2$ norm one. In each connected coordinate ball, convolution of a function with zero weak gradient is constant on smaller balls; overlapping balls force the constants to agree, so connectedness makes $w$ constant on $M^\circ$. Its trace is zero by [F4], whereas the trace of a nonzero constant is that same nonzero constant on the nonempty boundary. This contradiction proves the inequality.

Compactness of $M$ and positivity of $\gamma$ give $\gamma_*:=\min_M\gamma>0$. Thus $a_\gamma(w,z)=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)\,dV_g$ is bounded on $H_0^1(M)$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)\geq c\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2$ by step 1.1 and $\gamma_*$. By [F3], for any bounded conjugate-linear functional $G$ on $H_0^1(M)$ there is a unique $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $a_\gamma(w,z)=G(z)$ for all $z$.

Flatten each boundary chart, apply the local half-space trace lift, and patch the finitely many chart lifts with a smooth partition. The resulting $Ef\in H^1(M)$ has trace $f$ and norm bounded by $C\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\partial M)}$ by [F5]. For $h\in L^2(M)$ take $G(z)=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g-a_\gamma(Ef,z)$ in step 2.1 and set $v=Ef+w$. Then $v$ has trace $f$ and satisfies the weak equation. If $v_1,v_2$ are two such solutions, their difference $w$ lies in $H_0^1$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)=0$; since $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, $\nabla w=0$, and step 1.1 gives $w=0$.

Suppose $h$ and $f$ are smooth. By [F8], extend $f$ smoothly from the boundary into a collar and multiply by a cutoff to obtain a smooth extension $Ef$ on $M$. Then $w=v-Ef$ has zero trace and solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gw)=h-\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gEf)$, whose right-hand side is smooth. In each boundary chart, flatten the boundary and write the principal matrix as $|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}$; it is smooth and uniformly elliptic because $g$ is positive definite and $\gamma$ has a positive minimum. For the base case, localize $w$ by a cutoff; its equation has an $L^2$ right-hand side since $w\in H^1$, so [F6] gives local $H^2$ regularity. If $w\in H^{m+1}$, each cutoff commutator contains derivatives of $w$ of order at most $m+1$ with smooth bounded coefficients, hence lies in $H^m$; the localized right-hand side is therefore in $H^m$, and [F6] gives $H^{m+2}$ regularity. Induction over $m$ and a finite chart cover give $w\in H^m(M)$ for every integer $m$. By [F7], $w$ and hence $v=Ef+w$ are smooth up to the boundary.

citations.quote:
A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

derivations.claim: Embed the segment in a collar extension across $\partial M_0$ and cover it by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods. On an embedded subsegment, parallel transport an orthonormal normal frame and set $F(t,y)=\exp_{\gamma(t)}(\sum_\alpha y_\alpha E_\alpha(t))$. The inverse function theorem gives local Fermi coordinates with $g_{jk}(t,0)=\delta_{jk}$ and $\partial_i g_{jk}(t,0)=0$. This construction is along an interval and uses no orientation of $M_0$.

In one such chart, seek $v_s=e^{is\Theta}a$, $s=\tau+i\lambda$, with $\Theta(t,0)=t$ and $\operatorname{Im}\Theta(t,y)\geq c|y|^2$. Expand $\Theta$ into homogeneous transverse Taylor polynomials. The quadratic polynomial is $\frac12H(t)y\cdot y$; substituting into $g(d\Theta,d\Theta)=1$ gives the matrix Riccati equation $H'+H^2=F(t)$, where $F$ is determined by the second transverse Taylor coefficient of the inverse metric. An initial complex symmetric $H(t_0)$ with positive-definite imaginary part yields a smooth solution with positive imaginary part on a short subsegment. Each higher homogeneous phase term then solves a linear first-order ODE along $t$, because its newest coefficient occurs linearly in the eikonal equation.

Substituting $a=\tau^{(m-1)/4}\sum_{j=0}^N s^{-j}a_{-j}$ into $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)e^{is\Theta}a$ cancels successive powers of $s$ by linear transport ODEs for the transverse Taylor coefficients of each $a_{-j}$. The leading coefficient solves $a_0(t,0)=c_0\exp(-\frac12\int_{t_0}^t\operatorname{tr}H(r)\,dr)$. A finite Taylor realization to the order required for the fixed $K$ and a transverse cutoff produce a smooth local beam; Gaussian integration gives bounded $L^2$ norm and a residual that tends to zero faster than any prescribed power after increasing the Taylor order.

On an oriented transversal of dimension at least two, apply [F3] to complete the finite overlap matching and eliminate all distinct-branch cross terms. This gives the stated global family and limit; steps 1.1--2.1 describe its local ingredients, without claiming a new proof of the imported global estimates.

For a nonorientable transversal let $\pi:\widetilde M_0\to M_0$ be its orientation double cover, with deck involution $\sigma$, and lift $\gamma$ to $\widetilde\gamma$. Let $w_s$ be the oriented beam from [F3] along that lift. Define the descended function by $\pi^*v_s=w_s+\sigma^*w_s$. The residual and norm bounds follow by a finite sum and the covering integral formula. The two lifted segments have no common tangent branch: equality of position and velocity at different times would make the geodesic periodic, contrary to its nontangential boundary exit; opposite velocities at a repeated point would force a zero midpoint velocity by geodesic uniqueness. There are only finitely many crossing branches, by compactness and local uniqueness. The distinct-branch estimate in [F3], applied to these two lifts, therefore gives a zero mixed-term limit. For every continuous $\psi$ the covering formula is
$$\int_{M_0}|v_s|^2\psi\,dV=\int_{\widetilde M_0}|w_s|^2(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV+\operatorname{Re}\int_{\widetilde M_0}w_s\overline{\sigma^*w_s}(\psi\circ\pi)\,dV.$$
The first term has precisely the required ray limit and the second tends to zero. In particular there is no extra factor two in the normalization. The same argument works if the cover is disconnected.

If the transversal has dimension one, the component containing the segment is an interval with arclength coordinate $t$ beginning at its incoming endpoint. Set $v_s=e^{ist}$ on this component and zero on all other components. The residual is zero and the asserted integral formula is exact. In dimension zero the given unit-speed segment cannot exist. This covers the dimensions not needed in the CTA application as well.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\gamma>0$. There is a constant $C_P>0$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be real
Banach spaces, let $U \subseteq X \times Y$ be open for the product metric, let
$F : U \to Z$ be of class $C^k$ with $k \ge 1$
([[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]]), and let $(a,b) \in U$ with
$F(a,b) = 0$. Let $D_XF(a,b) := DF(a,b)\circ i_X$ and
$D_YF(a,b) := DF(a,b)\circ i_Y$ be the partial derivatives, where
$i_X(x) := (x,0)$ and $i_Y(y) := (0,y)$. If $D_YF(a,b) : Y \to Z$ is a bounded
linear isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $A \subseteq X$ of $a$
and $B \subseteq Y$ of $b$ and a unique map $g : A \to B$ of class $C^k$ such
that

$$\{\,(x,y) \in A \times B : F(x,y) = 0\,\} = \{\,(x,g(x)) : x \in A\,\},$$

and along the graph $Dg$ satisfies
$$Dg(x) = -\,D_YF\bigl(x,g(x)\bigr)^{-1}\,D_XF\bigl(x,g(x)\bigr) \qquad (x \in A).$$
In particular $g(a) = b$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

derivations.claim: For $q=0$, the Dirichlet kernel of $-\Delta_g$ is trivial: if $w\in H_0^1(M)$ is weakly harmonic, testing with $w$ gives $\int_M|\nabla w|^2dV_g=0$, and the zero-trace Poincare inequality in [F2] gives $w=0$. Thus [F3] supplies the zero-boundary inverse $G=(-\Delta_g)^{-1}:H^{s-2}(M)\to X_s$, where $X_s=\{w\in H^s(M):w\in H_0^1(M)\}$. The high-order estimate in [F3], together with its bounded $H^1$ inverse, makes $G$ bounded.

Since $s>n/2+2$, [F4] makes $H^s(M)$ an algebra by localizing to finitely many smooth charts, extending each localized representative to a bounded Euclidean chart domain, applying the Euclidean algebra estimate, and summing the finite norms. Thus the map $(\epsilon,w)\mapsto q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3$ is a continuous polynomial from $\mathbb R^m\times X_s$ into $H^{s-2}(M)$, where $f_\epsilon=\sum_j\epsilon_jh_j$ and $Ef_\epsilon$ is the smooth collar extension from [F7]. Define
$$\mathcal F(\epsilon,w)=w-G\big[\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon)-q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3\big]\in X_s.$$
It is $C^3$ (indeed polynomial plus bounded linear maps) and $\mathcal F(0,0)=0$.

At $(0,0)$, the derivative $D_w\mathcal F(0,0)$ is the identity on $X_s$, because the derivative of $u\mapsto q u^3$ at $u=0$ vanishes. By [F6], there is a neighborhood of $\epsilon=0$ and a unique $C^3$ map $w(\epsilon)\in X_s$ near zero such that $\mathcal F(\epsilon,w(\epsilon))=0$. The fixed-point equation is exactly $-\Delta_g(Ef_\epsilon+w)+q(Ef_\epsilon+w)^3=0$ with boundary trace $f_\epsilon$, so $u_\epsilon=Ef_\epsilon+w(\epsilon)$ gives the unique small solution.

By [F5], $u_\epsilon\in C^2(\overline M)$ and the outward normal derivative has a continuous boundary trace. The trace map from $C^1(\overline M)$ to $C^0(\partial M)$ is bounded in the chartwise norms, so composing the $C^3$ map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ with this bounded linear trace of $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$ proves $C^3$ dependence of the nonlinear DN data.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$ and $0<m<1<M$, and let $E$ be the closed real subspace of $L^\infty(\Omega)$ consisting of functions vanishing almost everywhere outside $B_\rho(0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Fix $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, $0<m<1<M$ and $A>0$. Let $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ be real conductivities on $\mathbb R^3$, with $a_j$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Let $\mathscr N_j$ be their boundary-mean-zero NtD maps on $S^2=\partial B_1$, and let
$$\delta=\left(\sum_{\ell\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{2\ell+1}\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)Y_{\ell k}\|_{L^2(S^2)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Then there is $C>0$ depending only on $s,\rho,m,M,A$ such that
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\left[\log(3+\delta^{-1})\right]^{-(s-3/2)}\qquad(\delta>0).$$
If $\delta=0$, the conductivities are equal. The zero-noise modulus is therefore defined to be zero. Restricting the left side to $B_1$ gives the same $H^1$ norm because the difference is supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For its elements, zero extension is bounded into $H^{s_1}(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F3]. Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|a\|_\infty\le C\|a\|_V$ because $s_1>3/2$. Thus $V$ embeds continuously into the bounded collared coefficient space. The set $\mathcal C-\sigma_0$ is convex and closed in $V$: convexity preserves the pointwise bounds, and uniform convergence from this embedding preserves them under a norm limit.

Choose a smooth scalar function $\vartheta$ with $0\le\vartheta\le1$, equal to one on $[m,M]$ and zero outside $(m/2,2M)$, and set $g(t)=1+\int_1^t\vartheta(u)du$. Then $g(t)=t$ on $[m,M]$, $g(1)=1$, and $m/2\le g(t)\le2M$ globally. All its first and second derivatives are bounded. Put $b(a):=g(\sigma_0+a)-1$. Since $\sigma_0+a=1$ outside $B_\rho$ and $g(1)=1$, $b(a)\in E$ for every $a\in V$. Moreover, $a\mapsto b(a)$ is globally Lipschitz from $V$ into $E$ and continuously Fréchet differentiable, with derivative $b'(a)h=g'(\sigma_0+a)h$ and globally Lipschitz derivative; its Taylor remainder is bounded by $\frac12\|g''\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty^2$.

$$\Gamma(a):=G_{m_*,M_*}(b(a))=G_{m_*,M_*}\bigl(g(\sigma_0+a)-1\bigr)\qquad(a\in V).$$
The chain rule gives $\Gamma'(a)h=G'_{m_*,M_*}(b(a))[g'(\sigma_0+a)h]$. The bounded and Lipschitz derivatives of $b$ and the Lipschitz derivative of the centered supplier give all the asserted global bounds for $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$. For $\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C$, $g(\sigma_0+a)=\sigma_0+a$, so this formula agrees with the centered physical observation.

The identities for $K,r,F$ and the inverse follow by direct substitution. Concavity and $\psi(0)=0$ imply subadditivity: for positive $a+b$, $\psi(a)\ge a\psi(a+b)/(a+b)$ and $\psi(b)\ge b\psi(a+b)/(a+b)$; summing gives $\psi(a+b)\le\psi(a)+\psi(b)$. Hence $C_\psi=1$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: The space $V$ is closed in the intrinsic Sobolev Hilbert space, since convergence there implies $L^2$ convergence and preserves vanishing on the collar. For its elements, zero extension is bounded into $H^{s_1}(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F3]. Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|a\|_\infty\le C\|a\|_V$ because $s_1>3/2$. Thus $V$ embeds continuously into the bounded collared coefficient space. The set $\mathcal C-\sigma_0$ is convex and closed in $V$: convexity preserves the pointwise bounds, and uniform convergence from this embedding preserves them under a norm limit.

Choose a smooth scalar function $\vartheta$ with $0\le\vartheta\le1$, equal to one on $[m,M]$ and zero outside $(m/2,2M)$, and set $g(t)=1+\int_1^t\vartheta(u)du$. Then $g(t)=t$ on $[m,M]$, $g(1)=1$, and $m/2\le g(t)\le2M$ globally. All its first and second derivatives are bounded. Put $b(a):=g(\sigma_0+a)-1$. Since $\sigma_0+a=1$ outside $B_\rho$ and $g(1)=1$, $b(a)\in E$ for every $a\in V$. Moreover, $a\mapsto b(a)$ is globally Lipschitz from $V$ into $E$ and continuously Fréchet differentiable, with derivative $b'(a)h=g'(\sigma_0+a)h$ and globally Lipschitz derivative; its Taylor remainder is bounded by $\frac12\|g''\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty^2$. Use the centered map [F1] with fixed strict ellipticity bounds $m_*:=m/4$ and $M_*:=4M$, and denote it by $G_{m_*,M_*}$. Since $m_*<m/2\le1+b(a)\le2M<M_*$, every $b(a)$ is admissible for that map. Define explicitly $$\Gamma(a):=G_{m_*,M_*}(b(a))=G_{m_*,M_*}\bigl(g(\sigma_0+a)-1\bigr)\qquad(a\in V).$$ The chain rule gives $\Gamma'(a)h=G'_{m_*,M_*}(b(a))[g'(\sigma_0+a)h]$. The bounded and Lipschitz derivatives of $b$ and the Lipschitz derivative of the centered supplier give all the asserted global bounds for $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$. For $\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C$, $g(\sigma_0+a)=\sigma_0+a$, so this formula agrees with the centered physical observation.

The identities for $K,r,F$ and the inverse follow by direct substitution. The map $T$ is globally Lipschitz with $L_T\le\operatorname{Lip}(\Gamma)+\|\Gamma'(0)\|$, so both $r$ and $r^{-1}$ have Lipschitz constant at most $1+L_T$ in the sum norm. In particular $\|Pr^{-1}(a,b)-Pr^{-1}(a',b')\|\le(1+L_T)\|(a,b)-(a',b')\|$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $\zeta=a+ib$. The null condition gives $|a|=|b|=:s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$ and $a\cdot b=0$. Choose an orthogonal map $U$ with $Ua=se_1$ and $Ub=se_2$. Work temporarily with $U\Omega$, $q\circ U^{-1}$, and the phase $U\zeta$, relabeling them $\Omega$, $q$, and $\zeta$ for the construction; the Euclidean Laplacian, Lebesgue norms, and null phase are invariant under this change, and the constructed remainder is pulled back by $U$ at the end. As $\Omega\subset B(0,R)$, choose $L>\max\{1,(R+1)/\pi\}$; then $\Omega\subset Q_L=(-\pi L,\pi L)^n$. Put $\eta_k=(k+\tfrac12e_2)/L$ and $w_k(x)=(2\pi L)^{-n/2}e^{i\eta_k\cdot x}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$. By [F1], these form an orthonormal basis on $Q_L$: they are the rescaled standard Fourier characters multiplied by the unitary factor $e^{ix_2/(2L)}$. For $A_\zeta=D^2+2\zeta\cdot D$, one has $A_\zeta w_k=p_kw_k$, where $p_k=|\eta_k|^2+2\zeta\cdot\eta_k$ and $|\operatorname{Im}p_k|=2s|k_2+\tfrac12|/L\geq s/L$. If $|\eta_k|\leq4s$, then $|p_k|\geq s/L$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|\leq4L$. If $|\eta_k|>4s$, then $|\operatorname{Re}p_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2-2s|\eta_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2/2$, so $|p_k|^{-1}<1/(8s^2)\leq L/s$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|<1/(2s)$. Thus $\sup_k|p_k|^{-1}\leq L/s$ and $\sup_k|\eta_k/p_k|\leq C_L$. Define $G_\zeta f=\sum_k p_k^{-1}(f,w_k)w_k$. Parseval [F1] gives $\|G_\zeta f\|_2\leq (L/s)\|f\|_2$ and $\|\nabla G_\zeta f\|_2\leq C_L\|f\|_2$. For finite Fourier sums $f_N$, the corresponding partial sums $G_\zeta f_N$ satisfy $A_\zeta G_\zeta f_N=f_N$ termwise. Parseval and the multiplier bounds give $f_N\to f$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and $G_\zeta f_N\to G_\zeta f$ in $H^1(Q_L)$. Since $A_\zeta:H^1(Q_L)\to H^{-1}_{\rm loc}(Q_L)$ continuously, passage to distributions yields $A_\zeta G_\zeta f=f$.

Extend $q$ and $F:=-q$ by zero from $\Omega$ to $Q_L$. Multiplication by $q$ is bounded on $L^2(Q_L)$, and
$$\|qG_\zeta\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq \|q\|_\infty L/s.$$
Choose $\tau_0$ large enough that $s\geq2L\|q\|_\infty$ and $s\geq1$ whenever $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$. Then the series $\widetilde F=\sum_{m=0}^\infty(-qG_\zeta)^mF$ converges in $L^2(Q_L)$, satisfies $(I+qG_\zeta)\widetilde F=F$, and has norm at most $2\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$. Set $r_\zeta=G_\zeta\widetilde F$ and restrict it to $\Omega$. Step 1.1 gives $A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=F=-q$ on $\Omega$, as well as $\|r_\zeta\|_2\leq (2L/s)\|q\|_2$ and $\|\nabla r_\zeta\|_2\leq2C_L\|q\|_2$.

Since $D=-i\nabla$, conjugation gives
$$e^{-i\zeta\cdot x}(-\Delta+q)e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta) =(D^2+2\zeta\cdot D+\zeta\cdot\zeta+q)(1+r_\zeta).$$
The null condition removes $\zeta\cdot\zeta$, the constant amplitude has zero derivatives, and step 2.1 makes the remaining expression $q+A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=0$. Multiplication by the smooth exponential preserves $H^1(\Omega)$ for this fixed $\zeta$, so $u_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega)$ and solves the equation distributionally. The estimates in step 2.1 have $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, giving the asserted bounds after changing the constant.

only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $\zeta=a+ib$. The null condition gives $|a|=|b|=:s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$ and $a\cdot b=0$. Choose an orthogonal map $U$ with $Ua=se_1$ and $Ub=se_2$. Work temporarily with $U\Omega$, $q\circ U^{-1}$, and the phase $U\zeta$, relabeling them $\Omega$, $q$, and $\zeta$ for the construction; the Euclidean Laplacian, Lebesgue norms, and null phase are invariant under this change, and the constructed remainder is pulled back by $U$ at the end. As $\Omega\subset B(0,R)$, choose $L>\max\{1,(R+1)/\pi\}$; then $\Omega\subset Q_L=(-\pi L,\pi L)^n$. Put $\eta_k=(k+\tfrac12e_2)/L$ and $w_k(x)=(2\pi L)^{-n/2}e^{i\eta_k\cdot x}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$. By [F1], these form an orthonormal basis on $Q_L$: they are the rescaled standard Fourier characters multiplied by the unitary factor $e^{ix_2/(2L)}$. For $A_\zeta=D^2+2\zeta\cdot D$, one has $A_\zeta w_k=p_kw_k$, where $p_k=|\eta_k|^2+2\zeta\cdot\eta_k$ and $|\operatorname{Im}p_k|=2s|k_2+\tfrac12|/L\geq s/L$. If $|\eta_k|\leq4s$, then $|p_k|\geq s/L$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|\leq4L$. If $|\eta_k|>4s$, then $|\operatorname{Re}p_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2-2s|\eta_k|\geq|\eta_k|^2/2$, so $|p_k|^{-1}<1/(8s^2)\leq L/s$ and $|\eta_k/p_k|<1/(2s)$. Thus $\sup_k|p_k|^{-1}\leq L/s$ and $\sup_k|\eta_k/p_k|\leq C_L$. Define $G_\zeta f=\sum_k p_k^{-1}(f,w_k)w_k$. Parseval [F1] gives $\|G_\zeta f\|_2\leq (L/s)\|f\|_2$ and $\|\nabla G_\zeta f\|_2\leq C_L\|f\|_2$. For finite Fourier sums $f_N$, the corresponding partial sums $G_\zeta f_N$ satisfy $A_\zeta G_\zeta f_N=f_N$ termwise. Parseval and the multiplier bounds give $f_N\to f$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and $G_\zeta f_N\to G_\zeta f$ in $H^1(Q_L)$. Since $A_\zeta:H^1(Q_L)\to H^{-1}_{\rm loc}(Q_L)$ continuously, passage to distributions yields $A_\zeta G_\zeta f=f$.

Extend $q$ and $F:=-q$ by zero from $\Omega$ to $Q_L$. Multiplication by $q$ is bounded on $L^2(Q_L)$, and $$\|qG_\zeta\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq \|q\|_\infty L/s.$$ Choose $\tau_0$ large enough that $s\geq2L\|q\|_\infty$ and $s\geq1$ whenever $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$. Then the series $\widetilde F=\sum_{m=0}^\infty(-qG_\zeta)^mF$ converges in $L^2(Q_L)$, satisfies $(I+qG_\zeta)\widetilde F=F$, and has norm at most $2\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$. Set $r_\zeta=G_\zeta\widetilde F$ and restrict it to $\Omega$. Step 1.1 gives $A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=F=-q$ on $\Omega$, as well as $\|r_\zeta\|_2\leq (2L/s)\|q\|_2$ and $\|\nabla r_\zeta\|_2\leq2C_L\|q\|_2$.

Since $D=-i\nabla$, conjugation gives $$e^{-i\zeta\cdot x}(-\Delta+q)e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta) =(D^2+2\zeta\cdot D+\zeta\cdot\zeta+q)(1+r_\zeta).$$ The null condition removes $\zeta\cdot\zeta$, the constant amplitude has zero derivatives, and step 2.1 makes the remaining expression $q+A_\zeta r_\zeta+q r_\zeta=0$. Multiplication by the smooth exponential preserves $H^1(\Omega)$ for this fixed $\zeta$, so $u_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega)$ and solves the equation distributionally. The estimates in step 2.1 have $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, giving the asserted bounds after changing the constant.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the boundary
conventions of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let
$0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix a
finite family of boundary charts: for each $j$ let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
be open and $\Phi_j:W_j\to\Phi_j(W_j)\subseteq B_j\times\mathbb R$ a
flattening chart as in
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], so that
$\Phi_j(\Omega\cap W_j)=\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ and the boundary corresponds
to the graph $\{t=0\}$; write $\Psi_j:=\pi\circ\Phi_j|_{\partial\Omega\cap W_j}$
for the induced parametrisation of $\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ by an open subset
$V_j:=\Psi_j(\partial\Omega\cap W_j)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and assume the
$\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ cover $\partial\Omega$. Fix a subordinate finite
ambient partition: nonnegative $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a
neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega$
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).
Finally let $\partial\Omega$ carry the chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], which fixes the
meaning of almost-everywhere equality and of $L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

For a Borel function $g:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb K$ put
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}:=\sum_j\bigl\|(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}\bigr\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})},$$
where the chart representation $(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}$ is read in graph
coordinates and extended by zero off $V_j$, and the norm on the right is that
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. The **fractional
Sobolev space of the boundary** is
$$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}<\infty\}.$$
The right-hand side is a finite sum of finite norms of compactly supported
chart representations, so $W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is exactly the
set of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ classes whose chart representations all lie in
the Euclidean space of
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]; that the resulting
space and the topology of the norm do not depend on the choices of atlas and
partition, up to equivalence of norms, is proved in
[[lem-fractional-boundary-norm-is-independent-of-atlas]] and is not assumed
here.

Three conventions belong to the definition. First, membership is a property of
the $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ class: $g$ is an almost-everywhere class with respect
to the surface measure, and the chart representations are classes in
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; representative independence for the Euclidean
factor is established together with the well-definedness lemma on this page
and is not presupposed here. Second, the norm is a finite sum
over a finite atlas, and each $\chi_jg$ is supported in the interior of the
chart, so the localisations are compactly supported and no boundary behaviour
of $\Psi_j^{-1}$ outside $V_j$ enters. Third, on this page the exponent used
is the trace exponent $s=\theta=1-1/p$ for $1<p<\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded
$C^1$ domain, $0<s<1$ and $1\le p<\infty$.

(i) If $\Psi:V\to V'$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open subsets of
$\mathbb R^{d}$, $d\ge1$, which is bi-Lipschitz and whose derivatives in both directions are bounded,
then for every measurable $u:V'\to\mathbb K$,
$$\|u\circ\Psi\|_{W^{s,p}(V)}\le C(\Psi,s,p)\,\|u\|_{W^{s,p}(V')}$$
and symmetrically with $\Psi^{-1}$; in particular the Slobodeckij norm
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{s,p}}$ of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]
is preserved up to equivalence by such coordinate changes. Here the norm on an open set uses the same double integral restricted to that set, with its $L^p$ term. Bounded derivatives alone on arbitrary open sets do not imply the bi-Lipschitz hypothesis.

(ii) Consequently two finite boundary chart families with subordinate
partitions, as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]], define
equivalent norms on $\partial\Omega$: the sum norms differ by multiplicative
constants depending only on the two atlases, the dimension and $s,p$, so
$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)$ is well defined as a set and its topology is
atlas-independent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open
and let $\Phi:U\to V$ be a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with inverse
$\Psi:=\Phi^{-1}:V\to U$. Fix open sets $U_0\subset\subset U$ and
$V_0\subset\subset V$ with $\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, and suppose that on
$\overline{U_0}$ the derivatives of $\Phi$ through order $k$ are bounded and
that on $\overline{V_0}$ the derivatives of $\Psi$ through order $k$ are
bounded; in the situation of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] these are exactly the compact
patches on which the flattening chart and its inverse have bounded derivatives
through order $k$. Then:

1. for every $u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K)$ the composition
$u\circ\Phi$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(U_0;\mathbb K)$, and for every
$1\le|\alpha|\le k$ its weak derivatives satisfy, almost everywhere on
$U_0$,
$$D^\alpha(u\circ\Phi)=\sum_{1\le|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\bigl((D^\beta u)\circ\Phi\bigr)\,P_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(D\Phi,\dots,D^k\Phi\bigr),$$
where $P_{\alpha\beta}$ is a universal polynomial with integer coefficients,
whose values on $\overline{U_0}$ are bounded by a constant depending only on
$n,k$ and the stated bounds for $\Phi$;

2. there is a constant $C$, depending only on $n$, $k$, $p$ and the two sets of
chart bounds, with
$$\|u\circ\Phi\|_{W^{k,p}(U_0)}\le C\,\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(V_0)}\qquad\text{for all }u\in W^{k,p}(V_0;\mathbb K).$$
If in addition $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$ (equivalently, under the stated
$\Phi(U_0)\subseteq V_0$, $\Phi(U_0)=V_0$), the same assertion holds for
composition with $\Psi$ from $W^{k,p}(U_0)$ to $W^{k,p}(V_0)$.

For $k=1$ only the first derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ enter, so bounded
$C^1$ chart and inverse data suffice; no $C^1$-only claim is made for $k>1$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$,
$H=\mathbb R^d\times(0,\infty)$, and let $T_+$ be the half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]]. Write
$|Du|^p:=\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}|D_ju|^p$ for the sum of the $p$-th powers of the
weak first derivatives, and $[\cdot]_{\theta,p}$ for the Slobodeckij seminorm
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. Then for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)$ with $g=T_+u$,
$$[g]_{\theta,p}^p\le C(d,p)\int_H|Du|^p\,dx=C(d,p)\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\|D_ju\|_{L^p(H)}^p\le C(d,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(H)}^p;$$
equivalently $T_+:W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)\to W^{\theta,p}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$
is a bounded operator.

The homogeneous estimate is scale invariant: for $r>0$ and
$u_r(x',t):=u(rx',rt)$ one has $g_{u_r}(x')=g(rx')$ and
$$[g_{u_r}]_{\theta,p}^p=r^{-d+p\theta}[g]_{\theta,p}^p,\qquad \int_H|Du_r|^p\,dx=r^{-d+p\theta}\int_H|Du|^p\,dx,$$
because $p\theta=p-1$; so both sides of the homogeneous estimate scale with
the same exponent $r^{-d+p\theta}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

derivations.claim: On the common smooth core, the identity between the fixed-atlas and Euclidean $W^{1,2}$ norms is bounded in both directions. Indeed, each fixed chart representative is obtained by multiplying by a fixed smooth cutoff and composing with a smooth flattening chart, so [F3] bounds the finite fixed-atlas sum by the Euclidean norm. Conversely, the finite partition of unity writes $u$ as the sum of its localized chart pieces; pull each piece back and use [F3] to bound the Euclidean $W^{1,2}$ norm by the fixed-atlas sum. The constants are finite because the atlas and partition are finite. By the density and completeness in [F3], the identity extends to bounded inverse maps on the completions. Since the two norms are equivalent on $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, their closures give the same zero-boundary subspace.

For $u\in H^1_{\rm fix}$, take its localized boundary-chart representatives in the fixed-atlas definition. Apply [F4] to each representative (reflecting $t<0$ to $t>0$ when required), and sum the finitely many resulting local traces. The fixed-atlas norm [F1] gives a bounded map $T:H^1_{\rm fix}\to H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$. For smooth $u$ this sum is the classical boundary restriction because the partition equals one near the boundary and the half-space traces agree with classical restriction. As an $L^2$-valued map, this trace agrees with the Euclidean trace [F5]: the maps are bounded into $L^2$ by [F2] and [F5], and the Euclidean and fixed $H^1$ norms are equivalent by step 1.1, so equality on the dense smooth core extends to all of $H^1$.

If $Tu=0$ in $H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$, it is zero as an $L^2$ class by [F2]; the $L^2$ trace agreement of step 1.2 and [F6] imply $u\in H^1_{0,\rm E}$. Step 1.1 identifies this with $H^1_{0,\rm fix}$. Conversely, if $u\in H^1_{0,\rm fix}$, approximate it in the fixed $H^1$ norm by interior compactly supported smooth functions. Each has zero classical trace, so continuity of $T$ gives $Tu=0$. Therefore $\ker T=H^1_{0,\rm fix}$.

By [F7] and the boundary-norm equivalence [F2], the Euclidean $L^2$ trace has a bounded right inverse $R:H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}(\partial\Omega)\to H^1_{\rm E}(\Omega)$. The norm equivalence of step 1.1 makes $R$ bounded into $H^1_{\rm fix}$ as well. For every boundary class $f$, the Euclidean trace of $Rf$ is $f$; by step 1.2 the fixed trace agrees with it in $L^2$, hence as an $H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$ class. So $T$ is onto. The kernel identity of step 2.1 induces a bounded bijection $\bar T:H^1_{\rm fix}/H^1_{0,\rm fix}\to H^{1/2}_{\rm fix}$. For any representative $u+v$ with $v\in H^1_{0,\rm fix}$, step 1.2 gives $\|Tu\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|u+v\|_{H^1_{\rm fix}}$; taking the infimum shows $\bar T$ is bounded. Also $\|\bar T^{-1}f\|\le\|Rf\|_{H^1_{\rm fix}}\le C_R\|f\|_{H^{1/2}}$, so its inverse is bounded. Composing with the quotient identity isomorphism of step 1.1 proves the asserted Euclidean quotient identification.
