citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ (Measurable spaces and measurable sets,
Probability measures and probability spaces). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
Law or distribution of a random element; it is a probability measure by
The law of a random element is a probability measure.

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of Carathéodory measurable sets.

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume, which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment (Statistical experiments), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra (Measurable spaces and measurable sets), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space (Randomized procedures as probability kernels). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
A randomized procedure has a measurable action law, so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable.
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

If $f$ has a possible singularity at $c\in(a,b)$, define
$$\int_a^b f:=\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f$$
only when the two one-sided improper integrals converge separately. Cancellation between divergent sides is not allowed.

Likewise, for any finite split point $s$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f:=\int_{-\infty}^{s}f+\int_s^\infty f$$
only when both tails converge. More generally, an interval with several singular ends is split into finitely many one-ended pieces, each of which must converge separately. Independence of the permitted split point is a theorem, not part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: By induction on $n$, every iterated ring $\mathbb R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is an integral domain: the base $\mathbb R$ is a field, hence a domain, and the successor step is exactly [F1]. In each iteration the new indeterminate has coefficient $1$ in degree $1$, whereas every preceding indeterminate is embedded as a constant polynomial; since $1\ne0$ in $\mathbb R$, all the $t_j$ are pairwise distinct.

For $d=1$, $V_d=[1]$ and the empty product is $1$, so the formula holds. For the inductive step let $d\ge2$ and suppose the formula holds in size $d-1$. Put $C=\mathbb R[t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}]$ and $T=t_d$, so the recursive construction identifies $\mathbb R[t_1,\ldots,t_d]=C[T]$. Regard $D_d:=\det V_d$ as a polynomial $f(T)\in C[T]$.

The Leibniz expansion in [F2] shows that only powers $T^0,\ldots,T^{d-1}$ occur in $f$, and that the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ is $D_{d-1}:=\det V_{d-1}$: precisely the terms with exponent $d-1$ in the last column are those permutations fixing the last row, and their remaining signed sum is the Leibniz determinant of $V_{d-1}$. For each $j<d$, substituting $T=t_j$ makes the last column equal column $j$, so alternation in [F2] gives $f(t_j)=0$.

The elements $t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}$ are distinct in the domain $C$ by step 1.1. Starting with $f$, apply [F3] successively at $t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}$. At stage $k$, if $f=\bigl(\prod_{j<k}(T-t_j)\bigr)g_k$, evaluation at $t_k$ gives
$$0=f(t_k)=\bigl(\prod_{j<k}(t_k-t_j)\bigr)g_k(t_k).$$
Every factor $t_k-t_j$ is nonzero, so their product is nonzero in the domain $C$; hence $g_k(t_k)=0$, and [F3] gives $T-t_k\mid g_k$. Induction over these finitely many stages yields
$$f(T)=g(T)\prod_{j<d}(T-t_j)$$
for some $g(T)\in C[T]$.

By the induction hypothesis, $D_{d-1}=\prod_{1\le p<q<d}(t_q-t_p)$, which is nonzero because each difference is nonzero in the domain $C$. Thus the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $f$ is nonzero. The product $\prod_{j<d}(T-t_j)$ is monic of degree $d-1$. If $g$ had any nonzero coefficient at a positive power, its highest such power times this monic product would give a nonzero coefficient of $f$ above degree $d-1$, contradicting step 2.1. Therefore $g$ is constant, and comparison of the $T^{d-1}$ coefficients gives $g=D_{d-1}$. This proves
$$D_d=D_{d-1}\prod_{j<d}(t_d-t_j)=\prod_{1\le p<q\le d}(t_q-t_p).$$
By induction the determinant formula holds for every $d\ge1$.

For distinct real nodes $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, the evaluation homomorphism in [F3] substitutes them into the formula and gives $\det V_d(s_1,\ldots,s_d)=\prod_{p<q}(s_q-s_p)\ne0$. By [F4], the square matrix with these moment-curve vectors as columns is invertible, hence has trivial coefficient kernel and linearly independent columns by [F5].

lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by The natural numbers exist: a smallest inductive set (the
Axiom of Infinity, The Axiom of Infinity: there is a set containing a set with no elements and closed under $y \mapsto y \cup \{y\}$, supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$, makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus

derivations.claim: By induction on $n$, every iterated ring $\mathbb R[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is an integral domain: the base $\mathbb R$ is a field, hence a domain, and the successor step is exactly [F1]. In each iteration the new indeterminate has coefficient $1$ in degree $1$, whereas every preceding indeterminate is embedded as a constant polynomial; since $1\ne0$ in $\mathbb R$, all the $t_j$ are pairwise distinct.

For $d=1$, $V_d=[1]$ and the empty product is $1$, so the formula holds. For the inductive step let $d\ge2$ and suppose the formula holds in size $d-1$. Put $C=\mathbb R[t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}]$ and $T=t_d$, so the recursive construction identifies $\mathbb R[t_1,\ldots,t_d]=C[T]$. Regard $D_d:=\det V_d$ as a polynomial $f(T)\in C[T]$.

The Leibniz expansion in [F2] shows that only powers $T^0,\ldots,T^{d-1}$ occur in $f$, and that the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ is $D_{d-1}:=\det V_{d-1}$: precisely the terms with exponent $d-1$ in the last column are those permutations fixing the last row, and their remaining signed sum is the Leibniz determinant of $V_{d-1}$. For each $j<d$, substituting $T=t_j$ makes the last column equal column $j$, so alternation in [F2] gives $f(t_j)=0$.

The elements $t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}$ are distinct in the domain $C$ by step 1.1. Starting with $f$, apply [F3] successively at $t_1,\ldots,t_{d-1}$. At stage $k$, if $f=\bigl(\prod_{j<k}(T-t_j)\bigr)g_k$, evaluation at $t_k$ gives $$0=f(t_k)=\bigl(\prod_{j<k}(t_k-t_j)\bigr)g_k(t_k).$$ Every factor $t_k-t_j$ is nonzero, so their product is nonzero in the domain $C$; hence $g_k(t_k)=0$, and [F3] gives $T-t_k\mid g_k$. Induction over these finitely many stages yields $$f(T)=g(T)\prod_{j<d}(T-t_j)$$ for some $g(T)\in C[T]$.

By the induction hypothesis, $D_{d-1}=\prod_{1\le p<q<d}(t_q-t_p)$, which is nonzero because each difference is nonzero in the domain $C$. Thus the coefficient of $T^{d-1}$ in $f$ is nonzero. The product $\prod_{j<d}(T-t_j)$ is monic of degree $d-1$. If $g$ had any nonzero coefficient at a positive power, its highest such power times this monic product would give a nonzero coefficient of $f$ above degree $d-1$, contradicting step 1.3. Therefore $g$ is constant, and comparison of the $T^{d-1}$ coefficients gives $g=D_{d-1}$. This proves $$D_d=D_{d-1}\prod_{j<d}(t_d-t_j)=\prod_{1\le p<q\le d}(t_q-t_p).$$ By induction the determinant formula holds for every $d\ge1$.

For distinct real nodes $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, the evaluation homomorphism in [F3] substitutes them into the formula and gives $\det V_d(s_1,\ldots,s_d)=\prod_{p<q}(s_q-s_p)\ne0$. By [F4], the square matrix with these moment-curve vectors as columns is invertible, hence has trivial coefficient kernel and linearly independent columns by [F5].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

derivations.claim: Label the crossing ports northwest $1$, northeast $2$, southeast $3$, and southwest $4$, in the chart of [F1]. The over-strand joins $4$ to $2$ and the under-strand joins $1$ to $3$. For the left exterior cap $(1,4)$ the remaining ports are $2,3$. Orient its through strand from $2$ to $3$: it traverses the over-strand northeast to southwest, then the cap, then the under-strand northwest to southeast. The tangent vectors may be taken as $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,-1)$, whose determinant is $2>0$. This is a positive kink. The A-pairing $(1,4)(2,3)$ closes one additional circle against the cap; the B-pairing $(1,2)(3,4)$ gives just the through arc. Hence its bracket factor is $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$. Reversing the component negates both tangent vectors and preserves the determinant.

For the top exterior cap $(1,2)$ the remaining ports are $4,3$. Orient its through strand from $4$ to $3$: it traverses the over-strand southwest to northeast, then the cap, then the under-strand northwest to southeast. The tangent vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ have determinant $-2<0$, so this is a negative kink. Here the A-pairing gives only the through arc, while the B-pairing closes one additional circle. Its factor is $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$. The right and bottom cap cases are the respective $180$-degree rotations; orientation-preserving chart changes and reversal of the component preserve the calculation. These are all oriented type-I variants. The calculation is inside the move disk and permits every exterior connectivity and any additional components. Deletion uses the reciprocal Laurent-unit factor.

The positive kink changes writhe from $w$ to $w+1$, and the negative kink changes it to $w-1$. Their respective normalized values are $$(-A^3)^{-(w+1)}(-A^3)\langle D\rangle=(-A^3)^{-w}\langle D\rangle,$$ and $$(-A^3)^{-(w-1)}(-A^{-3})\langle D\rangle=(-A^3)^{-w}\langle D\rangle.$$ Thus both type-I additions and their inverse deletions preserve $f_D$.

A type-II move creates or deletes two opposite signs, and a type-III move preserves all three signs, so writhe is unchanged. Their raw bracket is unchanged by [F4]. Planar isotopy transports the determinant crossing signs, smoothing states and state-circle counts bijectively. Therefore it preserves both factors of $f_D$, and the normalized value is invariant under every listed move.

citations.quote: Put $A=\mathbb Z[a^{\pm1},s,d^{\pm1}]/(s(d-1)-(a-a^{-1}))$. This ring is an integral domain and embeds in $\mathbb Q(i)(a,s)$ by $d\mapsto1+(a-a^{-1})/s$, where $i^2=-1$. A link diagram means a finite generic immersion of circles in the oriented plane with over/under data at its double points. Regular isotopy is generated by planar isotopy and Reidemeister moves II and III. A positive curl is a one-crossing curl whose oriented self-crossing has sign $+1$; its sign is independent of the direction chosen on its component. There is a unique function $P$ from link diagrams, including the empty diagram, to $A$ with $P(\varnothing)=1$, unchanged by regular isotopy, satisfying the following local rules: a positive or negative curl multiplies $P$ by $a$ or $a^{-1}$; a disjoint trivial circle multiplies $P$ by $d$; and $P(L_+)-P(L_-)=s(P(L_0)-P(L_\infty))$. Here in an oriented disk with four cyclically labelled endpoints $1,2,3,4$, $L_+$ connects $1$ to $3$ over the strand from $2$ to $4$, and the two smoothings are chosen so that the oriented smoothing for any orientation making this crossing positive is $L_0$; $L_-$ reverses the crossing and $L_\infty$ is the other smoothing. Rotating the disk interchanges both differences and preserves the rule. In particular the empty diagram freely generates the quotient of the free $A$-module on closed diagrams by these rules.

derivations.claim: Fix distinct components $K_r,K_s$ and let their projected shadows be $\gamma_r,\gamma_s$. After finitely many such smoothings, $\gamma_r$ is a finite disjoint union of embedded circles. As $\gamma_s$ traverses any embedded circle, every transverse intersection changes whether it is inside or outside that circle, and the closed traversal returns to its initial region. Hence the original number of mixed intersections of $K_r,K_s$ is even. Each determinant crossing sign is $+1$ or $-1$, both congruent to $1$ modulo $2$, so the signed mixed-crossing sum $S_{rs}$ is even. Summing over $s\ne r$ shows that the total mixed-crossing sum $S_r$ involving $K_r$ is even. Reversing $K_r$ leaves its self-crossing signs fixed by [F2] and negates its mixed crossing signs, so $w$ changes by $-2S_r\in4\mathbb Z$. Thus $i^w$ is unchanged; $c$ and the unoriented value $D$ are unchanged as well. Therefore the formula defining $L$ is independent of reversing $K_r$, and repeating for every component proves orientation independence.

For a positive curl, $D$ gains a factor $a$ and $w$ increases by $1$; substituting $a_D=-iA$ and $z_D=iZ$ in [F5] shows that $L$ gains the factor $i a_D=A$. For a negative curl, $D$ gains $a^{-1}$ and $w$ decreases by $1$, so $L$ gains $i^{-1}a_D^{-1}=A^{-1}$. Adding a disjoint trivial circle increases $c$ by $1$ and multiplies $D$ by $d$, so the factor $(-1)^c$ makes $L$ acquire the factor $-d$. Set $\delta_L=-d$. Under $a_D=-iA$ and $z_D=iZ$, the coefficient relation $z_D(d-1)=a_D-a_D^{-1}$ becomes $Z(1-d)=A+A^{-1}$, hence $Z(\delta_L+1)=A+A^{-1}$. This gives the Kauffman circle rule using the universal relation without inverting $Z$.

Consider a positive crossing and write $w=w(K_+)$ and $c=c(K_+)$. Switching it gives $w(K_-)=w-2$ and leaves $c$ fixed. Each smoothing deletes that crossing, so before any orientation adjustment its writhe is $w-1$. The orientation-preserving smoothing $K_0$ has $c+1$ components at a self-crossing and $c-1$ at a mixed crossing. The other smoothing $K_\infty$ has $c$ components at a self-crossing and $c-1$ at a mixed crossing. This changes signs at exactly the crossings between that component and the other split component or any remaining component; the pairwise sums are even by step 1.1, so $w(K_\infty)\equiv w-1\pmod4$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible smooth three-manifold with a supplied finite whole-star smooth manifold triangulation $T$. Let $\mathcal S$ be a finite disjoint family of incompressible smooth tori in its interior. There is a jointly smooth ambient isotopy, fixed near $\partial M$ and stationary near its time endpoints, after which the family misses the vertices, crosses edges transversely in finitely many points, meets every triangular face in finitely many disjoint arcs joining different edges, and meets each tetrahedron in finitely many proper disks whose boundary crosses each of its edges at most once. The boundary patterns are therefore the four triangle and three quadrilateral patterns. The finitely many balls cut out inside each tetrahedron by those disks have supplied ball parameters retaining their disk faces and face-cell corners. All tori are moved simultaneously; the family may be empty.

These are smooth surfaces in a specified compatible triangulation. No identification of an arbitrary topological marking with a smooth or PL structure is asserted.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold with a supplied finite whole-star smooth manifold triangulation. Let $\mathcal S$ be a finite disjoint two-sided closed smooth torus family in its interior, in normal disk position: each tetrahedron meets it in proper disks with the triangle or quadrilateral boundary patterns. Suppose all balls obtained by cutting individual tetrahedra along those disks have supplied ball parameters, with their disk faces and face-cell corners retained. Supply parameters of the rectangle face cells, taking their opposite edges on $\mathcal S$ as horizontal and their other two edges on triangulation edges as vertical.

Let $C$ be a connected component of $M$ cut open along $\mathcal S$ which meets every triangular face only in rectangle cells. Then $C$ is disjoint from $\partial M$ and is a topological interval bundle over a compact connected surface without boundary. Its bundle admits a locally flat embedded core surface $Q$, obtained as a section, and the base has a finite cellulation. If $C$ is not homeomorphic to $T^2\times I$, the core is one-sided and $C\setminus Q$ is connected. No choice axiom is assumed.

The conclusion is a topological interval-bundle parameterization from the specified finite data. It asserts neither smoothness nor compatibility with an unrelated marking.

Let $N$ be a connected Hausdorff topological three-manifold without boundary. Let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be finitely many disjoint compact connected locally flat embedded surfaces without boundary. They may be one-sided and nonorientable. If $N\setminus\bigcup_j S_j$ is connected, their canonical mod-two fundamental classes have linearly independent images in $H_2(N;\mathbb F_2)$. The manifold may be noncompact and nonorientable, and the family may be empty. No choice axiom or ambient triangulation is assumed.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible smooth three-manifold with nonempty boundary, and supply a finite compatible whole-star smooth manifold triangulation with $t$ triangular faces. Let $\mathcal S$ be a finite disjoint family of two-sided incompressible smooth interior tori. If no component of $M$ cut open along $\mathcal S$ is homeomorphic to $T^2\times I$, then
$$
|\mathcal S|\le 4t+\dim_{\mathbb F_2}H_2(M;\mathbb F_2)-1.
$$
Thus any process accumulating cuts whose every finite stage has this no-product property can make only finitely many cuts. The family may be empty.

The supplied triangulation is compatible with the smooth structure in the stated whole-star sense. This result asserts no compatibility of an arbitrary topological marking and does not alter the scope of any other finiteness item.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to the given finite torus family for the very triangulation in the Statement. Its smooth ambient isotopy retains incompressibility, all cut-component homeomorphism types and the no-product condition. It puts the family into actual normal disks in each parametrized tetrahedron and disjoint arcs in each triangular face, joining distinct edges. This invokes the accepted marked normal-position construction rather than treating a surgery that changes a torus as an isotopy.

In each triangular face group the arcs by the pair of distinct edges they join. Within each of the three types they occur in a parallel stack. Between consecutive arcs of a stack is a rectangle, and collapsing those strips leaves at most one arc of each type, hence at most four complementary regions. Every nonrectangular region survives distinctly in this collapsed picture, so there are at most $4t$ such regions over all faces. The successive finite face-disk cuts and the marked rectangle product maps are supplied by [F2] and [F5]; no unparametrized polygon or missing side matching is being assumed.

Let $m$ be the number of cut components meeting all faces only in rectangles. By [F3] each is an interval bundle. The torus-product possibility is excluded by hypothesis. Thus they have disjoint one-sided compact locally flat cores $Q_1,\ldots,Q_m$, and removing each core leaves its component connected. No ambient triangulation or smoothness of these cores is required.

Form the connected finite dual graph of all torus cuts, allowing loops, and choose a spanning tree. Let $k$ be the number of edges outside that tree. The corresponding $k$ tori, together with all the $Q_j$, have connected complement: remove the cores in the fully cut pieces, which remain connected by step2.1, and glue back the tree faces. A tree joins all the pieces and cannot create a new disconnection. Pass to $\operatorname{Int}M$ by the finite inward collar push in [F5], chosen disjoint from these compact surfaces; its homotopy fixes them and proves that the interior inclusion induces a homology isomorphism, while their complement remains connected. Now [F4] gives $k+m$ independent mod-two classes, so $k+m\le\beta$, where $\beta=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}H_2(M;\mathbb F_2)$. This number is finite because the supplied triangulation is finite and its simplicial homology computes singular homology.

Write $n=|\mathcal T|$ and let $v$ be the number of cut components. The dual graph has $n$ edges, $v$ vertices and $k=n-v+1$ non-tree edges; thus $v=n-k+1$. Each component other than the $m$ rectangular-only ones contains a nonrectangular face region. A physical region belongs to just one cut component: its two tetrahedral sides are glued through its interior, or it is a boundary face with only one incident side. Distinct components therefore use distinct such regions, and step1.2 gives $v\le m+4t$.

Combining these inequalities yields $n+1\le k+m+4t\le\beta+4t$, which is exactly the stated bound. It also holds for the empty family. If an accumulating cutting process continued past $4t+\beta-1$ cuts while each finite accumulated family retained the stated hypotheses, that stage would contradict the same bound for the fixed original triangulation. Thus no such process continues indefinitely. The proof retains the original countable-choice and smooth-compatible triangulation scope; it does not postulate an arbitrary unrelated TOP marking.

citations.quote: Let $K_0,K_1$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$, and let $I=[0,1]$. A smooth concordance from $K_0$ to $K_1$ is the image of a smooth proper embedding $f:S^1\times I\to S^3\times I$ whose lower and upper boundary circles are $K_0\times\{0\}$ and $K_1\times\{1\}$. The embedding has product collars at both ends: in a neighborhood of each boundary circle it is the corresponding knot embedding crossed with the interval coordinate. Orient the annulus so that its boundary, with the boundary-orientation convention, is $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$. The knots are smoothly concordant when such an annulus exists.

Let $K_0,K_1$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$, and let $I=[0,1]$. They are locally flat topologically concordant if there is a topological proper embedding $f:S^1\times I\to S^3\times I$ whose image is a locally flat annulus, whose boundary circles are $K_0\times\{0\}$ and $K_1\times\{1\}$, and whose annulus orientation induces the boundary $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$. The annulus must have product collars at both ends. No differentiability of the annulus is assumed.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be continuous, let $A\subseteq M$ be closed, and suppose $F$ is smooth on an open neighbourhood of $A$. Then there exist a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $A$ such that $\widetilde F=F$ on $W$ and $F$ is homotopic to $\widetilde F$ by a homotopy fixed on $W$, hence relative to $A$. No compactness of $A$ or its neighbourhood is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $M=S^3\times[0,1]$. Let $\alpha:[0,1]\to M$ be a locally flat proper embedding with endpoints $(p,0)$ and $(p,1)$ and with product collars at those endpoints. Then there is a continuous family of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, $t\in[0,1]$, such that $H_0$ is the identity, every $H_t$ preserves the two boundary levels and is the identity near them, and $H_1(\alpha([0,1]))=\{p\}\times[0,1]$. derivations.claim: First consider smooth concordances. Pick one point on each endpoint knot. By [F4], apply separate endpoint ambient isotopies carrying both marked points to a common point $p\in S^3$; extend them over disjoint product collars of the concordance and interpolate by the identity between the collars. This changes the representatives only within their ambient-isotopy classes. Choose a smooth spanning arc in each annulus joining the marked points and fixed in product collars. For one annulus, write this arc as $\alpha$ and the standard product arc as $\beta(s)=(p,s)$. Since $S^3\times(0,1)$ is simply connected by [F3], the middle portions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are homotopic rel endpoints after their common endpoint collars are deleted. Relative smooth approximation in [F3] gives a smooth homotopy $H(s,t)$ fixed on those collars. We now perturb this homotopy through a finite-dimensional family. First, local coordinate bumps whose $s$-derivatives span the four target coordinates at each zero of $\partial_sH$ make the total derivative family transverse to the zero section of the rank-four tangent bundle; its source has dimension two, so a generic parameter has $\partial_sH\ne0$ everywhere. Compactness then supplies a uniform $\delta>0$ for local injectivity of every slice when $|s-s'|<\delta$. On the compact configuration set $|s-s'|\ge\delta$, use two disjoint source-supported coordinate bumps near each pair to vary $H(s,t)$ and $H(s',t)$ independently. A finite cover of the possible diagonal preimage makes the total pair map transverse to the diagonal in $(S^3\times I)^2$. Its source-pair-time dimension is three and the diagonal has codimension four, so the generic slice has no double points. Both perturbations are supported away from the endpoint collars and can be chosen small enough to preserve immersion and local injectivity. Thus every time-slice is a smooth embedding, giving an isotopy of proper arcs rel collars. The isotopy is stationary on common source end collars, so restrict to the compact middle arcs containing its moving part; these lie in $S^3\times(0,1)$, a boundaryless smooth manifold. Apply [F3] there with support in the interior, choosing the extension to fix the adjacent stationary arc collars, and extend it by the identity across the fixed end collars. This gives an ambient isotopy of $S^3\times I$ fixed near both end levels and carrying the whole spanning arc to the vertical product arc without changing the concordance or its oriented endpoint knot types.

For each vertical arc, double the ambient product across its two boundary levels by gluing to a second copy of $S^3\times I$, and glue a second copy of the concordance annulus using its product collars. The doubled ambient manifold is $S^3\times S^1$ and the doubled annulus is a smooth embedded torus. Doubling the spanning arc across its endpoints gives a smooth embedded circle $C$ in that torus. Apply the tubular-neighborhood theorem to the closed torus in $S^3\times S^1$ and to $C$ inside the torus. Over $C$, the normal line of $C$ in the torus and the rank-two normal bundle of the torus in the ambient manifold are trivial, so their product gives a neighborhood $D^1\times D^2\times S^1$ of $C$ whose intersection with the torus is exactly $D^1\times S^1$. Restrict to the half corresponding to the original arc; this gives the required product neighborhood $D^3\times I$ meeting the original annulus exactly in $D^1\times I$, with product end faces from the collars. Removing the interior of this strip from each annulus leaves a rectangle. Remove the two product neighborhoods from two copies of $S^3\times I$ and glue their boundary cylinders $S^2\times I$ by the fixed product identification. At each level this glues two three-balls along their boundary spheres, giving $S^3\#S^3\cong S^3$; since the gluing is independent of the interval parameter, the resulting ambient cobordism is $S^3\times I$. Glue the two surface rectangles across the two side intervals in the connecting cylinder, choosing the side identifications to extend the orientations on the cut annuli. At the lower end the fixed orientation-reversing boundary map joins the incoming arcs with boundary orientation $-(K_0\#J_0)$; at the upper end the same product convention gives $K_1\#J_1$. The result is connected, orientable, has two boundary circles, and has Euler characteristic $0$ (two rectangles, each of Euler characteristic $1$, glued along two intervals); hence it is an annulus. The product collars give the required smooth concordance.
The preceding construction proves the smooth implication.

For the TOP implication, first code the actual input as compact metric data. Parametrize the two annuli by the standard compact annulus, and choose finitely many local pair charts covering each, together with their inverses and the given end-collar maps. Such a finite selection is possible by compactness and finite choice; using countably many relatively compact chart restrictions instead would require only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Include the endpoint knots and the chosen connected-sum representatives from [F2]. For these smooth knots and the finite smooth coordinate maps used in their sums, also code the derivatives of every finite order, their continuity moduli and rational difference-quotient remainder bounds; thus the inner model sees smooth knots, not merely continuous embeddings. Continuous maps on these standard metric domains are coded by their values on fixed countable rational dense sets and uniform continuity moduli on compact exhaustions; include inverse moduli for embeddings and chart inverses. All this countable numerical data is one real $r$.

We use certificates, not an unqualified assertion that homeomorphism existence is absolute. For every open chart domain record its rational-ball code (relative rational half-balls at a boundary chart), compact exhaustion, and positive-distance margins putting the images of exhaustion pieces in the corresponding open image. Record both map/inverse identities on dense sets. For the pair condition record the parametrization of the linear plane section and its identities with the annulus parametrization; on smaller charts also record positive separation from the compact remainder of the annulus outside that patch. A finite parameter-patch cover and a Lebesgue-number certificate cover the entire annulus. Properness is certified on the compact subannuli $S^1\times[1/j,1-1/j]$ by positive separation from the ambient end levels. Equalities with the oriented endpoint parametrizations and the product collars are dense-set equalities with their continuity moduli. The smooth derivative identities are certified by rational difference quotients and their coded remainder bounds at each finite order. These certificates express input validity using only rational inequalities, integer indices and quantification over natural numbers. They therefore have the same truth in $L[r]$ and in the ambient universe; in particular the coded input is valid in $L[r]$.

Apply [F6] inside $L[r]$, which satisfies full Choice by [F7]. It gives a locally flat annulus for the two connected sums. In that model choose its finite pair-chart cover, inverse maps, compact-exhaustion moduli, open-image margins and end-collar certificates of the same form as in step 4.2; collect them into a real $s\in L[r]$. Decode $s$ in the ambient universe by completion from the rational dense domains. The coded forward and inverse moduli give continuous inverse maps on their coded domains; the dense-set identities extend to all points, and the open-image and separation certificates make these actual local pair charts with no additional surface branch. The finite cover certificate, properness margins, and endpoint/collar identities likewise persist. Thus the decoded object is an actual oriented proper locally flat annulus in the ambient $S^3\times I$, with the required endpoint connected sums and product collars. This transfer uses arithmetic certificates for the particular compact objects, not preservation of arbitrary sets or homeomorphisms between inner models.

Steps 4.1–4.3 earn the required compact specialization of the external TOP input under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, without assuming ambient full AC. Together with the retained smooth construction in steps 1.1–3.1, this proves both implications in the unchanged Statement. No annulus-adapted transverse tube or ambient complement is inferred from the bare-arc theorem [F5]; that former local proof gap is bypassed by the explicitly external input [F6].

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].
