Fix a closed oriented marked surface $\Sigma$ with its Lagrangian and weighted anomaly data, and fix a marked handlebody $H$ with boundary $\Sigma$ and a complementary marked handlebody $H'$ so that their gluing is the standard oriented three-sphere. Specialize the framed-link Kauffman bracket skein module of $H$ to the coefficient field and root fixed above. For $x\in\mathcal K_A(H)$ and $y\in\mathcal K_A(H')$, define the handlebody pairing $B_\Sigma(x,y)$ by gluing the two framed skeins and evaluating the resulting closed marked three-manifold with the normalized root surgery invariant. Define

$$\operatorname{Rad}(B_\Sigma)=\{x\in\mathcal K_A(H):B_\Sigma(x,y)=0\text{ for every }y\in\mathcal K_A(H')\}, \qquad V_p(\Sigma)=\mathcal K_A(H)/\operatorname{Rad}(B_\Sigma).$$

This is the radical-quotient handlebody state-space construction for the specified marking and anomaly data. Independence of the marking, finite generation, nondegeneracy, and the gluing maps are separate mathematical obligations.

**External normalization input.** In this Definition the closed marked evaluation is the BHMV TQFT normalization, not merely the raw signature-normalized closed invariant $\theta_p$ of the Kirby lemma. BHMV §2 pp.897–898 and Gilmer–Masbaum §11 pp.23–25 give
$$Z_p(M,w)=\eta^{b_0(M)+b_1(M)}(\kappa^3)^w\theta_p(M),\qquad \Delta_\pm=\eta^{-1}\kappa^{\pm3}.$$
Thus $Z_p(S^3,0)=\eta$ and $Z_p(S^2\times S^1,0)=1$. These nonzero normalizations and the registered Wall-sign weight are part of the pairing. BHMV Proposition1.9, p.891, identifies EXACTLY this radical quotient computed with two complementary handlebodies with its universal state space. This external identification supplies well-definedness of the presented model; its finite basis and gluing are the separate following lemmas. The selected $\kappa$ remains a sixth root, with one weight step acting by its cube. The source itself is only used at these located statements/constructions, not as a claimed locally reconstructed universal-construction proof.

**Source hypotheses for this identification.** The normalized BHMV closed invariant is multiplicative and involutive, so BHMV Proposition 1.1 gives its cobordism-generated quantization functor at this fixed root; extend its coefficients to $\mathbb C$ as stated above. BHMV Theorem 1.7 supplies both hypotheses needed for Proposition 1.9: its Kauffman bracket relations let that proposition replace the free bordism module by the specialized skein module, and its surgery axioms give the surjectivity and radical-kernel description. The corresponding weighted Lagrangian version is the BHMV skein TQFT with integral weights and Lagrangians in place of $p_1$-structures, as described by Gilmer–Masbaum in §11; their one-weight square-root multiplier is matched to the selected BHMV sixth root by $\kappa_{\mathrm{GM}}=\kappa^3$. In that section Lemma 11.1 states the weighted surgery axiom and Remark 11.3 applies it to the handlebody skein presentation; the source refers the Lemma 11.1 proof to the BHMV argument rather than repeating it. These are imported source inputs, not a locally reconstructed proof, and they do not add another quotient or change the state-space interface.

Let $H$ be a handlebody with a fixed finite trivalent spine $G$, and let every edge carry one of the labels $0,\ldots,r-2$. Call a labeling admissible when the three labels at each trivalent vertex satisfy the root fusion rule. In the radical-quotient state space of $H$, the states represented by admissible labeled spines span, and the set of such labelings is finite. This statement asserts spanning, not linear independence.

For the fixed root parameter, let $\mathcal C_p$ denote the semisimplified Temperley–Lieb category with labels $0,\ldots,r-2$, pivotal dimensions $d_j=[j+1]$, and Hopf-link data inherited from the Kauffman bracket. Put $\mathcal D_p^2=\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}d_j^2$ and choose $\mathcal D_p\in\mathbb C$ with that square. Choose $\kappa\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\kappa^6=A^{-6-(p+1)p/2}$. The root-specific extended data are the weighted Lagrangian ribbon bordisms whose objects are closed oriented labeled surfaces with a Lagrangian subspace of real first homology and whose morphisms are collared oriented labeled ribbon bordisms with integer weights. If $M_1:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ and $M_2:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$ have relations $\Lambda_{M_1},\Lambda_{M_2}$ and boundary Lagrangians $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, define

$$K_1=\Lambda_{M_1}(\lambda_0),\qquad K_0=\lambda_1,\qquad K_2=\Lambda_{M_2}^{\,t}(\lambda_2), \qquad n(M_2\circ M_1)=n_2+n_1+\mu(K_1,K_0,K_2),$$

using the Wall-signature Maslov convention. The category composition, units, and anomaly weight are those specified by this formula and the weighted Lagrangian bordism definition; no ordinary oriented anomaly-free functor is part of this Definition.

derivations.claim: On a fixed finite spine, each admissible coloring gives a finite colored graph state. Gluing a pair of handlebodies evaluates the resulting closed colored graph using the specified root bracket and anomaly normalization.

By [F4], the radical quotients for the two orientations are finite-dimensional dual spaces and their normalized pairing is perfect. This is stronger than left nondegeneracy by the definition of a radical alone. Choose bases $v_i,w_j$ and let $B_{ij}$ be their pairing matrix. Its inverse gives the coevaluation tensor $\sum_{i,j}(B^{-1})_{ji}v_i\otimes w_j$; contraction with $B$ on either side is the identity. This finite linear-algebra identity is exactly the sewing contraction in the imported gluing theorem and is independent of the chosen dual bases.

The imported weighted gluing in [F5] gives the prescribed anomaly factor, with weight law [F3]. Its parameter is the cube of the selected sixth root, not an independently chosen square root with an unchecked sign. The real-Lagrangian transport in [F5] respects composition because the intervening reference cylinders cancel. Thus the inverse-pairing sewing maps satisfy precisely the registered weighted law. No unweighted anomaly cancellation or positivity of every complex-root Hermitian form is asserted.

Fix an even integer $p\ge4$ and a primitive $2p$-th root of unity $A\in\mathbb C$. Put

$$\zeta=A^2,\qquad q=-\zeta,\qquad r=p/2,\qquad \delta=-A^2-A^{-2}=q+q^{-1}.$$

The coefficient field after specialization is $\mathbb C$, and the Kauffman bracket loop coefficient is $\delta$ in the framed-link relation $[L\sqcup O]=\delta[L]$. Define the quantum integers by $[0]=0$, $[1]=1$, and $[j+1]=\delta[j]-[j-1]$ for $j\ge1$. Since $q^2=A^4$ has order $r\ge2$, these quantum integers also satisfy

$$[j]=\frac{q^j-q^{-j}}{q-q^{-1}}=(-1)^{j-1}\frac{A^{2j}-A^{-2j}}{A^2-A^{-2}}.$$

The BHMV simple-label convention is the finite set

$$\mathcal J_p=\{0,1,\ldots,r-2\}.$$

The pivotal loop and coefficient conventions throughout this page are the displayed $\delta$ and $\mathbb C$; no zero quantum integer is inverted.

Fix an even integer $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A\in\mathbb C$, $r=p/2$, and loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. Let $\mathcal T_\delta$ be the complex Temperley–Lieb diagram category with objects the nonnegative integers and morphisms finite linear combinations of perfect matchings of bottom and top boundary points with no intersecting arcs. Compose by stacking and remove each closed component with factor $\delta$. Define $\mathcal N_\delta(m,n)$ to be the subspace of morphisms $f:m\to n$ such that $\operatorname{Tr}_m(g\circ f)=0$ for every reverse morphism $g:n\to m$, where $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the unnormalized diagram-closure trace. Form the quotient category with the same objects and morphism spaces $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T_\delta}(m,n)/\mathcal N_\delta(m,n)$. Its additive envelope adjoins finite formal direct sums, with matrix morphisms and matrix composition. Its idempotent completion adjoins objects $(X,e)$ for idempotents $e\in\operatorname{End}(X)$ with $e^2=e$, and morphisms $(X,e)\to(Y,f)$ are morphisms $a:X\to Y$ satisfying $a=fae$. Juxtaposition, planar cup-cap duality, and the induced trace descend to this completed quotient. This definition makes no assertion that it is semisimple, that its simple objects have a specified label set, or that any braid, twist, or modularity identities hold.

Let $p\ge4$ be even, $A\in\mathbb C$ a primitive $2p$-th root, and $r=p/2$. In the BHMV Temperley–Lieb quotient with loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ and planar pivotal trace, the complete simple-label set is $\{0,1,\ldots,r-2\}$, represented by the surviving Jones–Wenzl projectors $p_a$ obtained from the standard recursion using unit denominators $[2],\ldots,[a]$. Every simple is self-dual. Its fusion multiplicities are

$$N_{ab}^{c}=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |a-b|\le c\le\min(a+b,\,2r-4-a-b) \ \text{and }a+b+c\text{ is even},$$

and are zero otherwise. With the BHMV overcrossing map $c_i=A1_i+A^{-1}U_i$, where $U_i$ is the cup-cap generator, the full-framing ribbon structure has planar quantum dimensions $d_a=[a+1]$ and simple-object twists $\theta_a=(-1)^aA^{a(a+2)}$. Here the quantum integers use the fixed BHMV recurrence. The unnormalized Hopf-link matrix, whose $(a,b)$ entry is the pivotal trace of the double braiding on $p_a\otimes p_b$, is nondegenerate. Here modular means that this finite semisimple ribbon category has an invertible unnormalized Hopf-link matrix.

For the fixed root parameter, let $\mathcal C_p$ denote the semisimplified Temperley–Lieb category with labels $0,\ldots,r-2$, pivotal dimensions $d_j=[j+1]$, and Hopf-link data inherited from the Kauffman bracket. Put $\mathcal D_p^2=\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}d_j^2$ and choose $\mathcal D_p\in\mathbb C$ with that square. Choose $\kappa\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\kappa^6=A^{-6-(p+1)p/2}$. The root-specific extended data are the weighted Lagrangian ribbon bordisms whose objects are closed oriented labeled surfaces with a Lagrangian subspace of real first homology and whose morphisms are collared oriented labeled ribbon bordisms with integer weights. If $M_1:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ and $M_2:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$ have relations $\Lambda_{M_1},\Lambda_{M_2}$ and boundary Lagrangians $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, define

$$K_1=\Lambda_{M_1}(\lambda_0),\qquad K_0=\lambda_1,\qquad K_2=\Lambda_{M_2}^{\,t}(\lambda_2), \qquad n(M_2\circ M_1)=n_2+n_1+\mu(K_1,K_0,K_2),$$

using the Wall-signature Maslov convention. The category composition, units, and anomaly weight are those specified by this formula and the weighted Lagrangian bordism definition; no ordinary oriented anomaly-free functor is part of this Definition.

derivations.claim: The label set is finite, so $\Omega_p$ is a finite linear combination of colored projectors. The normalized surgery expression is therefore a finite complex number whenever the displayed Gauss sums are nonzero.

By [F5], both Gauss sums are units, since $\eta$ and $\kappa$ are units. Framed isotopy preserves the ribbon bracket. The imported Kirby-color identity preserves its value under a handle slide, while the framing matrix changes by an integral congruence and hence has unchanged positive and negative indices. A split signed-unit unknot multiplies the numerator by $\Delta_\varepsilon$ and increases exactly the corresponding index by one. The denominator therefore cancels that factor. Deletion is the inverse operation. This proves the displayed surgery invariance with the exact normalization of the Statement.

The weighted interpretation is [F6]: the signature unit is $\nu=\kappa^3$, with the source's Maslov sign converted to the registered Wall order. The distinct additional $\eta^{b_0+b_1}$ normalization is retained when these closed values enter the TQFT pairing; no anomaly-free ordinary-oriented functor follows. The finite color and cancellation calculations add no choice assumption.

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]],
[[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let
$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$
The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the
principal localisation
$$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$
([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).
It is a commutative ring with unit $1=t^0$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]). Write
again $t$ for the image of the indeterminate under the localisation map; then
$t$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}$
([[prop-units-in-a-localisation]]). Every element of $\Lambda_1$ has a
representative
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,$$
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, obtained by writing a fraction
$p/t^N$ as a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of the powers
$t^{k-N}$; the finite coefficient sequence is unique: after multiplying two such sums
by a common sufficiently large power of $t$, equality becomes equality of
ordinary polynomials. The localisation map $\mathbb Z[t]\to\Lambda_1$ is
injective because $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain; hence their coefficients agree
([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]]). Equivalently, two such
sums are equal exactly when their coefficient sequences agree
([[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]).

**Universal property.** Let $A$ be a ring with unit and let
$\varphi\colon\mathbb Z[t]\to A$ be a unital ring homomorphism with
$\varphi(t)$ a unit of $A$. Then there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\widetilde\varphi\colon\Lambda_1\to A$ with
$\widetilde\varphi(t)=\varphi(t)$. Equivalently, for every unital ring $A$ and
every unit $u\in A$ there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\Lambda_1\to A$ with $t\mapsto u$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]],
[[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The cited localisation theorem treats commutative target rings. For the
possibly noncommutative target used here, define
$\sum_k a_kt^k\mapsto\sum_k(a_k1_A)u^k$. Unique Laurent coefficients make
this well defined. Integer multiples of $1_A$ are central, and
$u^ku^l=u^{k+l}$ for all integers $k,l$, so finite distributivity proves
additivity, multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Every unital
homomorphism must send $a_k$ to $a_k1_A$ and $t^k$ to $u^k$, proving
uniqueness. Taking $u=\varphi(t)$ gives the asserted extension of $\varphi$.

**Augmentation.** There is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$$\varepsilon\colon\Lambda_1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k\Bigr)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k,$$
the **sum-of-coefficients map** ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]]); it
is well defined because the coefficients are summable and their total sum is
unchanged along the relation of
[[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]. Its kernel is the
principal ideal $(t-1)$: indeed $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$, and if
$\varepsilon(x)=0$ then, writing $x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k$ with finite
support and using that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k=0$, one has
$$x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k(t^k-1)=(t-1)\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k\,(1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}),$$
where $1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}$ denotes the empty sum $0$ for $k=0$ and, for
$k=-j<0$, the negative sum
$-(t^{-1}+t^{-2}+\cdots+t^{-j})$, so that
$t^{-j}-1=-(t-1)(t^{-1}+\cdots+t^{-j})$; hence $x\in(t-1)$, and the reverse
inclusion is $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$.

**Caveats.** This item realises $\Lambda_1$ by localisation and does **not**
identify it with an integral group ring: the additive group underlying
$\Lambda_1$ is $\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z\,t^k$ and its multiplication
is the polynomial one ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]] is not
needed for the ring laws but records that $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain). The
deck-module structures on homology introduced later on this page are defined
separately, by the universal property above.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

Let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering with path-connected total space and path-connected locally path-connected base. Put

$$G=\pi_1(B,b_0),\qquad H=p_*\pi_1(E,e_0).$$

The following are equivalent:

1. $p$ is regular ([[def-regular-covering]]);
2. $H\trianglelefteq G$;
3. $\operatorname{Deck}(E/B)$ acts transitively on the fibre $p^{-1}(b_0)$.

No finiteness hypothesis is imposed on the fibre or on the index of $H$.

Let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a regular connected covering of a path-connected locally path-connected base. Put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$ and $H=p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Then

$$\operatorname{Deck}(E/B)\cong G/H.$$

For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ ([[def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces]]). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation ([[def-group]], [[def-group-action]]).

derivations.claim: **The boundary class.** The boundary circle $\partial S$ follows the inward conormal collar of $F$ once around $K$, so its projection to the core has degree $+1$. It bounds the oriented surface $S$ in $E$, hence maps to zero in $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)$. By [F2] it is the unique degree-one class in the boundary kernel, namely the preferred longitude. The collar removed from $F$ is an annulus, so [F3] also identifies $H_1(S;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$.

**Homology of the cut complement.** In an interior product chart $F\times(-\delta,\delta)$, the complement has the two half-collars $r<0$ and $r>0$; on either half replace $r$ during the homotopy by $(1-s)r+s\,\operatorname{sign}(r)\delta$ for $0\le s\le1$. At the boundary collar, the adapted tube gives the corresponding punctured half-disk fibers, and radial projection to their outer boundary arcs is the same deformation. These maps agree with the identity off the collar and exhibit the cut-open complement $Y$ as homotopy equivalent to $S^3\setminus F$. Since $H_2(F)=0$ by [F3], Alexander duality in [F4] gives $\widetilde H_0(S^3\setminus F)=0$, hence $Y$ is connected. In degree one, [F4] and the universal-coefficient sequence identify $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$. The natural duality map sends $[\gamma]$ to $([a]\mapsto\operatorname{lk}(\gamma,a))$; the meridian normalization in [F5] fixes its sign.

**The stacked space is the positive-linking cover.** Product neighborhoods of the cut faces show that the quotient map $\widetilde E_F\to E$ is a covering: away from $S$ it is the identity on a sheet, and at $S$ the two product half-collars of adjacent copies give the two half-neighborhoods of a point in $E$. The stack is connected because each $Y_n$ is connected by step 2.1 and consecutive copies meet along the connected surface $S$. The shift $t$ is a deck transformation with quotient group $\mathbb Z$. To fix the sign, let $k$ be the positive tangent to $K$ and $u$ the inward conormal of $F$ at its boundary. The outward-normal-first boundary convention makes $(k,u)$ positive in $TF$, so $(n,k,u)$ is positive in $TS^3$ for the declared positive normal $n$. The positive meridian disk then has oriented basis $(u,n)$; at its intersection with $F$ its positive boundary tangent is $n$, so it crosses from the negative to the positive side. Under the specified gluing this moves from $Y_n$ to $Y_{n+1}$ and has monodromy $+1$. Every loop's sheet change is its signed intersection with $S$, which equals its total linking with $K$ because $\partial S$ is parallel to $K$ and the omitted boundary collar misses loops in $E$. Therefore the cover subgroup is the kernel of the one-variable total-linking homomorphism, and [F7] identifies this as the cyclic cover with the stated positive deck generator.

**Mayer–Vietoris presentation.** Cover the stack by open thickenings of the copies $Y_n$; consecutive thickenings overlap in one copy of $S$ and nonconsecutive ones are disjoint. A singular chain has compact image and therefore meets only finitely many sheets, so the finite-chain Mayer–Vietoris sequences pass to the direct limit over finite consecutive stacks. Identifying translates with powers of $t$ gives the exact sequence
$$H_1(S;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda\xrightarrow{i_- -t i_+}H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda\longrightarrow H_1(\widetilde E_F;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_0(S;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda\xrightarrow{1-t}H_0(Y;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda.$$
Both $S$ and $Y$ are connected, so the last map is multiplication by $1-t$. If $q\in\Lambda$ and $(1-t)q=0$, a nonzero $q$ has a largest exponent $m$ with nonzero coefficient $q_m$, while the coefficient of $t^{m+1}$ in $(1-t)q$ is $-q_m\ne0$; hence $q=0$. The last map is therefore injective. Exactness makes the preceding map onto $H_1(\widetilde E_F)$ with kernel exactly the image of $i_- -t i_+$; using $H_1(S)\cong H_1(F)$ from step 1.1 gives the asserted cokernel presentation.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the

passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]],
[[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let
$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$
The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the
principal localisation
$$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$
([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).
It is a commutative ring with unit $1=t^0$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]). Write
again $t$ for the image of the indeterminate under the localisation map; then
$t$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}$
([[prop-units-in-a-localisation]]). Every element of $\Lambda_1$ has a
representative
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,$$
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, obtained by writing a fraction

([[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]).

**Universal property.** Let $A$ be a ring with unit and let
$\varphi\colon\mathbb Z[t]\to A$ be a unital ring homomorphism with
$\varphi(t)$ a unit of $A$. Then there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\widetilde\varphi\colon\Lambda_1\to A$ with
$\widetilde\varphi(t)=\varphi(t)$. Equivalently, for every unital ring $A$ and
every unit $u\in A$ there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\Lambda_1\to A$ with $t\mapsto u$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]],
[[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The cited localisation theorem treats commutative target rings. For the
possibly noncommutative target used here, define
$\sum_k a_kt^k\mapsto\sum_k(a_k1_A)u^k$. Unique Laurent coefficients make
this well defined. Integer multiples of $1_A$ are central, and
$u^ku^l=u^{k+l}$ for all integers $k,l$, so finite distributivity proves
additivity, multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Every unital
homomorphism must send $a_k$ to $a_k1_A$ and $t^k$ to $u^k$, proving
uniqueness. Taking $u=\varphi(t)$ gives the asserted extension of $\varphi$.

**Augmentation.** There is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$$\varepsilon\colon\Lambda_1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k\Bigr)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k,$$
the **sum-of-coefficients map** ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]]); it
is well defined because the coefficients are summable and their total sum is
unchanged along the relation of
[[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]. Its kernel is the
principal ideal $(t-1)$: indeed $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$, and if
$\varepsilon(x)=0$ then, writing $x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k$ with finite
support and using that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k=0$, one has
$$x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k(t^k-1)=(t-1)\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k\,(1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}),$$
where $1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}$ denotes the empty sum $0$ for $k=0$ and, for
$k=-j<0$, the negative sum
$-(t^{-1}+t^{-2}+\cdots+t^{-j})$, so that
$t^{-j}-1=-(t-1)(t^{-1}+\cdots+t^{-j})$; hence $x\in(t-1)$, and the reverse
inclusion is $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$.

is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

2. $H\trianglelefteq G$;

derivations.claim: **The boundary class.** The boundary circle $\partial S$ follows the inward conormal collar of $F$ once around $K$, so its projection to the core has degree $+1$. It bounds the oriented surface $S$ in $E$, hence maps to zero in $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)$. By [F2] it is the unique degree-one class in the boundary kernel, namely the preferred longitude. The collar removed from $F$ is an annulus, so [F3] also identifies $H_1(S;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$.

**Homology of the cut complement.** In an interior product chart $F\times(-\delta,\delta)$, the complement has the two half-collars $r<0$ and $r>0$; on either half replace $r$ during the homotopy by $(1-s)r+s\,\operatorname{sign}(r)\delta$ for $0\le s\le1$. At the boundary collar, the adapted tube gives the corresponding punctured half-disk fibers, and radial projection to their outer boundary arcs is the same deformation. These maps agree with the identity off the collar and exhibit the cut-open complement $Y$ as homotopy equivalent to $S^3\setminus F$. Since $H_2(F)=0$ by [F3], Alexander duality in [F4] gives $\widetilde H_0(S^3\setminus F)=0$, hence $Y$ is connected. In degree one, [F4] and the universal-coefficient sequence identify $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$. The natural duality map sends $[\gamma]$ to $([a]\mapsto\operatorname{lk}(\gamma,a))$; the meridian normalization in [F5] fixes its sign.

**The stacked space is the positive-linking cover.** Product neighborhoods of the cut faces show that the quotient map $\widetilde E_F\to E$ is a covering: away from $S$ it is the identity on a sheet, and at $S$ the two product half-collars of adjacent copies give the two half-neighborhoods of a point in $E$. The stack is connected because each $Y_n$ is connected by step 1.2 and consecutive copies meet along the connected surface $S$. The shift $t$ is a deck transformation with quotient group $\mathbb Z$. To fix the sign, let $k$ be the positive tangent to $K$ and $u$ the inward conormal of $F$ at its boundary. The outward-normal-first boundary convention makes $(k,u)$ positive in $TF$, so $(n,k,u)$ is positive in $TS^3$ for the declared positive normal $n$. The positive meridian disk then has oriented basis $(u,n)$; at its intersection with $F$ its positive boundary tangent is $n$, so it crosses from the negative to the positive side. Under the specified gluing this moves from $Y_n$ to $Y_{n+1}$ and has monodromy $+1$. Every loop's sheet change is its signed intersection with $S$, which equals its total linking with $K$ because $\partial S$ is parallel to $K$ and the omitted boundary collar misses loops in $E$. Therefore the cover subgroup is the kernel of the one-variable total-linking homomorphism, and [F7] identifies this as the cyclic cover with the stated positive deck generator.

**Mayer–Vietoris presentation.** Cover the stack by open thickenings of the copies $Y_n$; consecutive thickenings overlap in one copy of $S$ and nonconsecutive ones are disjoint. A singular chain has compact image and therefore meets only finitely many sheets, so the finite-chain Mayer–Vietoris sequences pass to the direct limit over finite consecutive stacks. Identifying translates with powers of $t$ gives the exact sequence $$H_1(S;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda\xrightarrow{i_- -t i_+}H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda\longrightarrow H_1(\widetilde E_F;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_0(S;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda\xrightarrow{1-t}H_0(Y;\mathbb Z)\otimes\Lambda.$$ Both $S$ and $Y$ are connected, so the last map is multiplication by $1-t$. Exactness makes the preceding map onto $H_1(\widetilde E_F)$ with kernel exactly the image of $i_- -t i_+$; using $H_1(S)\cong H_1(F)$ from step 1.1 gives the asserted cokernel presentation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be an even-order square matrix with integer entries, of size $n=2g$. A unimodular congruence replaces $V$ by $P^TVP$ for an integer matrix $P$ with determinant $+1$ or $-1$. For $x,y\in\mathbb Z^n$ as column vectors and $z\in\mathbb Z$, the two elementary enlargements of $V$ are
$$E_0(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_1(V;x,y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Two even-order integral matrices are **S-equivalent** if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of unimodular congruences, elementary enlargements, and reverse elementary enlargements.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume full AC when the form is obtained from a knot. For every integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, the class represented by $(H,-V)$ is the additive inverse of the class represented by $(H,V)$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
