citations.quote:
Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

If $A\subset X$ is a CW subcomplex and its inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ strongly deformation retracts onto $A$. Moreover, if $(Y,B)$ is a CW pair and $u_0,u_1:B\to Z$ are homotopic, then the adjunction spaces $Z\cup_{u_0}Y$ and $Z\cup_{u_1}Y$ are homotopy equivalent relative to their common subspace $Z$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Cut out disjoint small underpass intervals, one in each crossing box. The remaining projected arcs are embedded and pairwise disjoint: an interior double point would have an underpassing preimage, which has been removed. Put these arcs at height $1$, their ends in the plane $z=0$, and join each pair of ends of a removed underpass below that plane. This normalization preserves the complement pair. Indeed, inside a crossing box the two branches retain a strict height inequality while their heights interpolate; away from these boxes projection is injective and vertical interpolation cannot introduce intersections. A change of height $d(q)$ on a strand extends to a local ambient map $(q,z)\mapsto(q,z+\chi(z)d(q))$, subdividing the interpolation so that $1+\chi'(z)d(q)>0$. Finitely many disjoint strip charts, smooth cutoffs and parameter subdivisions suffice. Planar bends can likewise be straightened in their disjoint strip charts. All these maps are the identity in a common high collar.

For $c=0$, first compare the actual smooth knot with a polygon, rather than identifying embeddings merely from the code. Its projection is a smooth embedded circle $\gamma$, so the knot is $(\gamma(s),g(s))$. Apply the finite compact-tube construction [F2] to the flat curve $(\gamma(s),0)$: the planar slice of its normal tube is an injective strip $\Psi(s,r)=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $n$ the positive unit planar normal. In this strip the ambient map $(\Psi(s,r),z)\mapsto(\Psi(s,r),z-t\chi(r)g(s))$, with $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi$ zero near the strip boundary, is a homeomorphism for each $t$ (it is a translation on every vertical fibre), and is the identity outside the strip. It flattens the actual knot. Uniform continuity of the tangent and the finite tube bounds then give a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon: each chord stays in the strip and its projection to the circle is strictly increasing, since its tangent has positive scalar product with the nearby oriented circle tangents. The polygonal projection has one full turn, so it is bijective, and the polygon is the normal graph $r=f(s)$. Choose the subdivision so $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. This relates the actual embedding to the polygon without any later diagram-code supplier.

Here is a precise convenient tunnel model for the normalized knot. In each crossing box choose a small convex polygonal footprint $F_i$ and a convex lower cap $C_i=\{(q,z):q\in F_i,\ h_i(q)\le z\le0\},$ where $h_i$ is piecewise linear, negative inside $F_i$ and zero on its boundary. Take the lower arc to be the two straight segments from its two interior top-face endpoints to one interior point of $C_i$. This replacement of the underpass is realized by vertical interpolation of its negative graph, fixing its endpoints. Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. Thus it identifies a standard cylinder core with the two-segment arc and its two end disks with the designated exits. Attach product tubes along the disjoint upper arcs to those exits. The resulting neighborhood $N_*$ has one cap and one upper tube per underpass, joined in the same single cycle as $K$; its coordinates are a disk bundle around $K$, not an assumption about an arbitrary regular neighborhood. Corners and the core bends can be rounded inside disjoint smaller charts; retain the polygonal cap boundary, which is only used topologically.

The polygon's bounded side is supplied by [F6]. Triangulate it by diagonals: at a convex vertex use its neighbor triangle if it contains no other vertex; otherwise join it to a vertex in that triangle farthest from the opposite side. The smaller open triangle contains no intervening vertex, so the diagonal is internal; induction on the vertex count yields a finite triangulation. A leaf of its triangle-adjacency tree is an ear $uvw$, with ear tip $v$ and base $uw$. Remove any collinear vertices before this step. Put $q$ in the interior of $uw$. Choose $z_+=q+(1+\eta)(v-q)$ and $z_-=q-\epsilon(v-q)$, with small positive $\eta,\epsilon$, so the convex quadrilateral $Q=(u,z_+,w,z_-)$ meets the rest of the polygon only at $u,w$. Such bounds exist because the closed ear has no other polygon points, nonadjacent edges have positive separation, and the two remaining incident edges have a positive angle away from the ear; finite determinant and distance comparisons select the bounds. Both $v$ and $q$ are interior to $Q$. Triangulate $Q$ by the fan from $v$. On each fan triangle map its apex $v$ to $v_t=(1-t)v+tq$, fix its two boundary vertices, and interpolate affinely. Since $Q$ is convex and $v_t$ is always interior, the image triangles are a nondegenerate fan partition of the same quadrilateral. The resulting map is therefore injective, surjective and piecewise linear, fixes the whole boundary, and extends by the identity to an ambient plane isotopy. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement.

The model can be compared with the given sufficiently small normal tube without invoking a uniqueness theorem or choice. Make its disk-bundle chart smooth near the core and normalize its differential there to the given normal chart; the required linear change is fibrewise, with the tangential component removed by a change of core parameter. In finitely many charts the two resulting embeddings differ by $O(|v|^2)$, with derivative difference $O(|v|)$. Replace the model chart near $v=0$ by the given one using a radial cutoff supported where $|v|<2\delta$ and equal to one for $|v|\le\delta$. The derivative of the correction is $O(\delta)$; compactness and a finite minimum of the chart injectivity bounds therefore preserve a bundle embedding for small $\delta$. Injectivity between nonadjacent core charts follows from their positive separation. The modified chart equals the given normal chart for $|v|\le\delta$ and retains $N_*$ as its outer boundary. Choose the normal-tube radius $\rho<\delta$. In these product coordinates, replace every fibre radius $r\in[\rho,1]$ by $(1-s)r+s$ and fix the exterior of $N_*$. This is a strong deformation retraction from $E_K$ to $\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N_*$, fixed on its target. It agrees on the outer boundary and never enters the removed radius-$\rho$ tube.

Take a large ball $B_R$ containing $N_*$. Outside it, the homotopy $x\mapsto((1-s)+sR/|x|)x$, with the interior fixed, retracts the exterior to its truncation $X$ in $B_R$. Its outer sphere is retained. Write $A=X\cap\{z\ge0\}$. Below the plane, the exterior is exactly $B=\{(q,z):-\sqrt{R^2-|q|^2}\le z\le h(q)\},$ where $h=h_i$ on $F_i$ and is zero elsewhere; enlarge $R$ so every cap lies above the lower hemisphere. citations.quote:
Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

If $A\subset X$ is a CW subcomplex and its inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ strongly deformation retracts onto $A$. Moreover, if $(Y,B)$ is a CW pair and $u_0,u_1:B\to Z$ are homotopic, then the adjunction spaces $Z\cup_{u_0}Y$ and $Z\cup_{u_1}Y$ are homotopy equivalent relative to their common subspace $Z$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Cut out disjoint small underpass intervals, one in each crossing box. A change of height $d(q)$ on a strand extends to a local ambient map $(q,z)\mapsto(q,z+\chi(z)d(q))$, subdividing the interpolation so that $1+\chi'(z)d(q)>0$. Finitely many disjoint strip charts, smooth cutoffs and parameter subdivisions suffice. Planar bends can likewise be straightened in their disjoint strip charts. All these maps are the identity in a common high collar.

For $c=0$, first compare the actual smooth knot with a polygon, rather than identifying embeddings merely from the code. Its projection is a smooth embedded circle $\gamma$, so the knot is $(\gamma(s),g(s))$. It flattens the actual knot. Uniform continuity of the tangent and the finite tube bounds then give a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon: each chord stays in the strip and its projection to the circle is strictly increasing, since its tangent has positive scalar product with the nearby oriented circle tangents. The polygonal projection has one full turn, so it is bijective, and the polygon is the normal graph $r=f(s)$. Choose the subdivision so $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. This relates the actual embedding to the polygon without any later diagram-code supplier.

Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement.

For $v\in[-1,1]^3\setminus\{0\}$, the homotopy $$H_s(v)=\left(1-s+\frac{s}{\|v\|_\infty}\right)v$$ retracts onto the cube boundary, fixes both identified end faces pointwise, and therefore descends to the product quotient. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $|f|\le M$ pointwise for some finite $M\ge0$. With the convention
$$\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
one has
$$\left|\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ\right|\le 2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$
For every measurable $g:E\to\mathbb R$ with $0\le g\le M$ pointwise, one also has
$$\left|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ\right|\le M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}.$$
Both integral differences are zero when $M=0$.

Fix a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ and a bounded measurable functional
$f:E\to\mathbb R$, with $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|<\infty$. All
target laws below are probability measures on this same space. If a model or
discretization originally uses another state space, specify its measurable
embedding into $E$ and compare its pushforward law; no identification of
different state spaces is implicit. A **posterior law** here is the probability
law for the unknown at the specified computation stage, conditional on the same
fixed observed data. For a probability law $\mu$, write
$\mu(f):=\int_E f\,d\mu$.

Name the successive posterior laws as follows: $\mu_\star$ is the intended
target; $\mu_{\rm model}$ is the posterior under the selected statistical or
physical model; $\mu_{\rm solver}$ is the posterior after replacing the exact
forward or PDE solution by the declared numerical solver output; and
$\mu_{\rm disc}$ is the posterior after the declared finite-dimensional
discretization. These labels refer to the exact adjacent laws recorded for the
computation, even when two stages happen to agree.

Let $K$ be the implemented probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$. An
**invariant law** $\pi_K$ for $K$ is a probability measure satisfying
$$\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi_K(dx)=\pi_K(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal E).$$
Choose and report which invariant law is used if $K$ has more than one. If no
invariant law has been established, the invariant-kernel and burn-in terms
below are unavailable; they are not set to zero. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a
time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative to its
natural filtration, with initial probability law $\lambda$. For burn-in length
$b\ge0$ and retained sample size $N\ge1$, set
$$\bar f_{b,N}:=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N f(X_{b+j}),$$
and let $\mathbb E_\lambda$ denote expectation under this initial law and the
chain's transition randomness.

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $\theta=r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_m,\widetilde r$ be the finite scalar reference chain and returned value of [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]], with $m\ge0$. Then, pointwise,
$$\widetilde r-\theta=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(r_j-r_{j-1})+(\widetilde r-r_m),$$
and consequently
$$|\widetilde r-\theta|\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}|r_j-r_{j-1}|+|\widetilde r-r_m|.$$
The sum is empty when $m=0$. No independence, unbiasedness, or distributional assumption is needed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

For the stationary branch, set $Y_j=f(X_{b+j})-\pi_K(f)$. By [F4], each $Y_j$ has mean zero and $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=\gamma_{|i-j|}$. Expanding the finite square gives $\mathbb E[(N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N Y_j)^2]=N^{-2}(N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k)$: there are $N$ diagonal terms, and for each lag $k$ there are $N-k$ off-diagonal pairs, each counted twice.

Since $0\le N-k\le N$ and $\gamma_0=\operatorname{Var}(f(X_0))\ge0$, the expression in step 2.1 is at most $N^{-1}(\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}|\gamma_k|)$, which is bounded by the claimed infinite-series expression. Absolute summability makes the bound finite.

([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $\theta=r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_m,\widetilde r$ be the finite scalar reference chain and returned value of [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]], with $m\ge0$. Then, pointwise,
$$\widetilde r-\theta=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(r_j-r_{j-1})+(\widetilde r-r_m),$$
and consequently
$$|\widetilde r-\theta|\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}|r_j-r_{j-1}|+|\widetilde r-r_m|.$$
The sum is empty when $m=0$. No independence, unbiasedness, or distributional assumption is needed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Assume full AC. Let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ be the group of a smooth oriented knot exterior, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. For a finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$, the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ representation variety** is the algebraic set of tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ for which every relator matrix $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ equals the identity. The group $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ acts on this set by simultaneous conjugation. Its affine categorical quotient, whose coordinate ring is the invariant ring of regular functions, is the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety** $X(E_K)$. For a representation $\rho$, its character is the function $\gamma\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma))$. A representation is **reducible** if its matrices preserve a common one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$; otherwise it is irreducible. The peripheral torus group is $\pi_1(T_K)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, generated by the meridian and preferred longitude; its image in $G$ is generated by their commuting classes and need not be isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Their image under any representation is a commuting pair of matrices, so it has a common invariant line and is simultaneously triangularizable over $\mathbb C$. Choosing a common invariant line gives meridian and longitude eigenvalues $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$; the unordered boundary character identifies $(M,L)$ with $(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. Simultaneous diagonalizability is stronger than simultaneous triangularizability.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set
with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then:
(i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any
finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the
morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is
canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this
canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient
([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of
$\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so
is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with exterior $E_K$, positive meridian $\mu$, and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Define $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ to consist of all pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common invariant line on which $\rho(\mu)$ acts by $M$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ acts by $L$. The Zariski closure is the smallest Zariski-closed algebraic subset containing $\mathcal E_K$; let $V_K$ be the union of its one-dimensional irreducible components, where an irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed subset. Zero-dimensional image components are omitted. The **ordinary A-polynomial** $A_K(M,L)$ is the Laurent polynomial generating the vanishing ideal of $V_K$, chosen square-free (no repeated irreducible factors) and with primitive integer coefficients (their greatest common divisor is one). It is determined up to multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$ for $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. Its reduced curve includes the abelian component $L=1$; equivalently, its representative in $\mathbb Z[M,L]$ is divisible by $L-1$.

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. The restriction of representations of $\pi_1(E_K)$ to the peripheral torus gives an eigenvalue locus in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ with algebraic Zariski closure. Its one-dimensional reduced image components are exactly the curve components used in $A_K(M,L)$; isolated image points contribute no curve factor. Radical elimination of the representation, trace and eigenline coordinates from the finite presentation incidence equations, followed by retaining precisely the one-dimensional irreducible components, yields the Laurent ideal of that curve union, whose square-free primitive generator is $A_K$ up to $\pm M^aL^b$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

For homomorphisms $f:K\to G$ and $h:K\to H$, let $N$ be the normal closure in $G\ast H$ of $$\{j_G(f(k))j_H(h(k))^{-1}:k\in K\}.$$ Then $(G\ast H)/N$, with the induced factor maps $j_G$ and $j_H$, is a pushout of $f$ and $h$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

A smooth collar is a smooth embedding $c:\partial M\times[0,\varepsilon)\to M$ such that $c(p,0)=p$ and whose image is an open neighbourhood of $\partial M$ in $M$. Locally one may first use a positive smooth width depending on $p$.

derivations.claim: Inclusion of the boundary torus into the exterior gives a homomorphism of fundamental groups. Precomposing a representation with this homomorphism is polynomial in matrix entries, so it is a regular map of representation varieties and is equivariant for simultaneous conjugation.

Pullback along this equivariant map sends conjugation-invariant regular functions to conjugation-invariant regular functions, hence induces the algebraic restriction morphism on affine categorical quotients.

By [F2], the defining equation of the reduced curve union vanishes on each of its one-dimensional image components. The definition takes only those components, so an isolated image point outside their union is not added as a curve factor.

Write the attached solid torus as $V=D^2\times S^1$, let $A=\{0\}\times S^1$, and base at $(0,1)$. The retraction $r(z,w)=(0,w)$ and inclusion $i:A\hookrightarrow V$ satisfy $r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_A$, and the homotopy $((z,w),t)\mapsto((1-t)z,w)$ from $\operatorname{id}_V$ to $i\circ r$ fixes the basepoint. By [F5] and [F6], $\pi_1(V,(0,1))\cong\pi_1(S^1,1)\cong\mathbb Z$.

By [A1] and [F7], the exterior boundary has a collar; $V$ has its product collar. Thickening the two pieces across opposite halves of the gluing collar gives an open cover of the filled manifold whose sets retract to $E_K$ and $V$ and whose intersection retracts to the torus. These spaces are path connected, so [F4] identifies the filled fundamental group as their pushout.

Since $\mu,\lambda$ commute, the primitive class $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ is represented by $\mu^p\lambda^q$. It maps to the identity in $\pi_1(V)$ because it is the meridian. Complete $(p,q)$ to a unimodular basis of $\mathbb Z^2$ by Bézout; the complementary class has longitude coefficient $\pm1$ on $\partial V$, hence maps to a generator of $\pi_1(V)$ by step 2.1. The pushout from step 2.2 identifies this generator with the image of the complementary class in $\pi_1(E_K)$ and imposes only the relation $\mu^p\lambda^q=1$. Eliminating the generator gives $\pi_1(E_K(p/q))\cong\pi_1(E_K)/\langle\!\langle\mu^p\lambda^q\rangle\!\rangle$.

A homomorphism from this quotient is exactly a homomorphism from $\pi_1(E_K)$ that kills $\mu^p\lambda^q$. Since $\rho(\mu)$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ commute, this condition is the matrix equation $\rho(\mu)^p\rho(\lambda)^q=I_2$.

If the two peripheral matrices are simultaneously diagonalized, their product of powers is $\operatorname{diag}(M^pL^q,(M^pL^q)^{-1})$, which is the identity exactly when $M^pL^q=1$. For a merely triangular pair, the diagonal entries still give this necessary equation, but they do not determine the off-diagonal entries of the product; the matrix relation remains the exact test.

Require the resulting closed tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$ to be pairwise disjoint, and put $N(L)=\bigcup_{i=1}^rN(K_i)$ and $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(L)$, the resulting compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary. The tube choices are part of the input. Choose a basepoint $b\in E_L\subset X_L$. Orient each normal disk so that the positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the fixed orientation of $S^3$. A **positive meridian** $\mu_i$ of $K_i$ is the oriented boundary of the radius-$\epsilon_i$ normal disk in one fibre of $\nu(K_i)$; the curve lies on $\partial E_L$ and is disjoint from every component of $L$; its spanning normal disk meets $K_i$ transversely once with positive sign and misses every other component. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ and identifies the classes of $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ with its standard basis. $$A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z),$$

as a left $\Lambda_r$-module under the deck action. “Absolute” means this is ordinary homology of the covering space, not relative homology with respect to a fibre over the basepoint.

Let $\lambda(v)$ be the sum of edge labels along the unique spanning-tree path from the least vertex $v_0$ to $v$. Construct a simplicial cover with vertices $(v,g)$, $g\in\mathbb Z^r$, and with each oriented edge $e:v\to w$ lifting from $(v,g)$ to $(w,g+\ell(e))$. At each vertex $(v,g)$, each simplex incident to $v$ has a unique lift through $(v,g)$; therefore the open star maps homeomorphically to the open star of $v$, proving the covering condition. The spanning tree paths then connect every vertex in every other fiber to that fiber, hence the cover is connected. By [F9] the constructed cover is the maximal abelian cover.

The tree assignments select the vertex lifts $(v,\lambda(v))$. The procedure then selects each simplex lift through its anchor lift. For a face $\tau$ of $\sigma$, the difference between the exponent of this face occurrence and the selected lift of $\tau$ is exactly $g(\sigma,\tau)$ computed in instruction 3. These are the cellular face-incidence boundaries in the constructed cover, so the procedure matrices satisfy $\partial^2=0$ and form its lifted cellular chain complex.

e0$, the rational adjoint-twisted slope is

If $x$ is an ideal point of the smooth projective completion of this curve and the associated Culler-Shalen construction yields an essential surface of boundary slope $r$ in the fixed meridian-longitude convention, the limiting slope at $x$ is $-r$.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ have admissible adjoint local system, and let $v_\rho$ be a nonzero peripheral-adjoint-invariant vector for which $[v_\rho\otimes\lambda],[v_\rho\otimes\mu]$ form the specified ordered basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\operatorname{Ad}\rho)$. Rescaling $v_\rho$ or the kernel generator does not change this projective ratio. A rational function on an irreducible character component means an element of its function field, the fraction field of its coordinate domain. A projective-valued rational function means a point of the projective line over that field; it may be identically $\infty$. The slope's rational extension has this projective meaning. Assume full AC. Let $E$ be the compact exterior of a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Let $X$ be an irreducible one-dimensional component of its complex $SL_2$ character variety. Fix a one-dimensional peripheral eigenvalue-image component $Y$ arising from $X$, with coordinates $(M,L)$ ordered as (meridian,longitude), and an irreducible Laurent equation $P(M,L)=0$ for $Y$. Write $K=\mathbb C(X)$.

There is a finite extension $F/K$ with an actual generic representation $\rho:\pi_1(E)\to SL_2(F)$ and a choice of common peripheral eigenline whose eigenvalues are $M,L\in F^*$. These give the specified generic point of $Y$. Its actual intrinsic adjoint peripheral homology has a two-dimensional boundary basis ordered (longitude,meridian) and a one-dimensional inclusion kernel. With $\delta\in\{\lambda,\mu\}$ having distinct peripheral eigenvalues, set $u=\rho(\delta)-\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\delta))I/2$. In that basis its kernel is exactly
$$\ker\left\{F^2\longrightarrow\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C},\quad (a,b)\longmapsto a\,\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}+b\,\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right\}.$$
The two displayed differentials are not both zero. Thus its projective slope, with convention $s=-b/a$ for the kernel line, is
$$s=\left[\frac{\mathrm dL}{L}:\frac{\mathrm dM}{M}\right]=[-M P_M:L P_L]\ \in\mathbb P^1(F).$$
A ratio of one-forms here means their coordinate pair in any nonzero basis of the one-dimensional $F$-space $\Omega^1_{F/\mathbb C}$. The result is independent of that basis, the finite field model, the common eigenline and simultaneous conjugation, and is defined over $K$. It includes zero when $\mathrm dL=0$ and infinity when $\mathrm dM=0$. In particular a nonconstant meridian eigenvalue is not assumed.

This is an identity of rational projective maps. It agrees with the actual specialized homology slope on a nonempty dense rank-chart open. At every point where the rational extension and the peripheral restriction are evaluated and $(P_M,P_L)\ne(0,0)$, its projective value is $[-M P_M:L P_L]$; when $P_L\ne0$ this is the ordinary value $-M P_M/(L P_L)$. For the square-free ordinary A-polynomial, replacing $P$ by the full polynomial gives the same ratio at a point where its gradient is nonzero. No assertion that all specialized exterior homology ranks are constant outside that open, nor any ideal-point tree or essential-surface construction, is part of this lemma.

Assume full AC and let $G=\pi_1(E_K)=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$ be a finite presentation of a knot-exterior group. The set of homomorphisms $G\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is the affine algebraic subset of $SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ cut out by the matrix-entry equations $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=I_2$ for $1\le j\le m$. After each inverse letter is replaced by the adjugate of its determinant-one matrix, these equations have integer coefficients in the matrix-entry coordinates.

Assume also Dependent Choice for the cited minimal-prime existence theorem. Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the Nullstellensatz route. Every affine algebraic set $X$ has a finite irredundant decomposition into nonempty irreducible closed subsets, unique up to permutation. These are its maximal irreducible closed subsets. The empty set has the empty decomposition.

Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Then
$$ \dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K. $$

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with exterior $E_K$, positive meridian $\mu$, and preferred longitude $\lambda$. Define $\mathcal E_K\subset(\mathbb C^*)^2$ to consist of all pairs $(M,L)$ for which some representation $\rho:\pi_1(E_K)\to SL_2(\mathbb C)$ has a common invariant line on which $\rho(\mu)$ acts by $M$ and $\rho(\lambda)$ acts by $L$. The Zariski closure is the smallest Zariski-closed algebraic subset containing $\mathcal E_K$; let $V_K$ be the union of its one-dimensional irreducible components, where an irreducible component is a maximal irreducible closed subset. Zero-dimensional image components are omitted. The **ordinary A-polynomial** $A_K(M,L)$ is the Laurent polynomial generating the vanishing ideal of $V_K$, chosen square-free (no repeated irreducible factors) and with primitive integer coefficients (their greatest common divisor is one). It is determined up to multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$ for $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. Its reduced curve includes the abelian component $L=1$; equivalently, its representative in $\mathbb Z[M,L]$ is divisible by $L-1$.

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen compact exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$. A simple closed curve on a surface is **essential** if it is not null-homotopic there. A surface $S\subset E_K$ is properly embedded if $S\cap\partial E_K=\partial S$ and its interior lies in the interior of $E_K$. It is **incompressible** if it has no embedded disk with interior disjoint from $S$ and essential boundary in $S$; it is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no embedded disk whose boundary is the union of an arc in $S$ that does not cut off a disk and an arc in $\partial E_K$. derivations.claim: **The image curve is an actual A-component.** This instantiation requires excluding a larger peripheral image component. Take the actual generic matrices on an irreducible common-eigenline incidence chart of [F4], over its finitely generated function field $F$. A two-dimensional image would make $M,L$ algebraically independent and the meridian matrix nonparabolic. Over this field the trace form, cap boundary identity and pair exact sequence in [F3] give boundary dimension two and $2=\dim\ker i_*+\operatorname{rank}i_*=2\operatorname{rank}i_*$; hence its kernel is a line. Every $\mathbb C$-derivation $D$ of $F$ differentiates the actual relators to a cocycle. The explicit word/eigenbasis calculation in [F3] makes $(DL/L,DM/M)$ annihilate that SAME line. Extend $M,L$ to a finite transcendence basis and take its two coordinate derivations. Each extends through the finite algebraic extension to $F$ by $D\alpha=-(Dp)(\alpha)/p'(\alpha)$ at a minimal polynomial $p$; characteristic zero makes the denominator nonzero. Their two logarithmic pairs are independent, a contradiction. Generically reducible representations instead have $L=1$ by knot abelianization and cannot supply a two-dimensional image. Thus every peripheral-image component has dimension at most one. The closed irreducible nonconstant image curve $Y$ in the Statement is contained in their finite union, so it equals one of the one-dimensional components: a proper closed subset of an irreducible affine curve has dimension zero. Consequently [F5] supplies its defining Laurent factor $P$ in the full ordinary polynomial. No omitted two-dimensional component is presumed absent merely from the A-polynomial Definition.

**Variable order and sign.** Keep $M$ the meridian eigenvalue and $L$ the longitude eigenvalue. Writing $A_{\mathrm{BFR}}(L,M)=A_{\mathrm{library}}(M,L)$ only changes the order in which the arguments are displayed. Differentiation with respect to the NAMED variables therefore gives the same meridian derivative and the same longitude derivative, not their reciprocal. In the basis [F2], the generic kernel of $(a,b)\mapsto a\,dL/L+b\,dM/M$ has generator $(-dM/M,dL/L)$, so its slope is $(dL/L)/(dM/M)$. This fixes both the sign and the order of the quotient. A common invariant-vector rescaling changes neither coordinate ratio. Swapping the common eigenline inverts $M,L$ and changes both logarithmic differentials by minus one, preserving the projective ratio; [F3] already proves model/conjugation independence.

**Full-polynomial versus component derivatives.** Write $A=uPB$, where $u$ is a Laurent unit and $B$ is the product of the other distinct factors. At a point of $Y$ with both full derivatives nonzero, $B$ cannot vanish: if another factor vanished, every term of either product derivative would contain a vanishing factor, giving zero. On $P=0$ one has $A_M=uB P_M$ and $A_L=uB P_L$. Thus the two component derivatives are nonzero there and the common nonzero factor $uB$ cancels from their quotient. Multiplication of the whole representative by any further Laurent unit has the same effect, since its differentiated unit term is multiplied by $A=0$. This also proves that the stated derivative locus is intrinsic and avoids intersections of distinct peripheral factors. It does not exclude an extra character component with CONSTANT peripheral image at the same point.

**The complete rational instantiation.** The component formula in [F1] is $s^{\mathrm{rat}}=[-MP_M:LP_L]$. Combining steps1.2 and2.1 gives exactly $s^{\mathrm{rat}}=-M A_M/(L A_L)$ in the native BFR variable order wherever the displayed derivatives are nonzero. In particular it is finite there, and the projective extension still retains zero/infinity away from that affine locus. This instantiates the proved component theorem with the FULL square-free ordinary polynomial without changing either convention. It is so far an identity of the rational extension, not a proof about all exceptional actual kernels.

**Actual homology on the proved dense open.** Intersect the nonempty rank-chart open supplied by [F3] with the original smooth/derivative locus, whenever that latter locus is nonempty. The component is irreducible, so this intersection is dense and nonempty. At every point there, the finite homology specialization in [F3] identifies the rational line with the actual ordered peripheral inclusion kernel. Thus step3.1 proves the ACTUAL displayed formula on this open. This uses the direct generic/rank-chart construction, not an unverified extension of the separate rationality lemma beyond its stated dense scheme-smooth hypothesis. It does not assert that every smooth admissible point belongs to the chosen rank chart.

**The full stipulated ideal-point clause.** The curve in the preceding clause is the peripheral eigenvalue curve $Y$. Use its normalized smooth completion, exactly as in [F1], rather than replacing it by an arbitrary character ideal point with affine peripheral image. At its stipulated ideal point the actual local DVR has nonzero valuation pair $(v(L),v(M))$, and the finite representation-field valuation extends with one positive ramification factor. For a boundary circle $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ of the actual associated Culler–Shalen construction, [F1]'s inverse-image midpoint and boundary-preserving compression argument gives $a v(L)+b v(M)=0$. The logarithmic projective limit in [F1] is $[v(L):v(M)]=[-b:a]$. By [F2] this is $-b/a=-r$, including zero and infinity in the projective convention. This proves the ENTIRE conditional ideal-point clause: the construction/surface is stipulated by the original conditional, and no existence theorem for an arbitrary unrelated surface is imported or required.

**The actual exceptional-point clause uses the external theorem.** A reducible representation has longitude eigenvalue $L=1$ because its diagonal characters factor through the knot abelianization. Since $A=(L-1)Q$, its meridian derivative is $A_M=(L-1)Q_M$ and vanishes at every such peripheral point. The stipulated nonzero-derivative locus therefore contains only irreducible characters. At every actual admissible smooth point of that locus, including points outside the local rank chart, apply the ALL-character formula of the external Theorem 4.1 in [L1], in the actual homology convention of its Definitions 3.1–3.2. Steps1.2 and2.1 identify the named variables, signs and full square-free representative. This proves the first clause at its entire original locus; the exceptional specialization is supplied externally, not by a density argument.

Step4.2 already proves the full conditional ideal-point assertion with the stipulated associated surface; [L1]'s Theorem 5.2 independently gives the same valuation and sign convention. Together with step5.1 this establishes both original clauses without narrowing the admissible smooth locus or adding scheme-smoothness.

Differentiation with respect to the NAMED variables therefore gives the same meridian derivative and the same longitude derivative, not their reciprocal. In the basis [F2], the generic kernel of $(a,b)\mapsto a\,dL/L+b\,dM/M$ has generator $(-dM/M,dL/L)$, so its slope is $(dL/L)/(dM/M)$. This fixes both the sign and the order of the quotient. A common invariant-vector rescaling changes neither coordinate ratio. Swapping the common eigenline inverts $M,L$ and changes both logarithmic differentials by minus one, preserving the projective ratio; [F3] already proves model/conjugation independence.

**Full-polynomial versus component derivatives.** Write $A=uPB$, where $u$ is a Laurent unit and $B$ is the product of the other distinct factors. At a point of $Y$ with both full derivatives nonzero, $B$ cannot vanish: if another factor vanished, every term of either product derivative would contain a vanishing factor, giving zero. On $P=0$ one has $A_M=uB P_M$ and $A_L=uB P_L$. Thus the two component derivatives are nonzero there and the common nonzero factor $uB$ cancels from their quotient. Multiplication of the whole representative by any further Laurent unit has the same effect, since its differentiated unit term is multiplied by $A=0$. This also proves that the stated derivative locus is intrinsic and avoids intersections of distinct peripheral factors. It does not exclude an extra character component with CONSTANT peripheral image at the same point.

**The complete rational instantiation.** The component formula in [F1] is $s^{\mathrm{rat}}=[-MP_M:LP_L]$. Combining steps1.2 and2.1 gives exactly $s^{\mathrm{rat}}=-M A_M/(L A_L)$ in the native BFR variable order wherever the displayed derivatives are nonzero. In particular it is finite there, and the projective extension still retains zero/infinity away from that affine locus. This instantiates the proved component theorem with the FULL square-free ordinary polynomial without changing either convention. It is so far an identity of the rational extension, not a proof about all exceptional actual kernels.

**Actual homology on the proved dense open.** Intersect the nonempty rank-chart open supplied by [F3] with the original smooth/derivative locus, whenever that latter locus is nonempty. The component is irreducible, so this intersection is dense and nonempty. At every point there, the finite homology specialization in [F3] identifies the rational line with the actual ordered peripheral inclusion kernel. Thus step3.1 proves the ACTUAL displayed formula on this open. This uses the direct generic/rank-chart construction, not an unverified extension of the separate rationality lemma beyond its stated dense scheme-smooth hypothesis. It does not assert that every smooth admissible point belongs to the chosen rank chart.

**The full stipulated ideal-point clause.** The curve in the preceding clause is the peripheral eigenvalue curve $Y$. Use its normalized smooth completion, exactly as in [F1], rather than replacing it by an arbitrary character ideal point with affine peripheral image. At its stipulated ideal point the actual local DVR has nonzero valuation pair $(v(L),v(M))$, and the finite representation-field valuation extends with one positive ramification factor. For a boundary circle $a[\lambda]+b[\mu]$ of the actual associated Culler–Shalen construction, [F1]'s inverse-image midpoint and boundary-preserving compression argument gives $a v(L)+b v(M)=0$. The logarithmic projective limit in [F1] is $[v(L):v(M)]=[-b:a]$. By [F2] this is $-b/a=-r$, including zero and infinity in the projective convention. This proves the ENTIRE conditional ideal-point clause: the construction/surface is stipulated by the original conditional, and no existence theorem for an arbitrary unrelated surface is imported or required.

**The actual exceptional-point clause uses the external theorem.** A reducible representation has longitude eigenvalue $L=1$ because its diagonal characters factor through the knot abelianization. Since $A=(L-1)Q$, its meridian derivative is $A_M=(L-1)Q_M$ and vanishes at every such peripheral point. The stipulated nonzero-derivative locus therefore contains only irreducible characters. At every actual admissible smooth point of that locus, including points outside the local rank chart, apply the ALL-character formula of the external Theorem 4.1 in [L1], in the actual homology convention of its Definitions 3.1–3.2. Steps1.2 and2.1 identify the named variables, signs and full square-free representative. This proves the first clause at its entire original locus; the exceptional specialization is supplied externally, not by a density argument.

Step4.2 already proves the full conditional ideal-point assertion with the stipulated associated surface; [L1]'s Theorem 5.2 independently gives the same valuation and sign convention. Together with step5.1 this establishes both original clauses without narrowing the admissible smooth locus or adding scheme-smoothness.
