citations.quote:
A **rack** is a set $R$ with a binary operation $*:R\times R\to R$ such
that for every $y\in R$ the right translation $R_y(x)=x*y$ is a bijection
and $(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$ for all $x,y,z\in R$. A **quandle** is a rack
satisfying $x*x=x$ for every $x$. For either structure, write
$x\mathbin{\bar *}y=R_y^{-1}(x)$.

For a regular oriented link diagram $D$, let $A(D)$ be its finite set of
maximal under-arcs. Form the set of finite terms recursively: each symbol
$x_a$ for $a\in A(D)$ is a term, and if $s,t$ are terms then $s*t$ and
$s\mathbin{\bar *}t$ are terms. Let $\sim$ be the intersection of all
equivalence relations on these terms that are compatible with both operations
and contain the quandle identities: idempotency, right invertibility, and
right self-distributivity, together with the crossing relations.
At a crossing with source and target under-arcs $u,v$ and overarc $o$, the
crossing relation is $x_v=x_u*x_o$; reversing source and target gives the
equivalent relation with $\bar *$. The quotient term set $Q(D)$ is the
**diagram quandle**, or the diagram presentation of the **fundamental
quandle**. Its independence of diagram is proved in the Theorem.

For any quandle $Q$, its **adjoint group** $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ is the
group presentation with generators $e_q$ for all $q\in Q$ and relators
$e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$ for all $q,r\in Q$. A group presentation
$\langle X\mid S\rangle$ means the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the
normal closure of the relator words $S$.

The diagram presentation and the adjoint group are algebraic constructions;
this definition makes no completeness or knot-classification assertion.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Define a procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

derivations.claim: Under R1, the new underarc generator $y$ satisfies either $y=x*x$ or $x=y*x$ for the unchanged arc color $x$. In the first case idempotency gives $y=x$; in the second, $x=x*x$ and right invertibility give the unique solution $y=x$. Thus the new generator is eliminated. Under R2, each added underarc generator is uniquely solved from its neighboring arc and the overarc by $*$ or $\bar *$; the reverse move gives the inverse substitution. Thus these moves are quandle Tietze transformations.

Under R3, assigning boundary colors $x,y,z$ gives the two possible iterated labels $(x*y)*z$ and $(x*z)*(y*z)$; these agree by right self-distributivity. With the over-colors fixed, each under-color substitution is invertible by right invertibility, so the reverse replacements give inverse substitutions. The same calculation for reversed crossings follows by applying the inverse right translations, which preserve both operations by self-distributivity.

For the knot-group comparison assume $L=K$. Let $\Gamma$ be the finite planar graph obtained by taking the crossings as vertices and the strand pieces between consecutive crossings as edges. Choose disjoint small disks about the crossing vertices, each meeting $D$ only in its two transverse branches, and disjoint tubular strips around the compact edge pieces outside those disks. At a crossing, oriented local coordinates straighten the branches to two transverse axes. Choose a nearby rational point and two rational direction vectors, still transverse and in the same cyclic order as the original branches; the four rational half-segments give the coded crossing and its over/under choice. Extend each edge strip a short distance into its endpoint disks through the corresponding disjoint branch sectors, and choose rational bend ports there. In each strip choose a simple rational polygonal path that is a graph in strip coordinates and joins its ports; choose it fine enough that rounding its bends gives a small normal graph over the original edge. If there are no crossings, choose a simple rational polygon in a tubular annulus of the projected circle. Since there are finitely many compact edge pieces, nonincident pieces have positive separation, and each crossing is transverse; density of $\mathbb Q^2$ and a sufficiently fine finite subdivision therefore let all vertices and bends be rational while preserving the one-circle tracing, crossing cyclic orders, orientations, and over/under data, with no other intersections. The resulting record is a valid code by [F4]; smoothing its bends in disjoint disks gives a smooth regular diagram with the same crossing data by [F6]. To compare it with $D$, move each crossing point to its nearby rational point by an isotopy supported in its disk and the short branch sectors, fixed at the outer ends of the strips, and interpolate its four half-branches, within their disjoint sectors, through transverse direction pairs to the rational branches. This is an isotopy preserving the cyclic order and over/under choice. After these local adjustments, each rounded edge replacement is a sufficiently small normal graph $r=f(s)$ over the original edge in its strip, with $f=0$ at the ports. Choose the approximation so $|f|\,\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$ for a cutoff $\chi$ that is $1$ near the edge and $0$ near the strip boundary. Then $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r+t\chi(r)f(s))$, $0\le t\le1$, is a diffeomorphism in each strip, fixed at its boundary, and gives an ambient isotopy of that edge. These finitely many disk and strip isotopies paste to a compactly supported ambient isotopy of the plane. Its product with the identity in height carries a lift of $D$ to a realization of the code diagram, so the code represents the same knot $K$. The induced bijection on under-arcs preserves source, target, and overarc at each crossing because the positive over-normal and branch orientations are preserved. This finite construction uses no choice axiom.

For the knot-group comparison define $\phi:W(D)\to\operatorname{Adj}(Q(D))$ on generators by $\phi(g_a)=e_{x_a}$. The code from step 1.3 has the same under-arcs and crossing relations as $D$, so the constructor's relators in [F5] are exactly those of $W(D)$. At each crossing, $x_v=x_u*x_o$ in $Q(D)$, and the adjoint relation gives $e_{x_v}=e_{x_o}^{-1}e_{x_u}e_{x_o}$. Thus every relator of $W(D)$ maps to the identity; [F2] makes the homomorphism from the free group on its arc generators descend to $W(D)$.

The conjugation operation on $W(D)$ is idempotent because $g*g=g^{-1}gg=g$. Its right translation by $h$ is conjugation by $h^{-1}$, with inverse conjugation by $h$. It is right self-distributive because both $(g*h)*k$ and $(g*k)*(h*k)$ reduce to $k^{-1}h^{-1}ghk$. Thus $\operatorname{Conj}(W(D))$ is a quandle. Its generators $g_a$ satisfy the crossing equations by the relators of $W(D)$, so recursive evaluation of terms gives a quandle homomorphism $f:Q(D)\to\operatorname{Conj}(W(D))$. Define $\psi$ on adjoint generators by $\psi(e_q)=f(q)$. Since $f(q*r)=f(r)^{-1}f(q)f(r)$, every adjoint relator maps to the identity; [F2] therefore makes $\psi$ a group homomorphism.

By [F3], diagrams of $L$ are related by a finite sequence of these moves, and step 1.1 and step 1.2 identify the corresponding quandle presentations at each move. Their composites give an isomorphism between the two diagram quandles. Countable choice is used only for [F3]; these local presentation transformations use no choice.

The composites $\psi\phi$ fix each $g_a$. The other composite fixes each generator $e_q$: every $q\in Q(D)$ is represented by a term in the arc generators using $*$ and $\bar *$, and the adjoint relations give $e_{u*v}=e_v^{-1}e_ue_v$ and $e_{u\bar *v}=e_ve_ue_v^{-1}$, so induction on the term gives $\phi\psi(e_q)=e_q$. Hence $\phi$ and $\psi$ are inverse isomorphisms. By [F5] and step 1.3, $W(D)$ is the group of the Wirtinger constructor for a code of $K$, and is isomorphic to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$.

A **rack** is a set $R$ with a binary operation $*:R\times R\to R$ such
that for every $y\in R$ the right translation $R_y(x)=x*y$ is a bijection
and $(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$ for all $x,y,z\in R$. A **quandle** is a rack
satisfying $x*x=x$ for every $x$. For either structure, write
$x\mathbin{\bar *}y=R_y^{-1}(x)$.

For a regular oriented link diagram $D$, let $A(D)$ be its finite set of
maximal under-arcs. Form the set of finite terms recursively: each symbol
$x_a$ for $a\in A(D)$ is a term, and if $s,t$ are terms then $s*t$ and
$s\mathbin{\bar *}t$ are terms. Let $\sim$ be the intersection of all
equivalence relations on these terms that are compatible with both operations
and contain the quandle identities: idempotency, right invertibility, and
right self-distributivity, together with the crossing relations.
At a crossing with source and target under-arcs $u,v$ and overarc $o$, the
crossing relation is $x_v=x_u*x_o$; reversing source and target gives the
equivalent relation with $\bar *$. The quotient term set $Q(D)$ is the
**diagram quandle**, or the diagram presentation of the **fundamental
quandle**. Its independence of diagram is proved in the Theorem.

For any quandle $Q$, its **adjoint group** $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ is the
group presentation with generators $e_q$ for all $q\in Q$ and relators
$e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$ for all $q,r\in Q$. A group presentation
$\langle X\mid S\rangle$ means the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the
normal closure of the relator words $S$.

The diagram presentation and the adjoint group are algebraic constructions;
this definition makes no completeness or knot-classification assertion.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $D$ and $D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams.
Then $D$ and $D'$ represent equivalent oriented links if and only if $D'$ can be
obtained from $D$ by a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented
Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Define a procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

derivations.claim: Under R1, the new underarc generator $y$ satisfies either $y=x*x$ or $x=y*x$ for the unchanged arc color $x$. In the first case idempotency gives $y=x$; in the second, $x=x*x$ and right invertibility give the unique solution $y=x$. Thus the new generator is eliminated. Under R2, each added underarc generator is uniquely solved from its neighboring arc and the overarc by $*$ or $\bar *$; the reverse move gives the inverse substitution. Thus these moves are quandle Tietze transformations.

Under R3, assigning boundary colors $x,y,z$ gives the two possible iterated labels $(x*y)*z$ and $(x*z)*(y*z)$; these agree by right self-distributivity. With the over-colors fixed, each under-color substitution is invertible by right invertibility, so the reverse replacements give inverse substitutions. The same calculation for reversed crossings follows by applying the inverse right translations, which preserve both operations by self-distributivity.

For the knot-group comparison assume $L=K$. Let $\Gamma$ be the finite planar graph obtained by taking the crossings as vertices and the strand pieces between consecutive crossings as edges. Choose disjoint small disks about the crossing vertices, each meeting $D$ only in its two transverse branches, and disjoint tubular strips around the compact edge pieces outside those disks. At a crossing, oriented local coordinates straighten the branches to two transverse axes. Choose a nearby rational point and two rational direction vectors, still transverse and in the same cyclic order as the original branches; the four rational half-segments give the coded crossing and its over/under choice. Extend each edge strip a short distance into its endpoint disks through the corresponding disjoint branch sectors, and choose rational bend ports there. In each strip choose a simple rational polygonal path that is a graph in strip coordinates and joins its ports; choose it fine enough that rounding its bends gives a small normal graph over the original edge. If there are no crossings, choose a simple rational polygon in a tubular annulus of the projected circle. Since there are finitely many compact edge pieces, nonincident pieces have positive separation, and each crossing is transverse; density of $\mathbb Q^2$ and a sufficiently fine finite subdivision therefore let all vertices and bends be rational while preserving the one-circle tracing, crossing cyclic orders, orientations, and over/under data, with no other intersections. The resulting record is a valid code by [F4]; smoothing its bends in disjoint disks gives a smooth regular diagram with the same crossing data by [F6]. To compare it with $D$, move each crossing point to its nearby rational point by an isotopy supported in its disk and the short branch sectors, fixed at the outer ends of the strips, and interpolate its four half-branches, within their disjoint sectors, through transverse direction pairs to the rational branches. This is an isotopy preserving the cyclic order and over/under choice. After these local adjustments, each rounded edge replacement is a sufficiently small normal graph $r=f(s)$ over the original edge in its strip, with $f=0$ at the ports. Choose the approximation so $|f|\,\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$ for a cutoff $\chi$ that is $1$ near the edge and $0$ near the strip boundary. Then $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r+t\chi(r)f(s))$, $0\le t\le1$, is a diffeomorphism in each strip, fixed at its boundary, and gives an ambient isotopy of that edge. These finitely many disk and strip isotopies paste to a compactly supported ambient isotopy of the plane. Its product with the identity in height carries a lift of $D$ to a realization of the code diagram, so the code represents the same knot $K$. The induced bijection on under-arcs preserves source, target, and overarc at each crossing because the positive over-normal and branch orientations are preserved. This finite construction uses no choice axiom.

For the knot-group comparison define $\phi:W(D)\to\operatorname{Adj}(Q(D))$ on generators by $\phi(g_a)=e_{x_a}$. The code from step 1.3 has the same under-arcs and crossing relations as $D$, so the constructor's relators in [F5] are exactly those of $W(D)$. At each crossing, $x_v=x_u*x_o$ in $Q(D)$, and the adjoint relation gives $e_{x_v}=e_{x_o}^{-1}e_{x_u}e_{x_o}$. Thus every relator of $W(D)$ maps to the identity; [F2] makes the homomorphism from the free group on its arc generators descend to $W(D)$.

The conjugation operation on $W(D)$ is idempotent because $g*g=g^{-1}gg=g$. Its right translation by $h$ is conjugation by $h^{-1}$, with inverse conjugation by $h$. It is right self-distributive because both $(g*h)*k$ and $(g*k)*(h*k)$ reduce to $k^{-1}h^{-1}ghk$. Thus $\operatorname{Conj}(W(D))$ is a quandle. Its generators $g_a$ satisfy the crossing equations by the relators of $W(D)$, so recursive evaluation of terms gives a quandle homomorphism $f:Q(D)\to\operatorname{Conj}(W(D))$. Define $\psi$ on adjoint generators by $\psi(e_q)=f(q)$. Since $f(q*r)=f(r)^{-1}f(q)f(r)$, every adjoint relator maps to the identity; [F2] therefore makes $\psi$ a group homomorphism.

By [F3], diagrams of $L$ are related by a finite sequence of these moves, and step 1.1 and step 1.2 identify the corresponding quandle presentations at each move. Their composites give an isomorphism between the two diagram quandles. Countable choice is used only for [F3]; these local presentation transformations use no choice.

The composites $\psi\phi$ fix each $g_a$. The other composite fixes each generator $e_q$: every $q\in Q(D)$ is represented by a term in the arc generators using $*$ and $\bar *$, and the adjoint relations give $e_{u*v}=e_v^{-1}e_ue_v$ and $e_{u\bar *v}=e_ve_ue_v^{-1}$, so induction on the term gives $\phi\psi(e_q)=e_q$. Hence $\phi$ and $\psi$ are inverse isomorphisms. By [F5] and step 1.3, $W(D)$ is the group of the Wirtinger constructor for a code of $K$, and is isomorphic to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot and let $p,q$ be coprime integers, not both zero. The Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$ if and only if $q=0$, in which case $p=\pm1$ and the slope is the meridional slope $1/0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $S\subseteq N$ be a closed embedded submanifold, let $
u(S)$ be its normal bundle ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]), and let $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:\Omega	o N$ be two tubular neighbourhood embeddings of the same open disc bundle $\Omega=D(
u(S))$ whose restrictions to the zero section are the inclusion of $S$ ([[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Assume that $d\Phi_1$ and $d\Phi_2$ induce the same isomorphism from each vertical fibre $
u(S)_p$ to the ambient normal quotient $T_pN/T_pS$. (The usual normalization makes both induced maps the identity; merely fixing the zero section is insufficient.) Then, after shrinking $\Omega$ around the zero section, the two embeddings are isotopic through tubular neighbourhood embeddings fixing $S$ pointwise. Consequently, for every compact $A\subseteq S$ there is an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, compact support, $H_t\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$ (in particular $H_1\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_2$ there), and $H_t$ fixing a neighbourhood of $A$ in $S$ pointwise; when $S$ is compact one may take $A=S$ and obtain the agreement on a neighbourhood of all of $S$, with support in any prescribed neighbourhood of $\Phi_1(\Omega)\cup\Phi_2(\Omega)$.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For each $J\in\{K,K'\}$, the boundary $T_J$ is a circle bundle over the connected knot $J$ with connected fibres, hence is connected: a separation would split the boundary into saturated open sets whose projections, by local bundle charts, separate $J$. By [F10], $E_J$ is a compact smooth orientable $3$-manifold with boundary $T_J$. Since $T_J$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_J$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_J$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_J$ and $E_J$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F10]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus both exteriors are connected and, being manifolds, path-connected.

Suppose one knot is unknotted. By [F4] its standard radius-tube exterior is a solid torus with the displayed proper meridian disk. Use the ambient isotopy in the definition of unknotted to transport its chosen tube to a tube around the standard core $U$. Identify the transported and standard tube domains with the same normal bundle $
u(U)$. For each tubular embedding $\Phi_j$, its differential along the zero section induces an invertible smooth bundle map $L_j:
u(U)	o
u(U)$ on the normal quotient: invertibility follows because $\Phi_j$ is an embedding and is the identity on the zero section. Precompose $\Phi_j$ with the fibrewise map $L_j^{-1}$. After restricting to a common neighbourhood of the zero section, both induced normal maps are the identity; compactness of $U$ lets us choose one such neighbourhood for the whole core. Thus the hypotheses of [F5] hold. Under [A1], [L1] supplies its countable-choice premise, so an ambient isotopy identifies the tubes after shrinking. The standard disk transfers to the smaller chosen exterior. By [F6], the region between the smaller and original tube is a product boundary collar; trim or extend the disk across the product annulus so its boundary lies on the chosen exterior torus. The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pull that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ into the other exterior. Its parametrization is a continuous disk map with boundary in the target torus; the boundary class remains nontrivial because the boundary restriction is a homeomorphism. If the other knot were nontrivial, apply [F9] to its compact connected orientable smooth exterior (connectedness was proved in step 1.1), the whole smooth boundary torus as the boundary subsurface, and the trivial normal subgroup. The disk boundary lies in the relative interior of that torus, so [F9] gives a new smoothly properly embedded disk with essential boundary. This contradicts [F2]. No smoothing of the homeomorphic image disk and no replacement of $h$ by a diffeomorphism is required. Thus either both are unknotted or both are nontrivial.

Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. If $h$ preserves orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,w)$; if $h$ reverses orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,\overline w)$. In either case $g$ has the same orientation sign as $h$ and sends the source meridian to the target meridian. If $\phi:\partial W\to\partial E_K$ is the source gluing map, define the target gluing map by $\phi'=h\circ\phi\circ g^{-1}$. It is orientation-reversing because $\phi$ is and $g,h$ have the same sign; its meridian image is $h(\mu_K)$, so it defines the filling along $\gamma$. The maps $h$ and $g$ glue to a homeomorphism of the filled manifolds. The source filling is $S^3$, hence the target filling along $\gamma$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$. By [F1], $\gamma$ is the target meridian slope; [F7] then gives the boundary isotopy in the Statement.

If both are unknotted, [F8] gives ambient equivalences from each knot to the standard unknot; composing them gives an ambient equivalence between the knots. This conclusion is independent of whether the given $h$ preserves the knot-meridian slope.

Apply [F3] to the actual boundary restriction of $h$ and the two tubular solid tori. The extensions agree with $h$ on the common boundary and therefore glue to a homeomorphism of pairs $(S^3,K)\to(S^3,K')$. By [F3] the ambient orientation sign is the same as that of $h$. Together with steps 2.1, 2.2, and 3.1 this proves every case.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot and let $p,q$ be coprime integers, not both zero. The Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$ if and only if $q=0$, in which case $p=\pm1$ and the slope is the meridional slope $1/0$.

There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

u(S)$ be its normal bundle ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]), and let $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:\Omega	o N$ be two tubular neighbourhood embeddings of the same open disc bundle $\Omega=D(

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle

derivations.claim: For each $J\in\{K,K'\}$, the boundary $T_J$ is a circle bundle over the connected knot $J$ with connected fibres, hence is connected: a separation would split the boundary into saturated open sets whose projections, by local bundle charts, separate $J$. By [F10], $E_J$ is a compact smooth orientable $3$-manifold with boundary $T_J$. Since $T_J$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_J$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_J$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_J$ and $E_J$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F10]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus both exteriors are connected and, being manifolds, path-connected.

Suppose one knot is unknotted. By [F4] its standard radius-tube exterior is a solid torus with the displayed proper meridian disk. Use the ambient isotopy in the definition of unknotted to transport its chosen tube to a tube around the standard core $U$. Identify the transported and standard tube domains with the same normal bundle $
u(U)$. For each tubular embedding $\Phi_j$, its differential along the zero section induces an invertible smooth bundle map $L_j:
u(U)	o
u(U)$ on the normal quotient: invertibility follows because $\Phi_j$ is an embedding and is the identity on the zero section. Precompose $\Phi_j$ with the fibrewise map $L_j^{-1}$. After restricting to a common neighbourhood of the zero section, both induced normal maps are the identity; compactness of $U$ lets us choose one such neighbourhood for the whole core. Thus the hypotheses of [F5] hold. Under [A1], [L1] supplies its countable-choice premise, so an ambient isotopy identifies the tubes after shrinking. The standard disk transfers to the smaller chosen exterior. By [F6], the region between the smaller and original tube is a product boundary collar; trim or extend the disk across the product annulus so its boundary lies on the chosen exterior torus. The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pull that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ into the other exterior. Its parametrization is a continuous disk map with boundary in the target torus; the boundary class remains nontrivial because the boundary restriction is a homeomorphism. If the other knot were nontrivial, apply [F9] to its compact connected orientable smooth exterior (connectedness was proved in step 1.1), the whole smooth boundary torus as the boundary subsurface, and the trivial normal subgroup. The disk boundary lies in the relative interior of that torus, so [F9] gives a new smoothly properly embedded disk with essential boundary. This contradicts [F2]. No smoothing of the homeomorphic image disk and no replacement of $h$ by a diffeomorphism is required. Thus either both are unknotted or both are nontrivial.

Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. If $h$ preserves orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,w)$; if $h$ reverses orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,\overline w)$. In either case $g$ has the same orientation sign as $h$ and sends the source meridian to the target meridian. If $\phi:\partial W\to\partial E_K$ is the source gluing map, define the target gluing map by $\phi'=h\circ\phi\circ g^{-1}$. It is orientation-reversing because $\phi$ is and $g,h$ have the same sign; its meridian image is $h(\mu_K)$, so it defines the filling along $\gamma$. The maps $h$ and $g$ glue to a homeomorphism of the filled manifolds. The source filling is $S^3$, hence the target filling along $\gamma$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$. By [F1], $\gamma$ is the target meridian slope; [F7] then gives the boundary isotopy in the Statement.

If both are unknotted, [F8] gives ambient equivalences from each knot to the standard unknot; composing them gives an ambient equivalence between the knots. This conclusion is independent of whether the given $h$ preserves the knot-meridian slope.

Apply [F3] to the actual boundary restriction of $h$ and the two tubular solid tori. The extensions agree with $h$ on the common boundary and therefore glue to a homeomorphism of pairs $(S^3,K)\to(S^3,K')$. By [F3] the ambient orientation sign is the same as that of $h$. Together with steps 2.1, 1.2, and 3.1 this proves every case.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume AC. For a discrete group $G$, Milnor's $BG$ is connected and

$$ \pi_1(BG)\cong G,\qquad \pi_n(BG)=0\quad(n>1). $$

Consequently any connected CW model of $BG$ is an Eilenberg--Mac Lane space $K(G,1)$.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a Serre fibration over a path-connected CW complex and
let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. The skeletal filtration gives a
choice-free natural first-quadrant homological spectral sequence
$$E^2_{a,b}\cong H_a\bigl(B;\mathcal H_b(p;R)\bigr), \qquad d_r:E^r_{a,b}\longrightarrow E^r_{a-r,b+r-1},$$
strongly converging to $H_{a+b}(E;R)$ with the finite image filtration
$$F_aH_n(E;R)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_n(E_a;R)\to H_n(E;R)\bigr), \qquad 0=F_{-1}H_n\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_nH_n=H_n(E;R).$$
Its stable terms have the specified natural identifications
$$E^\infty_{a,n-a}\cong F_aH_n(E;R)/F_{a-1}H_n(E;R).$$
If $B$ is simply connected, transport between two fiber stalks is independent
of the path class, so after choosing one fiber identification the local
system is constant. The displayed spectral sequence then has
$E^2_{a,b}\cong H_a(B;H_b(F;R))$.

The chain filtration itself is not asserted to be degreewise finite. Strong
convergence follows from the argument below, not from the theorem for

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, let $\gamma,\widetilde\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, let $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, and let $\xi_0\in T_{x_0}^*\partial\Omega$ have unit norm in the induced boundary metric. Choose a sufficiently small boundary patch and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported there with $\chi=1$ near $x_0$. For every integer $N\geq1$ there are a smooth complex phase $\Phi$ in a collar of the patch and amplitudes $b_{\lambda,\gamma}$, $b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$, defined for $\lambda\geq1$, such that
$$v_{\lambda,\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\gamma},\qquad v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma},$$
have boundary values $\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\phi}\chi$, where $\phi$ is real with $|d\phi|=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, have $H^1(\Omega)$ norms bounded above and below by positive constants, and satisfy
$$\|\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} +\|\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
Here $\phi=\Phi|_{\partial\Omega}$ is real, $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$, and $\operatorname{Im}\Phi$ is comparable to the inward distance to the boundary on the collar. Let $u_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ be the exact conductivity solutions with the same respective boundary values. Their corrections satisfy
$$\|u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$ and continuous $F$ on $\overline\Omega$, choosing $N>k$ gives
$$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^k \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k F(x) \nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}}\,dx =c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,\qquad c_k=2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{k!}{2^k}>0.$$
The same limit holds with $v_{\lambda,\gamma},v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ replaced by their exact corrections.

derivations.claim:
Fix $x_0\in\partial\Omega$ and a sufficiently small patch. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported in the patch and equal to one near $x_0$, and use [F3] to construct approximate beams for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ with the same boundary trace. Let $u_{\lambda,j}$ be their exact conductivity solutions. Equality of the DN maps and [F2] give
$$\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_{\lambda,1}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\lambda,2}}\,dx=0.$$
Replacing each exact solution by its approximate beam changes this integral by $O(\lambda^{-N})$: the coefficient is bounded, the beam $H^1$ norms are uniformly bounded, and each exact correction is $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$ by [F3].

Set $k=0$ in [F3] and let $\lambda\to\infty$ in step 1.1. Since $c_0>0$,
$$\int_{\partial\Omega}(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)|\chi|^2\,dS=0.$$
If $\gamma_1-\gamma_2$ were positive or negative at any boundary point, continuity would give a patch on which it has that strict sign; choosing $\chi$ supported in that patch and equal to one near the point would make this integral nonzero. Thus $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Fix an integer $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $\partial_{x_n}^j(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)=0$ on a boundary patch for every $j<k$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the inward normal coordinate gives
$$\gamma_1(y,x_n)-\gamma_2(y,x_n)=x_n^kF_k(y,x_n),\qquad F_k(y,0)=\frac{\partial_{x_n}^k(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)(y,0)}{k!},$$
for a smooth $F_k$. Apply [F2] to the exact beams from [F3], replace them by their approximate beams, and multiply the resulting integral identity by $\lambda^k$. The replacement error is $O(\lambda^{k-N})$, since the weight $x_n^k$ is bounded and the corrections are $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$. Choose $N>k$ and apply the weighted limit in [F3]; then
$$c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F_k(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2\,dS(y)=0.$$
Since $c_k>0$, the same localized sign argument as in step 1.2 gives $F_k(y,0)=0$ throughout the patch. Therefore the $k$th inward normal derivatives agree there.

Step 1.2 is the base case for the induction. Step 2.1 proves each subsequent order on a patch that may be chosen around any prescribed boundary point. Thus every boundary point has a neighborhood on which the order-$k$ normal derivative difference is zero for every integer $k\geq0$, proving the full boundary-jet assertion.
