The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary. Write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. Let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite, so some $0<c\le C<\infty$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le \xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

The weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is the bilinear-form candidate $\Lambda_\gamma:\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega\to\mathbb R$ given, whenever the weak solution exists, by

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

where $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$ is any representative of $h$. The local anisotropic conductivity well-posedness lemma proves existence and uniqueness for every boundary class, independence of the representative $V_h$, and boundedness on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$; it therefore makes this candidate a bounded bilinear map. The map is the boundary energy form for the equation $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla u)=0$. Under the trace-quotient isomorphism and the local boundedness result, this form gives the usual weak map into the dual $H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ with the scalar convention.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary, let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le\xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for fixed $0<c\le C<\infty$, and let $f\in\mathcal B_\Omega=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the boundary trace-data class defined by the anisotropic weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. Then there is a unique $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and $\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla v\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. The energy formula defining $\Lambda_\gamma$ is independent of the chosen representative of its second boundary argument and is a bounded bilinear form on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

For smooth $F:M\to N$ and a Riemannian metric $h$ on $N$, its **pullback tensor** is $(F^*h)_p(v,w)=h_{F(p)}(dF_pv,dF_pw)$.

This is [[def-pullback-of-a-covariant-tensor-field]] for the tensor in [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]. It is always symmetric and positive semidefinite; the name does not assert positive definiteness. Smoothness and the precise immersion criterion are established next.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

In the Riemannian setting of the statement, the chain rule [F3] gives $d(u\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T(du\circ\Phi)$ in a coordinate chart, while [F8] gives $(\Phi^*g)=D\Phi^T(g\circ\Phi)D\Phi$. Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\varphi=\sigma x_1$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$. For $0<h\leq h_0$ define
$$P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}.$$
There is a constant $C$ such that every $w\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|P_{\varphi,h,q}w\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
Moreover, for every $F\in L^2(M)$ there is an $R\in L^2(M)$ solving $P_{\varphi,h,q}R=F$ in distributions on $M^\circ$ and satisfying
$$\|R\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
No boundary trace is prescribed for $R$.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

Put $\Phi=x_1+i\psi$. By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$,
$$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$
Direct conjugation gives
$$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$
The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. Hence the residual is $e^{-\tau\Phi}(-\Delta_g+q)a$.

Set $h=\tau^{-1}$ and conjugate by the real weight $e^{-\tau x_1}$. The equation for the correction is
$$P_{x_1,h,q}r_\tau=-h^2e^{-i\tau\psi}(-\Delta_g+q)a.$$
The right side is in $L^2$ and has norm $h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2$. By [F4]--[F5], with the equation divided by $h^2$, there is an $H^1$ correction (and hence a distributional) $r_\tau\in L^2(M)$ with
$$\|r_\tau\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2 =C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2.$$
Thus the asserted remainder estimate and the equation hold distributionally.

Choose the $H^1$ correction from step 1.2. Multiplication by the smooth exponentials preserves $H^1(M)$ for each fixed $\tau$, and the correction equation cancels the residual computed in step 1.1. Thus $u_\tau$ is exact, has the stated remainder bound, and has no imposed correction boundary value. The additional boundary regularity is the external input [F4], rather than a consequence asserted for the $L^2$ solver [F2].

boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

derivations.claim: Put $\Phi=x_1+i\psi$. By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$, $$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$ Direct conjugation gives $$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$ The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. Hence the residual is $e^{-\tau\Phi}(-\Delta_g+q)a$.

Set $h=\tau^{-1}$ and conjugate by the real weight $e^{-\tau x_1}$. The equation for the correction is $$P_{x_1,h,q}r_\tau=-h^2e^{-i\tau\psi}(-\Delta_g+q)a.$$ The right side is in $L^2$ and has norm $h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2$. By [F4]--[F5], with the equation divided by $h^2$, there is an $H^1$ correction (and hence a distributional) $r_\tau\in L^2(M)$ with $$\|r_\tau\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2 =C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2.$$ Thus the asserted remainder estimate and the equation hold distributionally.

Choose the $H^1$ correction from step 2.1. Multiplication by the smooth exponentials preserves $H^1(M)$ for each fixed $\tau$, and the correction equation cancels the residual computed in step 1.1. Thus $u_\tau$ is exact, has the stated remainder bound, and has no imposed correction boundary value. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

derivations.claim: For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$.

For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$: independence of the prior element from the noise element and independence within each coordinate family factor the probabilities of finite coordinate rectangles into the product of the pair marginals, and [F5] extends this factorization from the generating rectangles to the corresponding product-Borel events. Each $Y_j$ is a measurable function of its pair $(\theta_j,\xi_j)$, so $(\theta_J,Y_J)$ is independent of $Y_{J^c}$. For the finite block, put $D_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_j^2)_{j\in J}$ and $D_s=\operatorname{diag}(s_j)_{j\in J}$. [F2] gives posterior covariance
$$D_\tau-D_\tau D_s^T(D_sD_\tau D_s^T+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}D_sD_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(v_j)_{j\in J},$$
and posterior mean with coordinates $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$. Since each $v_j>0$, the Gaussian coordinates have zero cross-covariance, and repeated application of [F10] shows they are independent. Thus the finite-block conditional law is the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1. Independence of the complement makes this also the conditional law given the full data: the conditional identity first holds on data rectangles by finite-block conditioning and independence, and [F5] extends it to all product-Borel data events. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space.

Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation.

For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed.

Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity.

For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate.

$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

derivations.claim: For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$.

For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$: independence of the prior element from the noise element and independence within each coordinate family factor the probabilities of finite coordinate rectangles into the product of the pair marginals, and [F5] extends this factorization from the generating rectangles to the corresponding product-Borel events. Each $Y_j$ is a measurable function of its pair $(\theta_j,\xi_j)$, so $(\theta_J,Y_J)$ is independent of $Y_{J^c}$. For the finite block, put $D_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_j^2)_{j\in J}$ and $D_s=\operatorname{diag}(s_j)_{j\in J}$. [F2] gives posterior covariance $$D_\tau-D_\tau D_s^T(D_sD_\tau D_s^T+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}D_sD_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(v_j)_{j\in J},$$ and posterior mean with coordinates $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$. Since each $v_j>0$, the Gaussian coordinates have zero cross-covariance, and repeated application of [F10] shows they are independent. Thus the finite-block conditional law is the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1. Independence of the complement makes this also the conditional law given the full data: the conditional identity first holds on data rectangles by finite-block conditioning and independence, and [F5] extends it to all product-Borel data events. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space.

Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation.

For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed.

Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity.

For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $X_d(R)$ be the BV conductivity class for $d=2$ and the bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ class for $d\ge3$, with the same ellipticity and background collar in both cases. Then $X_2(R)$ is compact in $L^1(\Omega)$ and each $X_d(R)$ for $d\ge3$ is compact in $C^1(\overline\Omega)$. In dimension two there is an exponent $q>2$ and a constant $C$ such that
$$\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)}\le C\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\qquad(\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_2(R));$$
for $d\ge3$ the same kernel map is continuous in the $C^1(\overline\Omega)$ topology. Consequently the exact kernel image $\{\kappa_\gamma:\gamma\in X_d(R)\}$ is compact in $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, and let $X_d(R)$, $\kappa_\gamma$ and the concave modulus $\omega_\star$ be as in the mean-zero NTD observation and Hilbert extension statements. Regard $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ as a real Hilbert space with its complex $L^2$ norm. The exact-data inverse map
$$\Psi^\star:\{\kappa_\gamma:\gamma\in X_d(R)\}\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)=\gamma,$$
is well-defined and satisfies
$$\|\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)-\Psi^\star(\kappa_{\gamma_0})\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)}\le\omega_\star(\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)}).$$
Consequently the Hilbert-valued extension from the preceding theorem agrees with $\Psi^\star$ on the exact kernel image and retains this stability bound on the whole underlying real Hilbert space of complex-valued kernels. Each exact NtD kernel is real-valued, but the extension domain includes all complex-valued kernels.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A\subseteq H_1$, and let $g:A\to H_2$. If a continuous, nondecreasing, concave function $\omega_\star:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfies $\omega_\star(0)=0$ and
$$\|g(x)-g(y)\|_{H_2}\le\omega_\star(\|x-y\|_{H_1})\qquad(x,y\in A),$$
then the Hilbert-valued same-modulus extension theorem asserts that there is $\widetilde g:H_1\to H_2$ extending $g$ and satisfying the same inequality for every $x,y\in H_1$.

For the EIT inverse map, take the kernel input space to be $L^2(\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega;\mathbb C)$ viewed as a real Hilbert space with its usual complex $L^2$ norm. If IP-45 gives $\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_2\le C_0[\log(1/\min\{\delta,t_0\})]^{-\rho}$ for $\delta=\|\dot\Lambda_\gamma-\dot\Lambda_{\gamma_0}\|$, and the NTD kernel estimate transfers $\delta\le C_1\|\kappa_\gamma-\kappa_{\gamma_0}\|_2^{1/2}$, then after decreasing $t_0$ and, if necessary, enlarging $C_0$ the concave modulus
$$\omega_\star(0)=0,\qquad \omega_\star(s)=C_0\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{C_1\sqrt{s},t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(s>0)$$
is an admissible modulus for that inverse map and can be extended by the Hilbert same-modulus theorem to the whole underlying real Hilbert space of complex-valued kernels.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M=\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega$ for a nonempty bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, and let $a,b\in\mathbb N$ be positive finite channel dimensions. If $T:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)$ is continuous, then for every compact set $C\subset L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a generalized Fourier neural operator $\Psi:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)$ using a fixed smooth globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation and the boundary charts of the statement such that
$$\sup_{h\in C}\|T(h)-\Psi(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $K_\delta=\varnothing$ or $X_d(R)=\varnothing$, choose the zero generalized FNO; the uniform assertion is then vacuous. Otherwise, [A1] applies at the upstream conductivity, spectral and extension interfaces. [F1] and compactness of $K_\delta$ make $$Z_\delta:=\mathcal K_X+K_\delta=\{\kappa+\eta:\kappa\in\mathcal K_X,\ \eta\in K_\delta\}$$ compact in complex $L^2$, since it is the continuous image of $\mathcal K_X\times K_\delta$ under addition. The isometric realification $\mathfrak R(Z_\delta)$ is therefore compact in $L^2(M\times M;\mathbb R^2)$.

Apply [F4] to the continuous real-valued map $\widetilde\Psi^\star\circ\mathfrak R^{-1}$ on the compact set $\mathfrak R(Z_\delta)$ with tolerance $\varepsilon$. There is a two-input-channel generalized FNO $\Phi$ with $\sup_{z\in Z_\delta}\|\widetilde\Psi^\star(z)-\Phi(\mathfrak R z)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)}<\varepsilon$.

For $\gamma\in X_d(R)$ and $\eta\in K_\delta$, use [F2], the triangle inequality and monotonicity of $\omega_\star$ to obtain
$$\begin{aligned} \|\gamma-\Phi(\mathfrak R(\kappa_\gamma+\eta))\|_2 &\le\|\widetilde\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)-\widetilde\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma+\eta)\|_2\\ &\quad+\|\widetilde\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma+\eta)-\Phi(\mathfrak R(\kappa_\gamma+\eta))\|_2\\ &\le C_\star\omega_\star(\|\eta\|_2)+\varepsilon\\ &\le C_\star\omega_\star(\delta)+\varepsilon. \end{aligned}$$
Here $\widetilde\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)=\gamma$ because the extension agrees on the exact real kernel image, and the complex $L^2$ norm is preserved by $\mathfrak R$. Taking the supremum gives the claim.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\geq3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded smooth domain contained in a ball $B(0,R)$, and let $q\in L^\infty(\Omega,\mathbb C)$. There are constants $C>0$ and $\tau_0\geq1$, depending only on $n$, $R$, and $\|q\|_{L^\infty}$, such that for every $\zeta\in\mathbb C^n$ satisfying $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ and $|\zeta|\geq\tau_0$, there is $r_\zeta\in H^1(\Omega,\mathbb C)$ for which
$$u_\zeta(x)=e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta(x))$$
solves $(-\Delta+q)u_\zeta=0$ distributionally in $\Omega$, and
$$\|r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C|\zeta|^{-1}\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|\nabla r_\zeta\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\leq C\|q\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
The dot product in the null-phase condition is complex bilinear, and $|\zeta|=(\sum_{j=1}^n|\zeta_j|^2)^{1/2}$.
Assume AC. Finite complex Borel measures $\mu,\nu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with $\widehat\mu=\widehat\nu$ are equal. Here finite means finite total variation, and $n\ge1$.

derivations.claim: Set $Q=q_1-q_2$. For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ and define the Hermitian weak forms $a_j(v,w)=\int_\Omega(\nabla v\cdot\nabla\overline w+q_jv\overline w)\,dx$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(\Omega)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the two weak pairings gives $\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle=\int_\Omega Q u_1\overline{u_2}\,dx$. The maps agree on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, so this integral vanishes. This establishes the weak-trace extension of [F1] used here.

Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $n\geq3$, choose orthonormal $\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb R^n$ perpendicular to $\xi$; when $\xi=0$, choose any orthonormal pair. For $\tau\geq1$, set $\sigma_\tau=(\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4)^{1/2}$ and
$$\zeta_1=\tau\omega_1+i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2,\qquad \zeta_2=-\tau\omega_1-i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2.$$
The orthogonality gives $\zeta_j\cdot\zeta_j=\tau^2-\sigma_\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4=0$, $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=\xi$, and $|\zeta_j|\to\infty$. Apply [F2] to $q_1$ with phase $\zeta_1$ and to $q_2$ with phase $-\overline{\zeta_2}$; the latter is null, and reality of $q_2$ lets us conjugate the resulting solution. Thus
$$u_1=e^{i\zeta_1\cdot x}(1+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{-i\overline{\zeta_2}\cdot x}(1+r_2),\qquad \|r_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=O(\tau^{-1}).$$
Substitute in step 1.1. Since $Q\in L^2(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$,
$$\left|\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\big(r_1+\overline{r_2}+r_1\overline{r_2}\big)\,dx\right| \leq \|Q\|_2(\|r_1\|_2+\|r_2\|_2)+\|Q\|_\infty\|r_1\|_2\|r_2\|_2=O(\tau^{-1}).$$
Taking $\tau\to\infty$ proves $\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\,dx=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$.

Define the finite complex Borel measure $\mu(E)=\int_{E\cap\Omega}Q(x)\,dx$ on $\mathbb R^n$. It has finite total variation because $\Omega$ is bounded and $Q$ is bounded. The identity in step 2.1 gives $\widehat\mu(\eta)=0$ for every $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$ (take $\xi=-2\pi\eta$). By [F3], $\mu=0$. Hence $\int_E\operatorname{Re}Q\,dx=\int_E\operatorname{Im}Q\,dx=0$ for every Borel $E$; applying this to the sets $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\geq1/m\}$, $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\leq-1/m\}$, and their imaginary-part analogues shows $Q=0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $Q$ gives $Q=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

Since $Q\in L^2(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$, $$\left|\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\big(r_1+\overline{r_2}+r_1\overline{r_2}\big)\,dx\right| \leq \|Q\|_2(\|r_1\|_2+\|r_2\|_2)+\|Q\|_\infty\|r_1\|_2\|r_2\|_2=O(\tau^{-1}).$$ Taking $\tau\to\infty$ proves $\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\,dx=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$.

Define the finite complex Borel measure $\mu(E)=\int_{E\cap\Omega}Q(x)\,dx$ on $\mathbb R^n$. It has finite total variation because $\Omega$ is bounded and $Q$ is bounded. The identity in step 2.1 gives $\widehat\mu(\eta)=0$ for every $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$ (take $\xi=-2\pi\eta$). By [F3], $\mu=0$. Hence $\int_E\operatorname{Re}Q\,dx=\int_E\operatorname{Im}Q\,dx=0$ for every Borel $E$; applying this to the sets $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\geq1/m\}$, $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\leq-1/m\}$, and their imaginary-part analogues shows $Q=0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $Q$ gives $Q=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention. Input a prior covariance $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ symmetric positive semidefinite, a finite ordered list of raw candidate records $(A_d,\Gamma_d,c_d)_{d=1}^N$, and a real budget $B$. Each stored $A_d$ and $\Gamma_d$ is a finite real matrix, with its dimensions part of the input, and each declared cost $c_d$ is finite and real. A candidate is dimension-valid when $A_d$ has at least one row and exactly $n$ columns and $\Gamma_d$ is a symmetric square matrix whose dimension equals the row count of $A_d$; for a dimension-valid candidate write that common positive dimension as $m_d$. The prior mean is immaterial to the score.

Interpret each admissible candidate $d$ (dimension-valid with $\Gamma_d$ positive definite) as a separate singleton-design dominated inverse experiment with prior $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ for any $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, observation space $\mathbb R^{m_d}$ with Lebesgue measure, and observation $Y_d=A_d\theta+\eta_d$, where $\eta_d\sim N_{m_d}(0,\Gamma_d)$ is independent of $\theta$. Here $\operatorname{EIG}(d)$ is the expected information gain from the preceding definition for that singleton experiment. Different candidates may have different $m_d$ because each is evaluated on its own observation space. The score is independent of $m_0$.

In exact-real arithmetic, process the list in order. Mark a candidate inadmissible if it is not dimension-valid or if its noise covariance $\Gamma_d$ is not positive definite. For each remaining candidate with $c_d\le B$, compute the Cholesky factor $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ with positive diagonal, solve $L_dV_d=A_d$ by forward substitution, and form the symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$. Set $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ and compute its Cholesky factor $H_d=R_dR_d^T$. Assign the utility
$$U_d=\sum_{j=1}^{m_d}\log (R_d)_{jj}-c_d=\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)-c_d.$$
Initialize the stored best candidate as unset. For each admissible candidate meeting the budget, set it if unset; otherwise replace it exactly when the new utility is strictly greater than the stored utility. After the scan, return the stored candidate. This update rule preserves the first index in any tie. If every candidate is inadmissible, return `all-inadmissible`; if at least one candidate is admissible but none meets the budget, return `budget-exhausted`.

In floating-point mode, treat each finite stored floating-point matrix entry, cost, budget, and tolerance as the exact real number represented by that value; no uncertainty in these input data is included. Use failure-aware Cholesky and triangular-solve procedures, and take a certificate provider as part of the floating-point input. Each provider result is a finite, independently checkable certificate; if the provider cannot certify a required fact, it returns `unresolved`.

Process the candidates in list order. Test dimensions and symmetry exactly, marking a dimension-invalid candidate inadmissible. For each dimension-valid noise matrix $\Gamma_d$, call `CertifyPositiveDefiniteness(\Gamma_d)`. It returns `positive-definite` only with a checkable positive-definiteness certificate, `not-positive-definite` only with a checkable certificate, or `unresolved`. For example, an exact factorization $\Gamma_d=L L^T$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal certifies positive definiteness, while a nonzero vector $v$ with $v^T\Gamma_dv\le0$ certifies that it is not positive definite. A failed rounded Cholesky factorization is not a certificate of non-positive-definiteness. If any required status is unresolved, return `numerically-unresolved`. After all statuses are certified, return `all-inadmissible` if none is admissible. Compare each admissible stored cost to the stored budget exactly; if none meets it, return `budget-exhausted`.

For each feasible candidate $d$ in inherited order, call `CertifyScore(d)`. It first runs failure-aware rounded Cholesky on $\Gamma_d$ and, on success, failure-aware forward substitution on each column of $A_d$ in order; any operation failure or unmet range hypothesis returns `unresolved`. After forming a certified positive-semidefinite $\widehat Z_d$, it forms a stored matrix $\widehat H_d$ and certifies both that $\widehat H_d$ is symmetric positive definite and that $\|\widehat H_d-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\sigma_d$ for a rational bound $\sigma_d\ge0$. It then runs failure-aware rounded Cholesky on $\widehat H_d$; a failed definiteness check, factorization, or formation bound returns `unresolved`. The call then returns either `certified` with finite stored values $\widehat U_d$, $\widehat Z_d$, and $\widehat R_d$, nonnegative rational upper bounds $\delta_d,\rho_d,\lambda_d$, and certificates for all of the following, or `unresolved`:

- $\widehat Z_d$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d$, where $Z_d$ uses the exact Cholesky factor of the represented $\Gamma_d$. This bound includes rounding in forming the Cholesky factor and triangular solve for $\Gamma_d$, the covariance square root, and the matrix products.
- $\widehat R_d$ is a successful lower-triangular Cholesky factor with positive diagonal. If $\widetilde\rho_d$ is a certified upper bound for $\|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-\widehat H_d\|_2$, choose a rational $\rho_d\ge\widetilde\rho_d+\sigma_d$ with $\rho_d<1$; then $\|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d$.
- $\left|\widehat U_d-\left(\frac12\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-c_d\right)\right|\le\lambda_d$. Evaluate the exact expression as $\sum_j\log((\widehat R_d)_{jj})-c_d$ using the triangular determinant identity; $\lambda_d$ covers rounded logarithms, their summation, and cost evaluation.

The matrix radius may be certified by the published information-matrix perturbation bound in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I_n$ case. Factor $C$ as $C^{1/2}C^{1/2}$ and set $J_d=C^{1/2}V_d^T$; for a computed solve $\widehat V_d$, set $\widehat J_d=C^{1/2}\widehat V_d^T$. Then $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$ and $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$. The lemma's finite-design hypotheses hold for the one-point sensitivity maps $z\mapsto J_dz$ and $z\mapsto\widehat J_dz$ from $\mathbb R^{m_d}$ to $\mathbb R^n$, with weight $W=I_n$ and design weight $1$. If $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d$ may be any verified bound at least $2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$, enlarged by any separate matrix-formation residual. A rounded triangular-substitution bound may be used only after checking its $(m_d+3)u<1$ and normal-range, finite-operation hypotheses for every right-hand side. Convert its backward-error bound to the required forward matrix bound using verified conditioning; a solve backward-error bound alone does not certify $\eta_d$. For the published rounded-Cholesky normwise bound, verify success and its operationwise model, put $q=20m_d+20$ and $g=qu/(1-qu)$, and check $qu<1/5$ before using $100g\|\widehat R_d\|_F^2$ as a residual bound; if using its relative bound, also check $100\sqrt{m_d}g\le1/2$. The log-determinant perturbation bound is applied on the two symmetric matrix segments with eigenvalue floors $1$ and $1-\rho_d$. A missing or failed certificate returns `numerically-unresolved` and no optimum claim.

Set $\varepsilon_d=\frac{m_d}{2}\left(\delta_d+\frac{\rho_d}{1-\rho_d}\right)+\lambda_d$ and form the exact rational interval $[\widehat U_d-\varepsilon_d,\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_d]$. Given a finite nonnegative stored tolerance $\tau$, compute $M=\max_{d\text{ feasible}}\widehat U_d$ and return the first feasible candidate with $\widehat U_d\ge M-\tau$. Certify the comparisons exactly on the represented floating-point values and rational bounds; if any comparison needed for this branch or for its interval certificate is undecided, return `numerically-unresolved`. The returned candidate's true utility gap is at most $\tau+2\max_d\varepsilon_d$. If its lower interval endpoint exceeds every earlier candidate's upper endpoint and is at least every later candidate's upper endpoint, certify it as the first exact maximizer. The algorithm makes no bit-complexity claim for exact-real comparisons.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite and let
$A=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal.

1. For every right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$, the system $Ax=b$ is solved by
   first solving $Ly=b$ and then solving $L^*x=y$.
2. The two triangular solves cost $2n^2+O(n)$ scalar operations altogether, and
   the dense Cholesky factorisation costs
   $$\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   scalar operations, compared with
   $$\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   for dense LU factorisation without exploiting symmetry.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Use the finite observation designs of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]]. Suppose uniformly over $x\in\mathcal X$ that $\|J_x\|_2\le K$, $\|J_{h,x}-J_x\|_2\le\eta$, and $\|W_x\|_2\le w$, where $K,\eta,w\ge0$. For every approximate design $\xi$,
$$\|M_h(\xi)-M(\xi)\|_2\le\delta:=w(2K\eta+\eta^2),$$
where $M_h(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xJ_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}$. If $M(\xi)$ satisfies $v^TM(\xi)v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v$ with some $\alpha>\delta$, then
$$v^TM_h(\xi)v\ge(\alpha-\delta)\|v\|_2^2$$
for every $v$, so the computed information matrix remains positive definite.

Let $p\ge1$ and let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric. Put $E=B-A$ and $A_t=(1-t)A+tB$ for $0\le t\le1$. Suppose there is $\alpha>0$ such that $v^T A_t v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $t\in[0,1]$. Then $A_t$ is positive definite and
$$|\log\det B-\log\det A|\le\frac{p\|E\|_2}{\alpha}.$$

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A=A^*$ be positive definite in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. Suppose the rounded Cholesky algorithm succeeds with $\widehat L$. Put $m=20n+20$ and $g=\gamma_m=\frac{m u}{1-m u}$; assume $m u<1/5$. For $E=\widehat L\widehat L^*-A$, which is Hermitian, and with $|M|$ denoting entrywise absolute value for matrices,
$$|E|\le100g\,|\widehat L|\,|\widehat L|^*\quad\hbox{entrywise},\qquad \|E\|_F\le100g\|\widehat L\|_F^2,\qquad \|E\|_2\le100g\|\widehat L\|_F^2.$$
Thus $c_n(u)u=\frac{100m u}{1-m u}$. If also $100\sqrt n\,g\le1/2$, then
$$\|E\|_F\le200\sqrt n\,g\|A\|_F,\qquad \|E\|_2\le200\sqrt n\,g\|A\|_F.$$
These bounds apply on success only; positive definiteness does not guarantee rounded success.

Let $R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be upper triangular with stored floating-point entries and nonzero diagonal, and let $y\in\mathbb R^n$ have stored floating-point entries, where $n\ge1$ and $(n+3)u<1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]] at unit roundoff $u$. Compute descending substitution by the sequential rounded dot $s_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{j>i}R_{ij}\widehat x_j)$ (empty sum zero), $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(y_i-s_i)$, and $\widehat x_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/R_{ii})$. Assume each exact intermediate is zero or normal and each rounded result is finite, so every operation succeeds under that model. Then there is upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(R+\Delta R)\widehat x=y,\qquad |\Delta R|\le\gamma_{n+3}|R|,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|R\|_F.$$
In particular $\widehat x=0$ forces $y=0$. Forward substitution has the transposed conclusion.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: For a valid candidate, $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ and $V_d=L_d^{-1}A_d$, so $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Hence $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ is positive definite and has the Cholesky factor used by the exact algorithm.

Put $Q_d=A_dCA_d^T$ and $W_d=\Gamma_d^{-1/2}$. The square-root identity [F5] gives $\Gamma_d+Q_d=\Gamma_d^{1/2}(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)\Gamma_d^{1/2}$. By [F4], $\det(\Gamma_d+Q_d)=\det(\Gamma_d^{1/2})^2\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)=\det(\Gamma_d)\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)$. Also step 1.1 gives $\Gamma_d+Q_d=L_dH_dL_d^T$, so [F3]–[F4] give $\det(\Gamma_d+Q_d)=\det(\Gamma_d)\det(H_d)$ with $\det(\Gamma_d)=(\det L_d)^2>0$. Dividing proves $\det(I_{m_d}+W_dQ_dW_d)=\det(H_d)$. By [F2], the exact EIG is $\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)$. By [F3], $\det(H_d)=\det(R_dR_d^T)=(\prod_j(R_d)_{jj})^2$; all Cholesky diagonal entries are positive, so [F10] gives $\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)=\sum_j\log(R_d)_{jj}$. Thus the algorithm's exact score equals $U_d$.

For the exact scan, after the first feasible candidate the stored candidate is the first maximum of that one-element prefix. When the next candidate is processed, [F1] says a strictly larger score replaces it; an equal or smaller score leaves it in place, preserving the earliest maximizing index. Repeating this finite comparison through the ordered feasible list proves the final stored candidate is the first global maximizer. The validity and budget tests likewise make `all-inadmissible` and `budget-exhausted` exactly the two stated empty-feasible-set cases.

In floating-point mode, when $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$ and $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$, [F6] supplies $\delta_d\ge2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$ from certified bounds $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$; any rounded matrix-formation residual is included in the supplied $\delta_d$. Both $I+Z_d$ and $I+\widehat Z_d$ have eigenvalues at least $1$, and every matrix on their segment does too. Applying [F7] gives $|\log\det(I+\widehat Z_d)-\log\det(I+Z_d)|\le m_d\delta_d$.

Put $E_d=\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I+\widehat Z_d)$. Every matrix $I+\widehat Z_d+tE_d$ has quadratic form at least $(1-t\rho_d)\|v\|_2^2\ge(1-\rho_d)\|v\|_2^2$, since $I+\widehat Z_d\succeq I$ and $\|E_d\|_2\le\rho_d<1$. Applying [F7] on this segment yields $|\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-\log\det(I+\widehat Z_d)|\le m_d\rho_d/(1-\rho_d)$. Under the successful rounded-factorization hypotheses, [F8] provides such a residual radius. [F9] supplies only a backward-error constraint for triangular solves; any forward matrix error used in $\delta_d$ must additionally account for conditioning.

The certificate's $\lambda_d$ bounds the remaining rounded log, summation, and cost evaluation. Combining it with steps 3.1–3.2, the log-determinant perturbation [F7], and the factor $1/2$ in the EIG formula gives $|\widehat U_d-U_d|\le\varepsilon_d$.

Let $d^*$ maximize exact utility and let $\widehat d$ be the selected computed $\tau$-maximizer. By [F1] and the hypothesis, $\widehat U_{\widehat d}\ge\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau$. Then $U_{d^*}\le\widehat U_{d^*}+\varepsilon_{d^*}\le\max_d\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_{d^*}$, while $U_{\widehat d}\ge\widehat U_{\widehat d}-\varepsilon_{\widehat d}\ge\max_d\widehat U_d-\tau-\varepsilon_{\widehat d}$. Subtracting gives the stated gap bound.

If the selected interval's lower endpoint exceeds each earlier upper endpoint and is at least each later upper endpoint, then every earlier exact utility is strictly smaller and every later exact utility is no larger. Thus the selected candidate is the first exact maximizer.
