The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. A nontangential maximal geodesic segment is a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$, with $L>0$, whose initial velocity points strictly inward at $\partial M_0$, whose terminal velocity points strictly outward at $\partial M_0$, and whose points for $0<t<L$ lie in $M_0^\circ$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(M_0^\circ,\mathbb R)$ define its geodesic ray transform by $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=\int_0^L f(\gamma(t))\,dt$. The unweighted scalar ray transform is called injective on compactly supported smooth functions if $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=0$ for every such segment implies $f=0$. For complex-valued $f$, injectivity means injectivity of its real and imaginary parts separately.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$ be a unit-speed nontangential geodesic segment. For every real $\lambda$ and every $K>0$, there is a family $v_{\tau+i\lambda}\in C^\infty(M_0)$, $\tau\geq1$, such that
$$\|(-\Delta_{g_0}-(\tau+i\lambda)^2)v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(\tau^{-K}),\qquad \|v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(1),$$
and for every $\psi\in C(M_0)$,
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_{M_0}|v_{\tau+i\lambda}|^2\psi\,dV_{g_0} =\int_0^L e^{-2\lambda t}\psi(\gamma(t))\,dt.$$
The statement permits transversal manifolds without an orientability assumption and makes no boundary condition assertion for the quasimodes.

derivations.claim: For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ and define $a_j(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla_gv,\nabla_g\overline w)+q_jv\overline w)\,dV_g$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(M)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the weak pairings and using equality of the DN maps on all $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ gives $\int_M Q(x_1,x')u_1(x_1,x')\overline{u_2(x_1,x')}\,dV_g=0$, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. This derives the needed weak-trace extension of [F2]. Because $q_j\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ and $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$, extension of $Q$ by zero gives a smooth compactly supported function on $\mathbb R\times M_0$.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, put $s=\tau+i\lambda$, and choose the beam $v_s$ of [F6] with residual $O(\tau^{-K})$. Use the signed real-weight solver [F5] to obtain exact solutions
$$u_1=e^{-s x_1}(v_s+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{s x_1}(v_s+r_2)$$
for the respective potentials, with $r_j\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_j\|_2=O(\tau^{-1})$. Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Applying [F6] proves the attenuated ray identity for every $\lambda$ and every nontangential $\gamma$. This argument works on the base manifold; it does not assume injectivity of a ray transform on its orientation cover.

Step 2.1 supplies
$$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$
where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$. At $\lambda=0$, [F3] gives $\widehat Q_0=0$. Assume inductively that $\partial_\lambda^j\widehat Q_0=0$ for every $j<k$. Differentiate the ray identity $k$ times at $\lambda=0$. Differentiation under the finite geodesic integral is valid because $Q$ is smooth with compact $x_1$ support. Leibniz' rule leaves the unweighted ray integral of $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0$; all other terms contain lower derivatives and vanish by the induction hypothesis. Thus [F3], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0=0$. Induction proves that every Taylor coefficient of $\lambda\mapsto\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ vanishes for each fixed $x'$.

For each fixed $x'$, compact $x_1$ support makes $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ entire in $\lambda$, so its zero Taylor series implies it vanishes for all real $\lambda$. This is the Fourier transform of the $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function $Q(\cdot,x')$ at every frequency $2\lambda$; [F4] gives $Q(\cdot,x')=0$ almost everywhere. Smoothness of $Q$ then yields $Q=0$ on $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. A nontangential maximal geodesic segment is a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$, with $L>0$, whose initial velocity points strictly inward at $\partial M_0$, whose terminal velocity points strictly outward at $\partial M_0$, and whose points for $0<t<L$ lie in $M_0^\circ$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(M_0^\circ,\mathbb R)$ define its geodesic ray transform by $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=\int_0^L f(\gamma(t))\,dt$. The unweighted scalar ray transform is called injective on compactly supported smooth functions if $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=0$ for every such segment implies $f=0$. For complex-valued $f$, injectivity means injectivity of its real and imaginary parts separately.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$ be a unit-speed nontangential geodesic segment. For every real $\lambda$ and every $K>0$, there is a family $v_{\tau+i\lambda}\in C^\infty(M_0)$, $\tau\geq1$, such that
$$\|(-\Delta_{g_0}-(\tau+i\lambda)^2)v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(\tau^{-K}),\qquad \|v_{\tau+i\lambda}\|_{L^2(M_0)}=O(1),$$
and for every $\psi\in C(M_0)$,
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_{M_0}|v_{\tau+i\lambda}|^2\psi\,dV_{g_0} =\int_0^L e^{-2\lambda t}\psi(\gamma(t))\,dt.$$
The statement permits transversal manifolds without an orientability assumption and makes no boundary condition assertion for the quasimodes.

derivations.claim: For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ and define $a_j(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla_gv,\nabla_g\overline w)+q_jv\overline w)\,dV_g$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(M)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the weak pairings and using equality of the DN maps on all $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ gives $\int_M Q(x_1,x')u_1(x_1,x')\overline{u_2(x_1,x')}\,dV_g=0$, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. This derives the needed weak-trace extension of [F2]. Because $q_j\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ and $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$, extension of $Q$ by zero gives a smooth compactly supported function on $\mathbb R\times M_0$.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, put $s=\tau+i\lambda$, and choose the beam $v_s$ of [F6] with residual $O(\tau^{-K})$. Use the signed real-weight solver [F5] to obtain exact solutions $$u_1=e^{-s x_1}(v_s+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{s x_1}(v_s+r_2)$$ for the respective potentials, with $r_j\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_j\|_2=O(\tau^{-1})$. Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Applying [F6] proves the attenuated ray identity for every $\lambda$ and every nontangential $\gamma$. This argument works on the base manifold; it does not assume injectivity of a ray transform on its orientation cover.

Step 2.1 supplies $$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$ where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$. At $\lambda=0$, [F3] gives $\widehat Q_0=0$. Assume inductively that $\partial_\lambda^j\widehat Q_0=0$ for every $j<k$. Differentiate the ray identity $k$ times at $\lambda=0$. Differentiation under the finite geodesic integral is valid because $Q$ is smooth with compact $x_1$ support. Leibniz' rule leaves the unweighted ray integral of $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0$; all other terms contain lower derivatives and vanish by the induction hypothesis. Thus [F3], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0=0$. Induction proves that every Taylor coefficient of $\lambda\mapsto\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ vanishes for each fixed $x'$.

For each fixed $x'$, compact $x_1$ support makes $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ entire in $\lambda$, so its zero Taylor series implies it vanishes for all real $\lambda$. This is the Fourier transform of the $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function $Q(\cdot,x')$ at every frequency $2\lambda$; [F4] gives $Q(\cdot,x')=0$ almost everywhere. Smoothness of $Q$ then yields $Q=0$ on $M$.

citations.quote:
Assume countable choice. Let $\Sigma\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ be a compact smooth oriented cobordism from an oriented knot $K_0$ to an oriented knot $K_1$, with fixed product collars and fixed endpoint diagrams. Every generic movie $M$ of $\Sigma$ defines a map of bidegree $(0,\chi(\Sigma))$,
$$
Kh(M):Kh^{i,j}(K_0)\longrightarrow Kh^{i,j+\chi(\Sigma)}(K_1),
$$
where $\chi(\Sigma)$ is the Euler characteristic of the surface and the integral even Khovanov groups use the normalized crossing shifts. If two such movies represent cobordisms related by an ambient isotopy fixed on the boundary collars, their maps differ by multiplication by a single overall sign, independent of the input class. The resulting assignment is a functor after each morphism group is quotiented by the relation identifying a map with its negative; before that quotient the sign is not canonical.

Let $(W,\Sigma,\mathcal A)$ be a decorated knot cobordism from $(Y_0,K_0)$ to $(Y_1,K_1)$, and fix $\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$. Choose a parametrized Kirby decomposition of $W$, together with admissible Heegaard data and regular almost-complex structures for its elementary pieces. Intermediate pieces may contain links with several components or more than one pair of basepoints. Use the colored multipointed modules with $g+n-1$ attaching curves in $\operatorname{Sym}^{g+n-1}(S)$, and specialize all $w$-colors to $U$ and all $z$-colors to $V$; the displayed doubly pointed formula is the $n=1$ case. For a piece represented by a subordinate Heegaard triple $(S,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma,w,z)$, its triangle-count map has the form
$$
\mathbf x\longmapsto \sum_{\mathbf y}\ \sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\Theta^+_{\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\gamma},\mathbf y)\\ \mu(\phi)=0,\ \mathfrak s(\phi)=\mathfrak s}} \#_2\bigl(\mathcal M(\phi)\bigr)U^{n_w(\phi)}V^{n_z(\phi)}\mathbf y,
$$
where $\Theta^+_{\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\gamma}$ denotes a chosen cycle representative of the distinguished top-degree homology class of the appropriate standard auxiliary Heegaard pair, $\mathfrak s(\phi)$ is the Spin-c structure determined by the triangle class, and the other symbols and coefficient ring are as in the two-color target definition. For a chosen auxiliary cycle with finite support $\Theta=\sum_j p_j\theta_j$, with $p_j\in\mathbb F_2[U,V]$ and basis generators $\theta_j$, interpret the displayed formula by $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$-linearity as $\sum_j p_j F(\mathbf x,\theta_j)$ (or $\sum_j p_j F(\theta_j,\mathbf x)$ for the alpha-triple convention). The elementary 2-handle maps and band maps are triangle-count maps; the 0-, 1-, 3-, and 4-handle maps use the corresponding stabilization or destabilization maps; cylindrical changes of the dividing set use basepoint and quasi-stabilization maps. Compose the elementary maps in the chosen decomposition to obtain a representative
$$
\widetilde F_{W,\Sigma,\mathcal A,\mathfrak s,\mathcal K}: CFL^-_{UV}(Y_0,K_0,\mathfrak s|_{Y_0})\longrightarrow CFL^-_{UV}(Y_1,K_1,\mathfrak s|_{Y_1}).
$$
The subscript $\mathcal K$ records the chosen decomposition and auxiliary data. This is one map for one Spin-c structure; maps for different Spin-c structures are not summed unless a sum is explicitly specified. Independence from $\mathcal K$, regular data, and parametrization is a separate naturality assertion.

Let $(W,\Sigma,\mathcal A)$ be a decorated knot cobordism between doubly pointed knots in $S^3$, and let $\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$. The representative maps from any two parametrized Kirby decompositions and admissible regular Heegaard choices are filtered $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$-equivariantly chain homotopic. If the decorated cobordism is a composite of $(W_1,\Sigma_1,\mathcal A_1)$ followed by $(W_2,\Sigma_2,\mathcal A_2)$, then for fixed Spin-c structures $\mathfrak s_i$ on $W_i$,
$$
\widetilde F_{W_2,\Sigma_2,\mathcal A_2,\mathfrak s_2}\circ \widetilde F_{W_1,\Sigma_1,\mathcal A_1,\mathfrak s_1} \simeq \sum_{\substack{\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)\\ \mathfrak s|_{W_i}=\mathfrak s_i,\ i=1,2}} \widetilde F_{W,\Sigma,\mathcal A,\mathfrak s}.
$$
The sum is over Spin-c structures on the glued cobordism restricting to the specified structures on the two pieces. For $W=S^3\times[0,1]$, $\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$ has one element, so the sum has one term and the composition law is ordinary composition up to filtered equivariant chain homotopy.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the smooth oriented surface. Its target is ordinary even integral $Kh^{i,j}$, and identifying a map with its negative removes exactly the one sign ambiguity. Its isotopy and composition conclusions are the first assertion of the Statement.

For the separately decorated surface apply [F2], coloring all w-regions by $U$ and z-regions by $V$. The intermediate multiply based link modules and their endpoint naturality identifications are part of that construction. Zero curvature makes the endpoint objects the specified complexes, and external Theorem A gives filtered equivariant chain-homotopy invariance. This assertion has coefficient field $\mathbb F_2$ and its own decoration and Spin-c data; no integral Khovanov sign ambiguity or comparison between the two theories is transferred to it.

The general composition law is the extension sum in [F2]. On $S^3\times[0,1]$ the Spin-c set has one element, so composition has one term. Combining the two independently established assignments proves the entire Statement with its distinct targets, coefficients and equivalence relations. It asserts neither equality of the functors nor a canonical chain-level top generator, and requires no new local reconstruction of the imported Cerf checks.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $S\subseteq M$ be an embedded submanifold.

Equip $S$ with the smooth structure supplied by
[[lem-slice-chart-restrictions-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. The inclusion
$i:S\hookrightarrow M$ is then a smooth embedding by
[[prop-the-inclusion-of-an-embedded-submanifold-is-a-smooth-embedding]], so its
differential is defined. Identify $T_pS$ with the linear subspace
$di_p(T_pS)\subseteq T_pM$. Here the notation
$$TM|_S:=\coprod_{p\in S}T_pM,\qquad T^*M|_S:=\coprod_{p\in S}T_p^*M$$
means the fibrewise restriction of these disjoint unions to base points in
$S$; it does not invoke restriction to an open subset.

The **normal-bundle set** of $S$ in $M$ is the fibrewise quotient

$$\nu(S):=\coprod_{p\in S}T_pM/T_pS.$$

The **conormal-bundle set** of $S$ in $M$ is the fibrewise annihilator

$$N^*S:=\{\xi\in T^*M|_S:\xi|_{T_pS}=0\text{ for the base point }p\}.$$

Both are intrinsic constructions attached to the embedding $S\hookrightarrow M$.
The next proposition supplies their smooth vector-bundle structures.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Under countable choice [A1], [F5] supplies a product tubular map and a closed product disk tube with the stated norm and radius data for every smooth oriented knot.

Write $D_r^2=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:|z|\le r\}$ in the product coordinates and set $U=\Phi(S^1\times\{|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$ and $V=S^3\setminus\Phi(S^1\times D^2_{\epsilon/2})$. The set $U$ is open because its source is open in the tubular domain and $\Phi$ maps that domain diffeomorphically onto an open set. The removed disk image is compact, hence closed in Hausdorff $S^3$, so $V$ is open. They cover $S^3$, and $U\cap V=\Phi(S^1\times\{\epsilon/2<|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$.

Radial homotopies retract $U$ onto $N(K)$ by replacing each fibre radius $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\min(r,\epsilon)$, fixing the zero vector; retract $V$ onto $E_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\max(r,\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon/2<r<2\epsilon$ and fixing points outside the product tube; and retract $U\cap V$ onto $T_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\epsilon$. Each formula remains within its domain, agrees with the identity at the relevant boundary, and fixes its target. Thus these are deformation retractions.

On the overlap, composing its inclusion into $U$ with the first retraction gives radius $\min(r,\epsilon)$, while retracting first to $T_K$ and including into $N(K)$ gives radius $\epsilon$; linear interpolation stays in $N(K)$. For the inclusion into $V$, the corresponding radii are $\max(r,\epsilon)$ and $\epsilon$, and their interpolation stays in $E_K$. Hence, after the deformation-retraction identifications, the two maps in Mayer–Vietoris are the maps induced by $T_K\hookrightarrow N(K)$ and $T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$. By [F7], homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on homology.

By [F9], the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the open cover of step 2.1 has the segment $$H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U\cap V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z).$$ The outer groups vanish by [F6], so the middle map is an isomorphism. Under the identifications of step 4.1, it is induced by the two boundary inclusions.

By [F8], $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ with basis $([\mu],[\sigma])$. The product tube $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$ retracts to its core $S^1$ by contraction in each disk fibre, so homotopy invariance [F7] and [F6] give $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. Put $H=H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Steps 3.1–5.1 give $\mathbb Z^2\cong\mathbb Z\oplus H$. The isomorphism embeds $H$ as a subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$. Every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$ is free of rank at most two: projection to one coordinate has cyclic image; if nonzero, choose a preimage of its positive generator to split it off, and the kernel is a subgroup of $\mathbb Z$; if zero, the subgroup already lies in $\mathbb Z$. Since the complementary $\mathbb Z$ has rank one and the total rank is two, $H$ has rank one. Therefore $H\cong\mathbb Z$.

Choose $c$ to be the first component of the Mayer–Vietoris image of $[\sigma]$; it is a generator of $H_1(N(K);\mathbb Z)$ because the product section projects with degree one to the core of the product tube [F5, F8]. Choose a generator $h$ of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, which exists by step 6.1. The meridian maps to zero in the $N(K)$ component because it bounds its fibre disk. In the bases $([\mu],[\sigma])$ and $(c,h)$, the Mayer–Vietoris isomorphism of step 5.1 has first column $(0,a)$ for some integer $a$ and second column whose first coordinate is $1$. Its determinant is therefore $\pm a$; since the map is an isomorphism over $\mathbb Z$, $a=\pm1$. Thus $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer with $i_*[\sigma]=k[\mu]$, and put $[\lambda]=[\sigma]-k[\mu]$. Then $i_*[\lambda]=0$, $p_*[\lambda]=1$, and the change from the basis $([\mu],[\sigma])$ to $([\mu],[\lambda])$ has determinant $1$. In the new basis, $i_*(a[\mu]+b[\lambda])=a[\mu]$, so the kernel is exactly $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, a primitive rank-one direct summand. Every degree-one class is $[\sigma]+a[\mu]$ and maps to zero exactly when $a=-k$, proving uniqueness. The curve $t\mapsto(e^{2\pi it},e^{-2\pi ikt})$ is embedded in $S^1\times S^1$ because its first coordinate is injective on $S^1$; it represents $[\lambda]$ and is a preferred longitude.

Write $D_r^2=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:|z|\le r\}$ in the product coordinates and set $U=\Phi(S^1\times\{|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$ and $V=S^3\setminus\Phi(S^1\times D^2_{\epsilon/2})$. The set $U$ is open because its source is open in the tubular domain and $\Phi$ maps that domain diffeomorphically onto an open set. The removed disk image is compact, hence closed in Hausdorff $S^3$, so $V$ is open. They cover $S^3$, and $U\cap V=\Phi(S^1\times\{\epsilon/2<|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$.

Radial homotopies retract $U$ onto $N(K)$ by replacing each fibre radius $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\min(r,\epsilon)$, fixing the zero vector; retract $V$ onto $E_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\max(r,\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon/2<r<2\epsilon$ and fixing points outside the product tube; and retract $U\cap V$ onto $T_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\epsilon$. Each formula remains within its domain, agrees with the identity at the relevant boundary, and fixes its target. Thus these are deformation retractions.

On the overlap, composing its inclusion into $U$ with the first retraction gives radius $\min(r,\epsilon)$, while retracting first to $T_K$ and including into $N(K)$ gives radius $\epsilon$; linear interpolation stays in $N(K)$. By [F9], the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the open cover of step 1.2 has the segment $$H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U\cap V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(U;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S^3;\mathbb Z).$$ The outer groups vanish by [F6], so the middle map is an isomorphism. citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Let a balanced sutured manifold be taut. For a specified coherent orientation class, its integral sutured Floer homology has a direct summand isomorphic to the integers. More precisely, a finite good taut hierarchy terminating in product balls induces a split inclusion of the terminal product homology into the original homology, with orientation classes induced along the cuts.

Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, let $F$ be a genus-$g$ Seifert surface, and let $(M,\gamma)$ be the balanced sutured manifold obtained by cutting the compact exterior of $K$ along $F$. For a surface-adapted admissible sutured Heegaard diagram, the generator correspondence between the top Alexander summand of the knot Floer complex and the sutured Floer disk-count module identifies their disk-count differentials. Under the hypotheses of a horizontal decomposition, the induced chain map realizes Ni's horizontal decomposition formula. Under the hypotheses of a separating product annulus with connected $R_+$ and $R_-$, the induced chain map realizes Ni's product-annulus tensor formula. These assertions use the specified basepoint domains, periodic-domain admissibility, and exact characteristic-product-region hypotheses; they make no claim that generic Heegaard disk existence alone supplies the decomposition maps.

For the actual marked Seifert surface of genus g, oriented as minus the fiber for the cut, an adapted generator x has Alexander degree g minus the number of its interior polygon coordinates. Thus the top degree-g generators are exactly the outer generators and correspond to the cut diagram generators with their ordered intersection signs. If the integral top homology is one copy of the integers, the actual cut incidence matrix is unimodular, the cut is an integral homology product, and its periodic-domain group vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

For an actual weakly admissible balanced sutured diagram on a surface with boundary, the integral disk complex exists for each specified coherent orientation class. Its disk, triangle and quadrilateral moduli spaces admit finite signed counts and the corresponding oriented boundary identities on actual weakly admissible multidiagrams. Sphere and one-torus boundary bubbles are excluded by the zero boundary-region multiplicities. Orientation classes are transported rather than declared equivalent.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix a finite collection of admitted compact marked sutured diagrams, a finite sequence of diagram moves or surface cuts, and finite-dimensional parameter families of dimension at most two. Suppose the local Fredholm, finite-dimensional Sard, compactness and gluing constructions are supplied for their actual Cauchy–Riemann operators, including the prescribed endpoint and protected-neighborhood conditions. All selections needed to apply those constructions, choose coherent determinant orientations, and obtain simultaneous regular data can then be made under Countable Choice. In particular no uncountable choice of analytic charts or regular data is needed for these fixed finite integral Floer constructions.

derivations.claim: Choose a Seifert surface F realizing the least genus g=g(K), and let E be the compact exterior. The exterior is irreducible: a sphere in its interior bounds two balls in S³ by F1; the connected knot neighborhood lies entirely on one side, so the other ball is disjoint from it and lies in E. A small oriented meridian loop meets F once, so F is nonseparating: a separating two-sided surface would have algebraic intersection zero with every closed loop. Cut E along the connected F to obtain connected M with the product annular suture and the two F faces. Their Euler characteristics agree and the boundary meets that suture, so M is balanced. A sphere in M is disjoint from F in E. Its E-ball is also disjoint from F: since F is connected, disjoint from the sphere, and has its boundary on ∂E outside that interior ball, it lies entirely on the other side. Thus that ball remains a ball in M. This proves irreducibility of the actual cut without a general-Y irreducibility assertion.

The two faces are incompressible. A compression of F along a nonseparating essential circle produces a connected Seifert surface of genus g−1. A separating compression produces a boundary-bearing Seifert component and a closed component. The latter has positive genus, since otherwise the original compression circle bounded a disk on F; discarding it again gives a Seifert surface of genus strictly less than g. Both contradict minimality. A face compression in M would be such a compression in E. For g=0 the disk has no essential compression circle.

To prove the actual sutured norm-minimality, take any compact oriented properly embedded competitor T representing the positive face class in H₂(M,γ;Z). Its total oriented boundary in H₁(γ;Z) is one copy of the longitude. Put its boundary circles in the interior of the annular suture. Cap an innermost contractible boundary circle by its disk in the annulus, pushed into the boundary collar; this operation increases Euler characteristic and cannot increase the Thurston complexity. Continue until every boundary circle is essential. Whenever both orientations remain, choose an adjacent opposite pair. The annulus between them contains no other boundary circle. Glue it to T in a thin boundary collar and round the corners. This gives an embedded oriented surface and removes the pair. Euler characteristic is unchanged; if two components merge, the inequality max(0,−(χ₁+χ₂))≤max(0,−χ₁)+max(0,−χ₂) shows that total complexity cannot increase. For two circles on one component its Euler characteristic, hence complexity, is unchanged. The finite sequence ends with exactly one essential boundary circle, since its total winding is one. Delete all closed components, which also cannot increase complexity. The remaining connected surface embeds in E and extends across the knot collar to an actual Seifert surface for K of the same genus. Its genus is at least g by minimality. For g≥1 its complexity is therefore at least 2g−1=x(F); for g=0 it is at least zero=x(F). It follows that x(T)≥x(F). The same argument applies to the negative face. Thus M is the actual taut balanced sutured manifold, by irreducibility and norm-minimality. The boundary cancellations were used only to derive a lower bound and need not preserve the competitor's relative class after it is mapped to E.

Work under the full-Choice analytic framework F6 on the actual fixed finite hierarchy and marked adapted diagram. Its admitted sutured operator problems retain the boundary/divisor barriers, periodic-domain and area conditions and the specified coherent orientation class. With the regular data and compactification/gluing construction supplied at that scope, apply F3 to the marked Seifert surface F. Its meridional frame, rather than an unspecified closure framing, gives an admissible adapted representative. By F4 every generator has Alexander degree g−n_P(x), with n_P(x) a nonnegative integer. Hence its whole integral chain complex has no generator, and thus no homology, in a grading greater than g.

The entire degree-g summand is the outer summand, and F3 identifies its signed differential with the actual cut complex of M. Since M is taut, F2 gives that this cut homology contains a split copy of Z for the orientation class induced by the given knot complex. Consequently the integral knot Floer group at degree g is nonzero. This also covers g=0: the taut cut argument and the same signed chain map apply to the minimum disk, without a genus-one connected-sum or field-coefficient substitution.

Degree g is nonzero and every larger degree is zero, so the maximum of the stated nonvanishing degree set is exactly g(K). The proof uses only the literal S³ ball-side and minimum-Seifert-genus arguments above; it makes no claim of arbitrary general-Y Thurston norm detection.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth properly embedded disk with boundary knot
$K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$. Choose a product tubular neighborhood
$\nu(D)\cong D^2\times D^2$ whose intersection with $S^3$ is the chosen tube
$N(K)$, and let $X=\overline{B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu(D)}$. Then the
inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
carrying the positive meridian of $K$ to the positive normal-circle generator.

A smooth $f:M\to N$ is an immersion if $df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ is injective for every $p$, using the full tangent spaces. It is an embedding if it is an immersion and a homeomorphism onto its image. No neatness, properness, closed-image, or boundary-preservation condition is included.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Suppose $D\subset B_1$ is a smooth proper slice disk for $K$. Its oriented
normal $2$-plane bundle is trivial because $D$ is a disk. Choose a nowhere-zero
normal section and push $D$ slightly along it to a parallel disk $D'$ in the
exterior $X$ of a tubular neighborhood of $D$. The boundary $K'$ is a
degree-one parallel of $K$ in $E_K$, and it bounds $D'$ in $X$. By [F3], its
class in $H_1(E_K)$ is zero. By [F2], it is the preferred longitude.

A tubular neighborhood of $D$ is $D^2\times D^2$ and meets the other
hemisphere $B_2$ in the attaching region $S^1\times D^2$. Consequently
$B_2\cup\nu(D)$ is obtained from a $4$-ball by attaching one $0$-framed
$2$-handle along $K$, hence is diffeomorphic to $X_0(K)$ by [F1]. This union
is a smooth codimension-zero submanifold of $S^4$.

Conversely, suppose $i:X_0(K)\hookrightarrow S^4$ is a smooth
codimension-zero embedding. In the $0$-handle of $X_0(K)$ take the cone on $K$
from an interior point $p$, and join that cone disk to the core disk
$D^2\times\{0\}$ of the $2$-handle along their common boundary $K$. After
smoothing the join, this is a piecewise-smooth embedded $2$-sphere, smooth
away from the cone point $p$.

In oriented coordinates at $p$ and $i(p)$, the derivative of $i$ is
invertible by [F4], because its differential is injective and both dimensions
are four. By [F5], $i$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$. If its local
orientation sign is negative, compose it with a fixed orientation-reversing
reflection of the standard $S^4$; this preserves the existence of the
embedding and makes the local sign positive. Thus its derivative $A$ lies in
$\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$.

Identify the cone near $p$ with the radial cone on $K\subset S^3$. Along
each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target
distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative
uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for
all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$,
followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where
$\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to
the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite
$P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the
connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The
chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of
$\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection
restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$.
It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has
degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a
diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that
section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$.

Choose the coordinate ball bounded by that small sphere. Its complement
$W=S^4\setminus\operatorname{int}(B_\epsilon)$ is a standard $4$-ball. The
image sphere is smooth away from the cone point; transversality makes its
remainder after deleting the cone cap a smooth properly embedded disk in $W$
with product boundary collar and boundary $\Gamma_\epsilon$. Append the trace
annulus of the isotopy in step 2.3 inside a boundary collar of $W$, with the
isotopy stationary near its ends. The result is a smooth slice disk with
boundary exactly $K$.

citations.quote: Fix the orientation-reversing involution $r:S^3\to S^3$ given by reflection across a fixed equatorial two-sphere containing a chosen standard unknot $U$. For a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, its mirror is $\overline K:=r(K)$, with the orientation transported by $r$. A diagram of the mirror can be obtained by keeping the projected shadow fixed and interchanging the over- and under-crossing data at every crossing; equivalently, one may reflect the planar shadow while retaining the crossing data. These are alternative mirror conventions, not operations to perform together. Since $r^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $r(U)=U$, mirroring twice returns $K$, and $K$ is the unknot exactly when $\overline K$ is.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

Assume full AC. For every smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, there is a finite spectral sequence of abelian groups whose $E_2$ page, after forgetting the Khovanov bigrading, is $\widetilde{Kh}(\overline K;\mathbb Z)$ and which converges to $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. The intermediate pages are not asserted to be knot invariants.

Assume full AC. For every smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, the rational sutured instanton knot homology $KHI(K;\mathbb Q)$ is finite-dimensional and has dimension at least one; it has dimension one if and only if $K$ is the unknot. Moreover, excision gives an isomorphism $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Q)\cong KHI(K;\mathbb Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

derivations.claim: Suppose $\widetilde{Kh}(K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ as a total graded group. Set $J=\overline K$. By [F1], $\overline J=K$. The $E_2$ group in [A1] for $J$ is therefore $\mathbb Z$, so its rationalization has dimension one.

Put $S=\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Localization $S^{-1}(-)=(-)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ preserves exact sequences: if $f:A\to B$ is injective and $f(a)/s=0$, some $t\in S$ has $f(ta)=0$, hence $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$; if $g:B\to C$ follows $f$ and $g(b)/s=0$, choose $t\in S$ with $tb\in\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, say $f(a)=tb$, so $b/s=f(a)/(ts)$; if $g$ is surjective, each $c/s$ is the image of a lift divided by $s$. Thus localization commutes with kernels, images, and homology.

The spectral sequence in [A1] is obtained by taking successive homology pages of a finite filtered complex. Exact localization therefore identifies its rationalized pages with the pages of the rationalized filtered complex, and identifies the localized abutment with $I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)$. The $E_2$ page has rational dimension one by step 1.1.

On each finite-dimensional rational page, the next page is homology. For any differential $d$ on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, rank-nullity gives $\dim H(V,d)=\dim V-2\dim\operatorname{im}d\le\dim V$. Iterating this inequality over the finite spectral sequence bounds the total dimension of $E_\infty$ by its one-dimensional $E_2$ page; since the finite abutment filtration has associated graded $E_\infty$, its total dimension equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q} I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)\le1$.

By [A2], this target has dimension at least one, so it has dimension one. The rank-detection clause of [A2] implies that $\overline K$ is the unknot; applying the same reflection gives that $K$ is the unknot.

Conversely, for the crossingless one-circle unknot diagram the reduced complex has the single generator from [F2] and no differential. Its total cohomology is therefore $\mathbb Z$ in bidegree $(0,0)$. This proves the converse and hence the stated equivalence.

citations.quote: Fix the orientation-reversing involution $r:S^3\to S^3$ given by reflection across a fixed equatorial two-sphere containing a chosen standard unknot $U$. For a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, its mirror is $\overline K:=r(K)$, with the orientation transported by $r$. A diagram of the mirror can be obtained by keeping the projected shadow fixed and interchanging the over- and under-crossing data at every crossing; equivalently, one may reflect the planar shadow while retaining the crossing data. These are alternative mirror conventions, not operations to perform together. Since $r^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $r(U)=U$, mirroring twice returns $K$, and $K$ is the unknot exactly when $\overline K$ is.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

Assume full AC. For every smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, there is a finite spectral sequence of abelian groups whose $E_2$ page, after forgetting the Khovanov bigrading, is $\widetilde{Kh}(\overline K;\mathbb Z)$ and which converges to $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. The intermediate pages are not asserted to be knot invariants.

Assume full AC. For every smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, the rational sutured instanton knot homology $KHI(K;\mathbb Q)$ is finite-dimensional and has dimension at least one; it has dimension one if and only if $K$ is the unknot. Moreover, excision gives an isomorphism $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Q)\cong KHI(K;\mathbb Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

derivations.claim: Suppose $\widetilde{Kh}(K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ as a total graded group. Set $J=\overline K$. By [F1], $\overline J=K$. The $E_2$ group in [A1] for $J$ is therefore $\mathbb Z$, so its rationalization has dimension one.

Put $S=\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Localization $S^{-1}(-)=(-)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ preserves exact sequences: if $f:A\to B$ is injective and $f(a)/s=0$, some $t\in S$ has $f(ta)=0$, hence $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$; if $g:B\to C$ follows $f$ and $g(b)/s=0$, choose $t\in S$ with $tb\in\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, say $f(a)=tb$, so $b/s=f(a)/(ts)$; if $g$ is surjective, each $c/s$ is the image of a lift divided by $s$. Thus localization commutes with kernels, images, and homology.

The spectral sequence in [A1] is obtained by taking successive homology pages of a finite filtered complex. Exact localization therefore identifies its rationalized pages with the pages of the rationalized filtered complex, and identifies the localized abutment with $I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)$. The $E_2$ page has rational dimension one by step 1.1.

On each finite-dimensional rational page, the next page is homology. For any differential $d$ on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, rank-nullity gives $\dim H(V,d)=\dim V-2\dim\operatorname{im}d\le\dim V$. Iterating this inequality over the finite spectral sequence bounds the total dimension of $E_\infty$ by its one-dimensional $E_2$ page; since the finite abutment filtration has associated graded $E_\infty$, its total dimension equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q} I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)\le1$.

By [A2], this target has dimension at least one, so it has dimension one. The rank-detection clause of [A2] implies that $\overline K$ is the unknot; applying the same reflection gives that $K$ is the unknot.

Conversely, for the crossingless one-circle unknot diagram the reduced complex has the single generator from [F2] and no differential. Its total cohomology is therefore $\mathbb Z$ in bidegree $(0,0)$. This proves the converse and hence the stated equivalence.

finite_checks.claim: The crossingless one-circle quotient has a single Z generator in bidegree (0,0).
A one-dimensional E2 page gives total E-infinity dimension at most one; finite convergence identifies this with abutment dimension.
