The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$, let
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ have length at least two, and let $b,b'$ be any two
based meridian-longitude word systems used in the preceding definition. Then
the based residue candidates $\bar\mu_L^b(I)$ and $\bar\mu_L^{b'}(I)$ agree
under the canonical identification of their residue groups. If $L$ and $L'$ are
related by a finite sequence of self-crossing changes, the same residue is
preserved whenever the entries of $I$ are pairwise distinct. No invariance for
repeated-index sequences under self-crossing changes is asserted.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and give $C=D^2\times[0,1]$ the product orientation. An $r$-component string link is an ordered family of pairwise disjoint smooth proper embeddings $\tau_i:[0,1]\to C$, for $1\le i\le r$, with fixed distinct endpoints $\tau_i(0)=(p_i,0)$ and $\tau_i(1)=(p_i,1)$ and fixed product collars at the endpoints. Orient each interval from bottom to top. The exterior $X_\tau$ is obtained by removing the relative interiors of chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes around the intervals. The bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$ are the copies of $D^2$ with the interiors of the endpoint tube disks removed.

Choose a basepoint on the outer boundary of $P_-$, a path in the side boundary of $C$ to the corresponding top basepoint, and basing paths from these points to the component meridians. Each end inclusion, with the chosen connecting path for the top end, induces a based homomorphism $\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For each string component choose a parallel path on its tube boundary from the bottom endpoint to the top endpoint, and choose access paths that close it to a based loop using the fixed side connector. The resulting element of $\pi_1(X_\tau)$ is its based string-link longitude; the parallel and access paths are part of the peripheral datum. The positively oriented boundaries of the endpoint tube disks are the designated meridian loops. Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars; closure joins each top endpoint to the matching bottom endpoint outside $C$ and retains the component labels.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedded submanifold, and let $Y$ be a
smooth vector field along $S$, meaning that $Y(p)\in T_pM$ for each $p\in S$
and $Y$ depends smoothly on $p$ in slice charts. Then:

1. there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $S$ in $M$ and a smooth vector field
   $\widetilde Y$ on $U$ with $\widetilde Y|_S=Y$;
2. if $S$ is closed in $M$, then there is a global smooth vector field
   $\widehat Y$ on $M$ with $\widehat Y|_S=Y$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $A$ be a closed subset of a smooth manifold $M$, and let $U\subseteq M$ be open with $A\subseteq U$. Then there exists a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that $f=1$ on an open neighbourhood of $A$ and $\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq U$.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ such that

$$ \bigcup_{t\in J}\operatorname{supp}(X_t) $$

is contained in a compact subset $K\subseteq M$. Then there is a global evolution
operator $\Psi_{t,s}:M\to M$ for all $s,t\in J$.

derivations.claim: Let $\tau_t$ be the given smooth isotopy through string links, fixed on common endpoint collars. Reparametrize it to be stationary near $t=0,1$. Choose fixed disjoint smooth closure arcs outside $C=D^2\times[0,1]$, using the closure construction in the based-string-link definition, and adjoin them to the moving intervals. The result is a smooth family of closed links in $S^3$, constant on the closure arcs and endpoint collars; extend it constantly in time outside $[0,1]$. The map $\Theta:\mathbb R\times\bigsqcup_i S^1\to\mathbb R\times S^3$, $\Theta(t,s)=(t,\overline\tau_t(s))$, is an injective immersion and is proper: injectivity and immersion follow from the time coordinate and the embedding of each link slice, while the preimage of a compact set lies in a compact time interval times the finite union of circles. Thus its image is a closed embedded submanifold. The vector field $Y(t,\overline\tau_t(s))=(0,\partial_t\overline\tau_t(s))$ along this graph is smooth and vanishes on the fixed closure arcs and endpoint collars. Since the motion is confined to a compact subinterval of each string component away from its endpoint collars, choose a compact set $K\subset\operatorname{int}C$ containing every point where this velocity can be nonzero. By [A1] and [L1], [F4] extends $Y$ to a global smooth vector field on $\mathbb R\times S^3$. Let $X_t$ be its $S^3$ component. By [F5] choose $\chi:S^3\to[0,1]$ equal to one near $K$ and supported in $\operatorname{int}C$, and replace $X_t$ by $\chi X_t$. This field still equals the prescribed velocity along the entire closed link: it is unchanged wherever the velocity is nonzero and is zero on the stationary arcs. Its supports lie in the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset\operatorname{int}C$. Integrate it by [F6]. Uniqueness of the flow gives an ambient isotopy $H_t$ with $H_t\overline\tau_0=\overline\tau_t$; its support in $\operatorname{int}C$ makes $H_t$ the identity near $\partial C$, so it preserves $C$ and fixes the endpoint collars, bottom basepoint, and side connector. This is the relative based isotopy-extension argument for string links.

Restricting $H_1$ gives a based homeomorphism of string-link exteriors that transports the selected tubes, positive meridians, parallels, and access paths. It fixes the endpoint basepoints and side connector, so the two end inclusions commute with the induced based group isomorphisms. By [F1], the longitude has a unique preimage in each finite bottom-end quotient; naturality carries that preimage to the corresponding class for the isotopic string link. The Magnus expansion is the same homomorphism on the transported meridian symbols, so every integer coefficient agrees.

Under [A1], an ambient isotopy of closed links induces the peripheral correspondence in [F3]. Applying that correspondence to the based word-lift data gives the transported based residue candidate. The first assertion of [F2] proves independence of every meridian basing and finite longitude-word lift, with exactly equal lower-coefficient ideals. Applying it to the transported word data proves that the two closed-link residues agree in the same residue group.

Under [A1], a link-homotopy is generated by ambient isotopies and self-crossing changes. For pairwise-distinct indices, ambient isotopy is handled by step 2.1 and each self-crossing change is the second assertion of [F2]. Each move identifies the lower-coefficient ideals by [F2]; composing these finitely many equalities proves the asserted residue equality. No repeated-index conclusion is drawn.

expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$, let
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ have length at least two, and let $b,b'$ be any two
based meridian-longitude word systems used in the preceding definition. Then
the based residue candidates $\bar\mu_L^b(I)$ and $\bar\mu_L^{b'}(I)$ agree
under the canonical identification of their residue groups. If $L$ and $L'$ are
related by a finite sequence of self-crossing changes, the same residue is
preserved whenever the entries of $I$ are pairwise distinct. No invariance for
repeated-index sequences under self-crossing changes is asserted.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and give $C=D^2\times[0,1]$ the product orientation. An $r$-component string link is an ordered family of pairwise disjoint smooth proper embeddings $\tau_i:[0,1]\to C$, for $1\le i\le r$, with fixed distinct endpoints $\tau_i(0)=(p_i,0)$ and $\tau_i(1)=(p_i,1)$ and fixed product collars at the endpoints. Orient each interval from bottom to top. The exterior $X_\tau$ is obtained by removing the relative interiors of chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes around the intervals. The bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$ are the copies of $D^2$ with the interiors of the endpoint tube disks removed.

Choose a basepoint on the outer boundary of $P_-$, a path in the side boundary of $C$ to the corresponding top basepoint, and basing paths from these points to the component meridians. Each end inclusion, with the chosen connecting path for the top end, induces a based homomorphism $\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For each string component choose a parallel path on its tube boundary from the bottom endpoint to the top endpoint, and choose access paths that close it to a based loop using the fixed side connector. The resulting element of $\pi_1(X_\tau)$ is its based string-link longitude; the parallel and access paths are part of the peripheral datum. The positively oriented boundaries of the endpoint tube disks are the designated meridian loops. Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars; closure joins each top endpoint to the matching bottom endpoint outside $C$ and retains the component labels.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedded submanifold, and let $Y$ be a
smooth vector field along $S$, meaning that $Y(p)\in T_pM$ for each $p\in S$
and $Y$ depends smoothly on $p$ in slice charts. Then:

1. there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $S$ in $M$ and a smooth vector field
   $\widetilde Y$ on $U$ with $\widetilde Y|_S=Y$;
2. if $S$ is closed in $M$, then there is a global smooth vector field
   $\widehat Y$ on $M$ with $\widehat Y|_S=Y$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $A$ be a closed subset of a smooth manifold $M$, and let $U\subseteq M$ be open with $A\subseteq U$. Then there exists a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that $f=1$ on an open neighbourhood of $A$ and $\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq U$.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ such that

$$ \bigcup_{t\in J}\operatorname{supp}(X_t) $$

is contained in a compact subset $K\subseteq M$. Then there is a global evolution
operator $\Psi_{t,s}:M\to M$ for all $s,t\in J$.

derivations.claim: Let $\tau_t$ be the given smooth isotopy through string links, fixed on common endpoint collars. Reparametrize it to be stationary near $t=0,1$. Choose fixed disjoint smooth closure arcs outside $C=D^2\times[0,1]$, using the closure construction in the based-string-link definition, and adjoin them to the moving intervals. The result is a smooth family of closed links in $S^3$, constant on the closure arcs and endpoint collars; extend it constantly in time outside $[0,1]$. The map $\Theta:\mathbb R\times\bigsqcup_i S^1\to\mathbb R\times S^3$, $\Theta(t,s)=(t,\overline\tau_t(s))$, is an injective immersion and is proper: injectivity and immersion follow from the time coordinate and the embedding of each link slice, while the preimage of a compact set lies in a compact time interval times the finite union of circles. Thus its image is a closed embedded submanifold. The vector field $Y(t,\overline\tau_t(s))=(0,\partial_t\overline\tau_t(s))$ along this graph is smooth and vanishes on the fixed closure arcs and endpoint collars. Since the motion is confined to a compact subinterval of each string component away from its endpoint collars, choose a compact set $K\subset\operatorname{int}C$ containing every point where this velocity can be nonzero. By [A1] and [L1], [F4] extends $Y$ to a global smooth vector field on $\mathbb R\times S^3$. Let $X_t$ be its $S^3$ component. By [F5] choose $\chi:S^3\to[0,1]$ equal to one near $K$ and supported in $\operatorname{int}C$, and replace $X_t$ by $\chi X_t$. This field still equals the prescribed velocity along the entire closed link: it is unchanged wherever the velocity is nonzero and is zero on the stationary arcs. Its supports lie in the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset\operatorname{int}C$. Integrate it by [F6]. Uniqueness of the flow gives an ambient isotopy $H_t$ with $H_t\overline\tau_0=\overline\tau_t$; its support in $\operatorname{int}C$ makes $H_t$ the identity near $\partial C$, so it preserves $C$ and fixes the endpoint collars, bottom basepoint, and side connector. This is the relative based isotopy-extension argument for string links.

Restricting $H_1$ gives a based homeomorphism of string-link exteriors that transports the selected tubes, positive meridians, parallels, and access paths. It fixes the endpoint basepoints and side connector, so the two end inclusions commute with the induced based group isomorphisms. By [F1], the longitude has a unique preimage in each finite bottom-end quotient; naturality carries that preimage to the corresponding class for the isotopic string link. The Magnus expansion is the same homomorphism on the transported meridian symbols, so every integer coefficient agrees.

Under [A1], an ambient isotopy of closed links induces the peripheral correspondence in [F3]. Applying that correspondence to the based word-lift data gives the transported based residue candidate. The first assertion of [F2] proves independence of every meridian basing and finite longitude-word lift, with exactly equal lower-coefficient ideals. Applying it to the transported word data proves that the two closed-link residues agree in the same residue group.

Under [A1], a link-homotopy is generated by ambient isotopies and self-crossing changes. For pairwise-distinct indices, ambient isotopy is handled by step 3.1 and each self-crossing change is the second assertion of [F2]. Each move identifies the lower-coefficient ideals by [F2]; composing these finitely many equalities proves the asserted residue equality. No repeated-index conclusion is drawn.

Let $D$ be a finite regular diagram of a nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$ with ordered crossing set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The resolution cube has vertices $I\in\{0,1\}^n$, and $D(I)$ is obtained by applying the indicated local smoothing at every crossing. The link-surgery filtered module associated to $D$ is the direct sum
$$
C_D=\bigoplus_{I\in\{0,1\}^n}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2),
$$
with the summand for $I$ in increasing filtration degree $n-|I|$. Choose the subordinate Heegaard multi-diagram, compatible perturbation data and top-generator cycles for successive attaching-curve systems. The diagonal component of the candidate differential is the ordinary hat disk differential. For $I<J$ coordinatewise, sum over every ordered path $I=I_0<I_1<\cdots<I_r=J$ changing one coordinate at each step. Its summand counts the zero-dimensional holomorphic $(r+2)$-gon spaces with input at the $I$ vertex, the selected top-generator cycles between each pair of successive attaching systems, and output at the $J$ vertex. The count includes the allowed source conformal parameters and imposes zero basepoint multiplicity. These are the surgery polygon maps; the component is zero if $I\nleq J$. Thus changing several crossings is a sum over paths and polygon counts, not an arbitrary direct edge map. The increasing filtration is $F_pC_D=\bigoplus_{|I|\ge n-p}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2)$, extended by zero below $0$ and by $C_D$ at and above $n$. Thus a component increasing $|I|$ lowers its filtration degree and preserves every $F_p$. The cube direction and the reduced Khovanov cochain degree remain separate indices. The polygon-count finiteness, square-zero, and total-homology identifications are justified by the surgery lemma, which labels its actual Ozsváth–Szabó construction and top-input/filling calculations as external inputs, separately from the retained local analytic theorem and finite filtration algebra.

The local smoothing labels are those of Ozsváth–Szabó Figure1: in the chart with northwest–southeast over-strand, 0 joins the two left and two right endpoints, and 1 joins the two top and two bottom endpoints. These become A and B on the mirror chart, respectively. This fixes the convention for the consumers without a diagram-invariance assertion. The general surgery lemma also applies to links in arbitrary closed connected oriented smooth three-manifolds; this definition is only its branched-cover instance.

Assume the countable-choice Heegaard Floer analytic package. Let $Y$ be any closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold and let $\mathbb L$ be an ordered framed $n$-component link in $Y$. On its $i$th exterior boundary torus let $\mu_i$ be the meridian and $\lambda_i$ the chosen framing longitude. Use the three filling slopes $\lambda_i$, $\mu_i+\lambda_i$ and $\mu_i$, labelled $0,1,\infty$, respectively; $\infty$ restores the original unfilled component. For $I\in\{0,1,\infty\}^n$ let $Y(I)$ be the simultaneous filling specified by $I$. Fix an admissible pointed Heegaard multi-diagram subordinate to these surgeries and the compatible perturbation and top-generator choices used by the polygon construction. The mod-two polygon maps on
$$C(\mathbb L)=\bigoplus_{I\in\{0,1\}^n}\widehat{CF}(Y(I);\mathbb F_2)$$
form a differential with components only from $I$ to $J\ge I$ coordinatewise. It preserves the increasing filtration
$$F_pC(\mathbb L)=\bigoplus_{|I|\ge n-p}\widehat{CF}(Y(I);\mathbb F_2),$$
extended by zero below zero and by the whole module at and above $n$. Its total homology is isomorphic to $\widehat{HF}(Y(\infty,\ldots,\infty);\mathbb F_2)=\widehat{HF}(Y;\mathbb F_2)$. For $n=1$, the total complex is the mapping cone of the $0$-to-$1$ surgery map and is quasi-isomorphic to the hat complex of the third, $\infty$ filling; this yields the long exact surgery sequence for every surgery triad, with its cyclic ordering. For $n=0$ the cube is the single hat complex of $Y$. No filtered quasi-isomorphism between distinct surgery presentations is included.

Assume ACω. For every closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold $Y$, the homology of the hat Heegaard Floer complex over $\mathbb F_2$ is independent, up to isomorphism, of the pointed admissible Heegaard diagram used to define it. The assertion is invariance of the group $\widehat{HF}(Y;\mathbb F_2)$; it does not assert a diagram-independent filtered chain homotopy type.

For a fixed finite regular diagram $D$ of a nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$, with $n$ crossings and a basepoint $p\in D$ away from the crossings, choose an admissible pointed Heegaard multi-diagram subordinate to the branched-cover surgeries and the compatible perturbation data and top-generator cycles of the link-surgery construction. Its first page and first differential are isomorphic as a cochain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ to the reduced Khovanov cochain complex of the mirror diagram $\overline D$, based at the corresponding point, in the specified normalized grading shifts. The resulting second page is therefore the based reduced Khovanov cohomology of $\overline D$. The isomorphism is for this fixed diagram and makes no claim about filtered chain complexes for different diagrams.

Let $(C,d,F)$ be a filtered chain complex over a field with an increasing filtration $0=F_{-1}C\subseteq F_0C\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_nC=C$ and $d(F_pC)\subseteq F_pC$. Its spectral sequence stabilizes and abuts to $H(C)$ with the image filtration, without any uniform bound outside the finite range $0\le p\le n$. If a particular filtered complex has been constructed from a fixed link diagram, this convergence assertion does not itself identify filtered complexes arising from different diagrams.

derivations.claim: The crossing resolutions of $D$ give the vertices of the cube, and the surgery maps give the differential components. By [F2] these components square to zero and preserve the increasing cube filtration, so the associated spectral sequence is defined.

The filtration has only the $n+1$ levels $0,\ldots,n$, where $n$ is the number of crossings. By [F4] the spectral sequence stabilizes and abuts to the image filtration on the total homology, which [F2] identifies with $\widehat{HF}(\Sigma(L);\mathbb F_2)$.

The associated graded vertex groups form the $E_1$ page, and their first differential is the sum of the single-crossing edge maps. By [F3], this complex is isomorphic to the reduced Khovanov complex of the mirror diagram; taking its cohomology gives the stated $E_2$ page.

The proof used one fixed $D$ and the finite filtration only. It supplies no filtered map between the constructions for two diagrams, so it establishes the stated fixed-diagram spectral sequence but no diagram-independent filtered quasi-isomorphism. Here [F2] uses the explicitly external OS surgery construction and filling comparison, and [F3] uses its actual compatible unlink maps with the proved finite reduced-algebra binding. Those imports retain their stated scope; no missing geometric map is inferred from finite convergence.

For $I<J$ coordinatewise, sum over every ordered path $I=I_0<I_1<\cdots<I_r=J$ changing one coordinate at each step. Its summand counts the zero-dimensional holomorphic $(r+2)$-gon spaces with input at the $I$ vertex, the selected top-generator cycles between each pair of successive attaching systems, and output at the $J$ vertex. The count includes the allowed source conformal parameters and imposes zero basepoint multiplicity. These are the surgery polygon maps; the component is zero if $I\nleq J$. Thus changing several crossings is a sum over paths and polygon counts, not an arbitrary direct edge map. The increasing filtration is $F_pC_D=\bigoplus_{|I|\ge n-p}\widehat{CF}(\Sigma(D(I));\mathbb F_2)$, extended by zero below $0$ and by $C_D$ at and above $n$. The local smoothing labels are those of Ozsváth–Szabó Figure1: in the chart with northwest–southeast over-strand, 0 joins the two left and two right endpoints, and 1 joins the two top and two bottom endpoints. Use the three filling slopes $\lambda_i$, $\mu_i+\lambda_i$ and $\mu_i$, labelled $0,1,\infty$, respectively; $\infty$ restores the original unfilled component. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. There exists a dualizable framed handle link $(B,G,R)$ whose associated
handlebody is diffeomorphic to both zero-traces $X_0(C)$ and $X_0(K_P)$, with
the component orientations and zero-framings compatible with the diagrams
defining $C$ and $K_P$.

Assume countable choice. Over $\mathbb Q$, the Rasmussen invariants of the
oriented Conway knot $C$ and its Piccirillo partner $K_P$ are
$$s(C)=0,\qquad s(K_P)=2.$$
The calculation is the finite Lee-filtered Khovanov calculation on the two
specified diagrams, including the rational Khovanov ranks and the surviving
Lee filtration levels needed to determine these values.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, choose a closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$; assume $E_K$ is connected. Let $\mu$ be the oriented boundary of a normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented tangent to $K$, agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. Let $\lambda$ be a simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose degree under the normal-tube projection $T_K\to K$ is $+1$ and whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; such a curve is a preferred longitude. Assume $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero, let $E_K(p/q)$ be the filling whose attached solid-torus meridian maps to $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Then
$$H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z,&p\ne0,\\[2pt]\mathbb Z,&p=0.\end{cases}$$

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot, and let $p,q$ be coprime integers with $|p|=1$ and $q\ne0$. For the Dehn filling $Y_{p/q}=E_K(p/q)$ whose attached solid-torus meridian is identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ admits a homomorphism to $SU(2)$ with noncyclic image.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Let $\mu$ be the oriented boundary of a normal disk whose orientation, preceded by the oriented tangent to $K$, agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. Let $\lambda$ be a simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose degree under the normal-tube projection $T_K\to K$ is $+1$ and whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero; such a curve is a preferred longitude. Assume $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. For coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero, let $E_K(p/q)$ be the filling whose attached solid-torus meridian maps to $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. Then
$$H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z,&p\ne0,\\[2pt]\mathbb Z,&p=0.\end{cases}$$

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$

A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.

A **rack** is a set $R$ with a binary operation $*:R\times R\to R$ such
that for every $y\in R$ the right translation $R_y(x)=x*y$ is a bijection
and $(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$ for all $x,y,z\in R$. A **quandle** is a rack
satisfying $x*x=x$ for every $x$. For either structure, write
$x\mathbin{\bar *}y=R_y^{-1}(x)$.

For a regular oriented link diagram $D$, let $A(D)$ be its finite set of
maximal under-arcs. Form the set of finite terms recursively: each symbol
$x_a$ for $a\in A(D)$ is a term, and if $s,t$ are terms then $s*t$ and
$s\mathbin{\bar *}t$ are terms. Let $\sim$ be the intersection of all
equivalence relations on these terms that are compatible with both operations
and contain the quandle identities: idempotency, right invertibility, and
right self-distributivity, together with the crossing relations.
At a crossing with source and target under-arcs $u,v$ and overarc $o$, the
crossing relation is $x_v=x_u*x_o$; reversing source and target gives the
equivalent relation with $\bar *$. The quotient term set $Q(D)$ is the
**diagram quandle**, or the diagram presentation of the **fundamental
quandle**. Its independence of diagram is proved in the Theorem.

For any quandle $Q$, its **adjoint group** $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ is the
group presentation with generators $e_q$ for all $q\in Q$ and relators
$e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$ for all $q,r\in Q$. A group presentation
$\langle X\mid S\rangle$ means the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the
normal closure of the relator words $S$.

The diagram presentation and the adjoint group are algebraic constructions;
this definition makes no completeness or knot-classification assertion.

Let $R$ be a rack, with right translations $R_y(x)=x*y$. The kink map
$\pi:R\to R$, $\pi(x)=x*x$, is a bijection. Its inverse is
$\pi^{-1}(z)=R_z^{-1}(z)$.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a knot $K$ with blackboard framing $b_D$. The self-linking number of the
framed knot $(K,b_D)$ equals the diagram writhe:
$$\operatorname{sl}(K,b_D)=\operatorname{wr}(D).$$
For a link component $K_i$, the corresponding self-linking number is its
self-writhe $\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$. Total writhe of a link still includes
the signs of mixed crossings, while the sum of component self-linking numbers
uses only self-crossings.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: At an R2 move, hold the overarc color $y$ fixed. The underarc label is changed by $R_y$ at one crossing and by $R_y^{-1}$ at the other, so the two boundary colorings determine one another uniquely. Reversing the move gives the inverse correspondence.

For a braid-like R3 move, use the crossing map $B(x,y)=(y,x*y)$. Its inverse is $B^{-1}(u,v)=(v\mathbin{\bar *}u,u)$ by right invertibility. The two sides send $(x,y,z)$ respectively to $(z,y*z,(x*y)*z)$ and $(z,y*z,(x*z)*(y*z))$; the last coordinates agree by rack self-distributivity. For every $z$, $R_z(x*y)=(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$, so $R_z$ preserves $*$. If $u=a\mathbin{\bar *}b$, then $u*b=a$; applying $R_z$ gives $R_z(u)*R_z(b)=R_z(a)$, and uniqueness of right division yields $R_z(u)=R_z(a)\mathbin{\bar *}R_z(b)$. Thus $R_z$ and its inverse preserve both operations. For either operation $\star_1,\star_2\in\{*,\bar *\}$, this gives $(x\star_1 y)\star_2 z=(x\star_2 z)\star_1(y\star_2 z)$, the corresponding mixed R3 equation. The bijective crossing maps then give the extension bijection for every orientation variant. A planar isotopy transports arc labels.

Write the under-tangent as $a v_{\rm over}+b n_o$. Its determinant sign is the sign of $b$, so at a positive crossing the oriented underpass goes from source to target. In a positive curl with incoming label $x$ and outgoing label $y$, either the overarc is the incoming arc and $y=x*x$, or it is the outgoing arc and $y=x*y$. In the latter case self-distributivity gives $R_yR_x=R_{x*y}R_y=R_yR_y$, hence $R_x=R_y$; therefore $y=x*y=x*x=\pi(x)$. Conversely $y=\pi(x)$ solves the equation since $R_{\pi(x)}=R_x$ by the kink-map proof. Thus both positive curl shapes have unique transport $y=\pi(x)$. In a negative curl the same equations are read backwards and give $y=\pi^{-1}(x)$. This checks both choices of which boundary arc is the overarc, independently of a picture.

For a single unframed curl with boundary color $x$, extension requires $x=\pi(x)$; if $\pi$ is the identity, this condition holds uniquely for every $x$. Conversely, if every boundary color extends uniquely, every $x$ is fixed by $\pi$, so $x*x=x$ for all $x$ and the rack is a quandle.

The kink shift propagates through any crossing. Self-distributivity gives $\pi(x*y)=(x*y)*(x*y)=(x*x)*y$, hence $\pi R_y=R_y\pi$. It also gives $(x*y)*y=(x*y)*(y*y)$ for every $x$. Since $R_y$ is surjective, this implies $R_{\pi(y)}=R_y$. By [F2], $\pi$ is bijective, so these identities hold for its inverse as well: $\pi^kR_y^{\delta}=R_y^{\delta}\pi^k$ and $R_{\pi^{\ell}(y)}^{\delta}=R_y^{\delta}$ for all $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$ and $\delta\in\{1,-1\}$. In particular, if a crossing obeys $x_t=R_y(x_s)$, independently shifting its two under-colors by the same $\pi^k$ and its over-color by $\pi^{\ell}$ preserves it, because $R_{\pi^{\ell}(y)}(\pi^k x_s)=\pi^kR_y(x_s)=\pi^k x_t$. The reversed crossing relation is preserved by the same calculation with $R_y^{-1}$.

A compensated pair creates two curls on the same oriented component, or removes their inverse configuration. If its blackboard framing is preserved, [F4] forces the two created crossing signs to sum to zero; the same holds when opposite signed framing changes are specified directly. Choose either of the two component intervals between the sites and traverse it in the component orientation, writing $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ for the sign of its first curl; the second has sign $-\epsilon$. Starting from an old coloring, retain every color off this interval and replace every old color on it by $\pi^{\epsilon}$ of that color, splitting an old under-arc at the two sites if needed. Insert the unique local curl labels from step1.3. At the first site the transport changes the old incoming label to its $\pi^{\epsilon}$-shift; at the second the transport $\pi^{-\epsilon}$ restores the old outgoing label. Thus the prescribed labels agree along every new maximal under-arc.

At any old crossing, the selected component interval contains both local halves of the underpassing branch or neither, since its endpoints are away from crossings. Thus the source and target under-colors have the same shift exponent $k\in\{0,\epsilon\}$. Independently the overpassing branch has shift exponent $\ell\in\{0,\epsilon\}$. Step1.5 preserves the crossing relation for all four possibilities, including a self-crossing at which the interval contains exactly one of the two visits. The old crossing relations therefore all hold after the recoloring. Conversely, start with any coloring of the twice-curled diagram, undo the $\pi^{\epsilon}$ shift on that same marked component interval, and remove the two uniquely determined curl portions using step1.3; step1.5 again preserves every intervening relation. The endpoint transports now cancel in the inverse order. citations.quote:
A **rack** is a set $R$ with a binary operation $*:R\times R\to R$ such
that for every $y\in R$ the right translation $R_y(x)=x*y$ is a bijection
and $(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$ for all $x,y,z\in R$. A **quandle** is a rack
satisfying $x*x=x$ for every $x$. For either structure, write
$x\mathbin{\bar *}y=R_y^{-1}(x)$.

For a regular oriented link diagram $D$, let $A(D)$ be its finite set of
maximal under-arcs. Form the set of finite terms recursively: each symbol
$x_a$ for $a\in A(D)$ is a term, and if $s,t$ are terms then $s*t$ and
$s\mathbin{\bar *}t$ are terms. Let $\sim$ be the intersection of all
equivalence relations on these terms that are compatible with both operations
and contain the quandle identities: idempotency, right invertibility, and
right self-distributivity, together with the crossing relations.
At a crossing with source and target under-arcs $u,v$ and overarc $o$, the
crossing relation is $x_v=x_u*x_o$; reversing source and target gives the
equivalent relation with $\bar *$. The quotient term set $Q(D)$ is the
**diagram quandle**, or the diagram presentation of the **fundamental
quandle**. Its independence of diagram is proved in the Theorem.

For any quandle $Q$, its **adjoint group** $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ is the
group presentation with generators $e_q$ for all $q\in Q$ and relators
$e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$ for all $q,r\in Q$. A group presentation
$\langle X\mid S\rangle$ means the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the
normal closure of the relator words $S$.

The diagram presentation and the adjoint group are algebraic constructions;
this definition makes no completeness or knot-classification assertion.

Let $R$ be a rack, with right translations $R_y(x)=x*y$. The kink map
$\pi:R\to R$, $\pi(x)=x*x$, is a bijection. Its inverse is
$\pi^{-1}(z)=R_z^{-1}(z)$.

An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a knot $K$ with blackboard framing $b_D$. The self-linking number of the
framed knot $(K,b_D)$ equals the diagram writhe:
$$\operatorname{sl}(K,b_D)=\operatorname{wr}(D).$$
For a link component $K_i$, the corresponding self-linking number is its
self-writhe $\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$. Total writhe of a link still includes
the signs of mixed crossings, while the sum of component self-linking numbers
uses only self-crossings.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: At an R2 move, hold the overarc color $y$ fixed. The underarc label is changed by $R_y$ at one crossing and by $R_y^{-1}$ at the other, so the two boundary colorings determine one another uniquely. Reversing the move gives the inverse correspondence.

For a braid-like R3 move, use the crossing map $B(x,y)=(y,x*y)$. Its inverse is $B^{-1}(u,v)=(v\mathbin{\bar *}u,u)$ by right invertibility. The two sides send $(x,y,z)$ respectively to $(z,y*z,(x*y)*z)$ and $(z,y*z,(x*z)*(y*z))$; the last coordinates agree by rack self-distributivity. For every $z$, $R_z(x*y)=(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$, so $R_z$ preserves $*$. If $u=a\mathbin{\bar *}b$, then $u*b=a$; applying $R_z$ gives $R_z(u)*R_z(b)=R_z(a)$, and uniqueness of right division yields $R_z(u)=R_z(a)\mathbin{\bar *}R_z(b)$. Thus $R_z$ and its inverse preserve both operations. For either operation $\star_1,\star_2\in\{*,\bar *\}$, this gives $(x\star_1 y)\star_2 z=(x\star_2 z)\star_1(y\star_2 z)$, the corresponding mixed R3 equation. The bijective crossing maps then give the extension bijection for every orientation variant. A planar isotopy transports arc labels.

Write the under-tangent as $a v_{\rm over}+b n_o$. Its determinant sign is the sign of $b$, so at a positive crossing the oriented underpass goes from source to target. In a positive curl with incoming label $x$ and outgoing label $y$, either the overarc is the incoming arc and $y=x*x$, or it is the outgoing arc and $y=x*y$. In the latter case self-distributivity gives $R_yR_x=R_{x*y}R_y=R_yR_y$, hence $R_x=R_y$; therefore $y=x*y=x*x=\pi(x)$. Conversely $y=\pi(x)$ solves the equation since $R_{\pi(x)}=R_x$ by the kink-map proof. Thus both positive curl shapes have unique transport $y=\pi(x)$. In a negative curl the same equations are read backwards and give $y=\pi^{-1}(x)$. This checks both choices of which boundary arc is the overarc, independently of a picture.

For a single unframed curl with boundary color $x$, extension requires $x=\pi(x)$; if $\pi$ is the identity, this condition holds uniquely for every $x$. Conversely, if every boundary color extends uniquely, every $x$ is fixed by $\pi$, so $x*x=x$ for all $x$ and the rack is a quandle.

The kink shift propagates through any crossing. Self-distributivity gives $\pi(x*y)=(x*y)*(x*y)=(x*x)*y$, hence $\pi R_y=R_y\pi$. It also gives $(x*y)*y=(x*y)*(y*y)$ for every $x$. Since $R_y$ is surjective, this implies $R_{\pi(y)}=R_y$. By [F2], $\pi$ is bijective, so these identities hold for its inverse as well: $\pi^kR_y^{\delta}=R_y^{\delta}\pi^k$ and $R_{\pi^{\ell}(y)}^{\delta}=R_y^{\delta}$ for all $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$ and $\delta\in\{1,-1\}$. In particular, if a crossing obeys $x_t=R_y(x_s)$, independently shifting its two under-colors by the same $\pi^k$ and its over-color by $\pi^{\ell}$ preserves it, because $R_{\pi^{\ell}(y)}(\pi^k x_s)=\pi^kR_y(x_s)=\pi^k x_t$. The reversed crossing relation is preserved by the same calculation with $R_y^{-1}$.

A compensated pair creates two curls on the same oriented component, or removes their inverse configuration. If its blackboard framing is preserved, [F4] forces the two created crossing signs to sum to zero; the same holds when opposite signed framing changes are specified directly. Choose either of the two component intervals between the sites and traverse it in the component orientation, writing $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ for the sign of its first curl; the second has sign $-\epsilon$. Starting from an old coloring, retain every color off this interval and replace every old color on it by $\pi^{\epsilon}$ of that color, splitting an old under-arc at the two sites if needed. Insert the unique local curl labels from step1.3. At the first site the transport changes the old incoming label to its $\pi^{\epsilon}$-shift; at the second the transport $\pi^{-\epsilon}$ restores the old outgoing label. Thus the prescribed labels agree along every new maximal under-arc.

At any old crossing, the selected component interval contains both local halves of the underpassing branch or neither, since its endpoints are away from crossings. Thus the source and target under-colors have the same shift exponent $k\in\{0,\epsilon\}$. Independently the overpassing branch has shift exponent $\ell\in\{0,\epsilon\}$. Step1.5 preserves the crossing relation for all four possibilities, including a self-crossing at which the interval contains exactly one of the two visits. The old crossing relations therefore all hold after the recoloring. Conversely, start with any coloring of the twice-curled diagram, undo the $\pi^{\epsilon}$ shift on that same marked component interval, and remove the two uniquely determined curl portions using step1.3; step1.5 again preserves every intervening relation. The endpoint transports now cancel in the inverse order. These constructions are inverse on every arc label, so give the required bijection for arbitrarily separated opposite curls, not only adjacent curls. The removal move uses the inverse bijection.

Steps 1.1–1.2 give the R2, R3 and planar-isotopy bijections; steps 2.1, 3.1 give the compensation bijection. A finite rack admits only finitely many assignments on a finite diagram, so the cardinalities are preserved. Step 1.4 proves exactly when the individual unframed R1 bijection is available. The algebraic assertions use no choice; only the smooth framing interpretation uses [A1].
