The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D_0$ and $D_1$ be finite integral framed-link surgery diagrams in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, with surgery results $M_0$ and $M_1$. Then $M_0$ and $M_1$ are orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic if and only if $D_0$ and $D_1$ are related by a finite sequence of ambient isotopies, framed handle slides, and additions or deletions of split $\pm1$-framed unknots.

Fix even $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A$, the BHMV semisimplified category, and its quantum dimensions $d_j$ and twists $\theta_j$ for $0\le j\le r-2$. Put $\Omega_p=\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}d_jp_j$, $\Delta_+=\sum_jd_j^2\theta_j$, and $\Delta_-=\sum_jd_j^2\theta_j^{-1}$. The Statement asserts that both $\Delta_+$ and $\Delta_-$ are nonzero. For a finite integral framed link $L$ in the oriented three-sphere, color each surgery component by $\Omega_p$ and normalize the bracket evaluation by $\Delta_+^{b_+(L)}\Delta_-^{b_-(L)}$, where $b_\pm(L)$ are the positive and negative indices of the framing matrix. With the stated BHMV root and weighted anomaly convention, the resulting value is unchanged under framed isotopy, handle slides, and addition or deletion of a split $\pm1$-framed unknot.

For the fixed root parameter, the normalized double-handlebody pairing on the admissible spine states of a marked handlebody is nondegenerate after quotienting by its radical. The inverse pairing defines the sewing map for gluing along a closed marked surface, and these maps satisfy the stated weighted Lagrangian anomaly correction.

Assume full AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the surface intersection and boundary-kernel duality suppliers.

An object is a closed oriented surface $\Sigma$ with a fixed finite collection of marked points carrying simple labels of the complex modular ribbon fusion category and pairwise disjoint oriented embedded interval germs through those points (the ribbon-end arcs), together with a Lagrangian subspace $\lambda\subset H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb R)$ for the signed intersection form. An elementary morphism is an oriented compact smooth 3-bordism $M:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ with product collars and fixed boundary parametrizations, a properly embedded colored ribbon graph whose ends match the marked labels and, in the fixed product collars, are exactly the products of those ribbon-end arcs with the collar interval, and an integer weight $n\in\mathbb Z$. Boundary parametrizations preserve these oriented arc germs. Reversing a boundary orientation dualizes its labels and reverses its oriented ribbon-end arcs. Composition glues the identical product ribbon germs through the common parametrized surface, with no interpolating twist.

For any closed oriented surface $\Sigma$, the intersection convention is $\omega_\Sigma([\alpha],[\beta])=$ the signed intersection number in which the tangent to $\alpha$ followed by the tangent to $\beta$ gives the surface orientation. For a bordism $M:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$, write $j_r$ for the inclusion maps into $H_1(M;\mathbb R)$ and set

$$\Lambda_M=\{(x_0,x_1)\in H_1(\Sigma_0;\mathbb R)\oplus H_1(\Sigma_1;\mathbb R):j_0x_0=j_1x_1\}.$$

Give the product the form $-\omega_{\Sigma_0}\oplus\omega_{\Sigma_1}$. The boundary-kernel lemma applied to $\partial M$ gives the relation with $j_0x_0=-j_1x_1$; changing the sign of the second coordinate is symplectic and gives exactly $\Lambda_M$. Hence $\Lambda_M$ is Lagrangian ([[lem-3-manifold-boundary-kernel-is-lagrangian]]).

For composable bordisms $M_1:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ and $M_2:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$, put $A=\Lambda_{M_1}$ and $B=\Lambda_{M_2}$. For a relation $R\subseteq\overline V\oplus W$, write $R(L)=\{w:\exists v\in L,(v,w)\in R\}$ and $R^t(Q)=\{v:\exists w\in Q,(v,w)\in R\}$. These use the inclusion maps into each individual bordism. The three Lagrangians for composition lie in the middle surface:

$$K_1=A(\lambda_0),\qquad K_0=\lambda_1,\qquad K_2=B^t(\lambda_2)\quad\subseteq H_1(\Sigma_1;\mathbb R).$$

They are Lagrangian by [[lem-lagrangian-relation-sends-lagrangian-to-lagrangian]], applied also to the transposed relation. With the Wall-form sign fixed in [[lem-maslov-index-four-lagrangian-cocycle]], define

$$n(M_2\circ M_1)=n_2+n_1+\mu(K_1,K_0,K_2).$$

For mapping cylinders of symplectic maps $f_1,f_2$, the index is $\mu(f_1\lambda_0,\lambda_1,f_2^{-1}\lambda_2)=\mu(f_2f_1\lambda_0,f_2\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$. This is Walker's prescribed sign and order. For arbitrary bordisms, replacing the individual relations by homology maps into the glued manifold is not part of the definition.

Identity bordisms are cylinders with the product ribbons on the specified arcs and weight zero. Disjoint union takes the disjoint union of geometric data, the direct sum of the surface Lagrangians, and the sum of weights. The empty surface is the monoidal unit. Bordisms are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms respecting collars, parametrizations, ribbon data and weights; smoothing glued collars is understood up to these identifications. Associativity and the weight, unit and disjoint-union laws follow from the relation identity in [[lem-maslov-correction-composes-for-lagrangian-relations]] and the proof below. This defines the weighted category before any RT functor is asserted. The equality between its correction and a surgery-signature defect remains a separate obligation of [[thm-weighted-rt-tqft-and-factorization]]; no unweighted TQFT is asserted.

For bordisms, use the BHMV additional $\eta^{b_0+b_1}$ normalization specified in the state-space Definition, not the raw closed invariant alone. The finite state spaces, perfect pairing and actual surgery/sewing maps are [F3], whose external BHMV/Gilmer–Masbaum input supplies the TQFT construction at the exact even root and complex specialization. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D_0$ and $D_1$ be finite integral framed-link surgery diagrams in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, with surgery results $M_0$ and $M_1$. Then $M_0$ and $M_1$ are orientation-preservingly diffeomorphic if and only if $D_0$ and $D_1$ are related by a finite sequence of ambient isotopies, framed handle slides, and additions or deletions of split $\pm1$-framed unknots.

Fix even $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A$, the BHMV semisimplified category, and its quantum dimensions $d_j$ and twists $\theta_j$ for $0\le j\le r-2$. Put $\Omega_p=\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}d_jp_j$, $\Delta_+=\sum_jd_j^2\theta_j$, and $\Delta_-=\sum_jd_j^2\theta_j^{-1}$. The Statement asserts that both $\Delta_+$ and $\Delta_-$ are nonzero. For a finite integral framed link $L$ in the oriented three-sphere, color each surgery component by $\Omega_p$ and normalize the bracket evaluation by $\Delta_+^{b_+(L)}\Delta_-^{b_-(L)}$, where $b_\pm(L)$ are the positive and negative indices of the framing matrix. With the stated BHMV root and weighted anomaly convention, the resulting value is unchanged under framed isotopy, handle slides, and addition or deletion of a split $\pm1$-framed unknot.

For the fixed root parameter, the normalized double-handlebody pairing on the admissible spine states of a marked handlebody is nondegenerate after quotienting by its radical. The inverse pairing defines the sewing map for gluing along a closed marked surface, and these maps satisfy the stated weighted Lagrangian anomaly correction.

Assume full AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the surface intersection and boundary-kernel duality suppliers.

An object is a closed oriented surface $\Sigma$ with a fixed finite collection of marked points carrying simple labels of the complex modular ribbon fusion category and pairwise disjoint oriented embedded interval germs through those points (the ribbon-end arcs), together with a Lagrangian subspace $\lambda\subset H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb R)$ for the signed intersection form. An elementary morphism is an oriented compact smooth 3-bordism $M:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ with product collars and fixed boundary parametrizations, a properly embedded colored ribbon graph whose ends match the marked labels and, in the fixed product collars, are exactly the products of those ribbon-end arcs with the collar interval, and an integer weight $n\in\mathbb Z$. Boundary parametrizations preserve these oriented arc germs. Reversing a boundary orientation dualizes its labels and reverses its oriented ribbon-end arcs. Composition glues the identical product ribbon germs through the common parametrized surface, with no interpolating twist.

For any closed oriented surface $\Sigma$, the intersection convention is $\omega_\Sigma([\alpha],[\beta])=$ the signed intersection number in which the tangent to $\alpha$ followed by the tangent to $\beta$ gives the surface orientation. For a bordism $M:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$, write $j_r$ for the inclusion maps into $H_1(M;\mathbb R)$ and set

$$\Lambda_M=\{(x_0,x_1)\in H_1(\Sigma_0;\mathbb R)\oplus H_1(\Sigma_1;\mathbb R):j_0x_0=j_1x_1\}.$$

Give the product the form $-\omega_{\Sigma_0}\oplus\omega_{\Sigma_1}$. The boundary-kernel lemma applied to $\partial M$ gives the relation with $j_0x_0=-j_1x_1$; changing the sign of the second coordinate is symplectic and gives exactly $\Lambda_M$. Hence $\Lambda_M$ is Lagrangian ([[lem-3-manifold-boundary-kernel-is-lagrangian]]).

For composable bordisms $M_1:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ and $M_2:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$, put $A=\Lambda_{M_1}$ and $B=\Lambda_{M_2}$. For a relation $R\subseteq\overline V\oplus W$, write $R(L)=\{w:\exists v\in L,(v,w)\in R\}$ and $R^t(Q)=\{v:\exists w\in Q,(v,w)\in R\}$. These use the inclusion maps into each individual bordism. The three Lagrangians for composition lie in the middle surface:

$$K_1=A(\lambda_0),\qquad K_0=\lambda_1,\qquad K_2=B^t(\lambda_2)\quad\subseteq H_1(\Sigma_1;\mathbb R).$$

They are Lagrangian by [[lem-lagrangian-relation-sends-lagrangian-to-lagrangian]], applied also to the transposed relation. With the Wall-form sign fixed in [[lem-maslov-index-four-lagrangian-cocycle]], define

$$n(M_2\circ M_1)=n_2+n_1+\mu(K_1,K_0,K_2).$$

For mapping cylinders of symplectic maps $f_1,f_2$, the index is $\mu(f_1\lambda_0,\lambda_1,f_2^{-1}\lambda_2)=\mu(f_2f_1\lambda_0,f_2\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$. This is Walker's prescribed sign and order. For arbitrary bordisms, replacing the individual relations by homology maps into the glued manifold is not part of the definition.

Identity bordisms are cylinders with the product ribbons on the specified arcs and weight zero. Disjoint union takes the disjoint union of geometric data, the direct sum of the surface Lagrangians, and the sum of weights. The empty surface is the monoidal unit. Bordisms are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms respecting collars, parametrizations, ribbon data and weights; smoothing glued collars is understood up to these identifications. Associativity and the weight, unit and disjoint-union laws follow from the relation identity in [[lem-maslov-correction-composes-for-lagrangian-relations]] and the proof below. This defines the weighted category before any RT functor is asserted. The equality between its correction and a surgery-signature defect remains a separate obligation of [[thm-weighted-rt-tqft-and-factorization]]; no unweighted TQFT is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the oriented $S^3$ with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism and fix the standard height $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$. Its only critical points are the two poles, and each regular level is a 2-sphere. A **Morse representative** of a smooth oriented knot $K$ is a knot ambient isotopic to $K$ on which $h$ has only nondegenerate critical points. Define the **bridge number** $b(K)$ as the minimum number of local maxima of $h$ on a Morse representative of $K$. The standard unknot is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate 2-plane of $S^3$.

A **regular oriented diagram** is a projection of a smooth oriented knot with finitely many transverse double points, no other multiple points, and an over/under choice at each double point. A **crossing change** switches which branch is over at one chosen double point and leaves the projection and strand orientations unchanged. Define the **unknotting number** $u(K)$ as the minimum number of crossing changes needed to turn some regular diagram of a representative of $K$ into a diagram of the standard unknot. Both minima are taken in subsets of $\mathbb N$. The Morse-representative set is nonempty by the first well-definedness result below; under countable choice the regular-diagram existence result and the descending-diagram theorem below make the unknotting set nonempty. The bridge-number definition and the least-element argument in $\mathbb N$ require no choice; countable choice is used only to invoke the stated regular-projection supplier for $u(K)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. Let $A\subset M$ be a connected properly embedded incompressible annulus with $\partial A\subset\partial M$. If $A$ is boundary-compressible, then $A$ is boundary-parallel.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

For $n=2,3$, a given smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ into a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold is isotopic through embeddings to a small coordinate round ball, and that embedding isotopy extends ambiently with compact support. For a parametrized smooth $n$-ball $B$ and a parametrized smooth boundary $(n-1)$-disk $W$, the pair $(B,W)$ is diffeomorphic to the standard ball with a hemispherical window. The diffeomorphism can retain the specified window parameter, using stereographic parameters on the standard hemisphere and allowing the necessary orientation of that parameter. No choice axiom is assumed.

Consequently, attaching a parametrized smooth $n$-ball to a smooth $n$-manifold along such a window does not change its diffeomorphism type, provided an attaching collar and corner rounding are supplied. The resulting diffeomorphism is supported in the added ball and an arbitrarily small receiving collar. The inverse assertion holds for removing a ball that meets the boundary in exactly one such window with the supplied collar charts. In dimension two the windows are intervals.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smoothly embedded sphere transverse to $K$ in exactly two points. Cutting along $S$ gives two properly embedded arcs; cap each arc by an orientation-compatible simple arc on $S$, pushed slightly into the corresponding boundary collar to obtain oriented knots $K_1$ and $K_2$. Then the oriented isotopy class of $K$ is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the bridge-number definition. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard $S^3$, $b(K)=1$ if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the fixed oriented coordinate circle used as the standard unknot.

derivations.claim: We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$.
Choose bridge representatives realizing $b(K)$ and $b(J)$, which is possible by [F1] and step 1.1. Each comes with its bridge sphere and disjoint upper and lower bridge-spanning disks.

Choose one point of each knot on its bridge sphere where an upper bridge arc and a lower bridge arc meet. Take product-coordinate balls around the two points so each ball meets the sphere in a disk, the knot in one short arc crossing that disk once, and each of the two incident bridge-spanning disks in a half-disk. Remove the ball interiors and glue the punctured spheres by the connected-sum map from [F2]. The two selected upper bridge arcs join into one proper upper arc, and the two selected lower bridge arcs join into one proper lower arc. The new upper spanning disk is the union of the two punctured upper disks and the gluing rectangle; two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk. The same construction gives the lower spanning disk. Every unselected bridge arc and disk remains unchanged and disjoint from these disks. Thus the connected-sum position has $b(K)+b(J)-1$ upper arcs, so $b(K\#J)\le b(K)+b(J)-1$.

If either factor is the unknot, [F8] gives equality immediately. Suppose therefore both are nontrivial. Choose a bridge sphere $S$ of $L=K\#J$ with $b=b(L)$ upper arcs, by step 1.1. Transport the connected-sum construction's two-puncture sphere through the representative isotopy; this gives a smooth sphere $P$ cutting $L$ into the specified factors. Choose a sufficiently small product tube adapted to its two transverse punctures and form $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$. The annulus core is a positive or negative meridian in the tube: both its boundary components bound the normal disks $P\cap N(L)$ and its core is homotopic within $A$ to either boundary. By [F4], composing $\pi_1(A)=\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(E_L)$ with abelianization sends its generator to $\pm1\in\mathbb Z$. The inclusion is therefore injective.

There is no boundary compression of $A$. If there were, [F5] would give a parallelism to one of the two annuli $A_0$ on the boundary torus between its meridional boundaries. This implies that one factor is the unknot, as can be checked with the markings: write the tube over the corresponding subinterval of the core knot as $D^2\times I$, with side $A_0=\partial D^2\times I$ and end disks the two disks $P\cap N(L)$. Attach the annulus parallelism to this side, retaining its rim collars. It merely enlarges the radial disk coordinate in each $I$-fiber, so the result is a ball with boundary the original $P$ after rounding. Its knot arc is the core $\{0\}\times I$, and it cobounds with an arc on that ball's boundary a disk given by a fixed radial interval times $I$, rounded at its ends. Capping this arc on $P$ produces an unknot. The same construction works for either complementary annulus of the torus; it uses its actual product parameter, not just a homological slope. By [F8] the resulting unknot is one of the given factors, contradicting nontriviality. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold for this particular $P$, and we may apply its isotopy and disk changes without changing $(L,S)$ or the specified factors.

In the resulting normal form $P\cap S=C$ is one circle disjoint from $L$. The two disks $P_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$ each contain one puncture. Indeed the two disk-intersection arcs of [F3] have their puncture endpoints one on each side, as in that lemma's final normalization. Each $P_\pm$ is a proper disk cutting its bridge ball into two balls: cap it by either of the two disks on $\partial B_\pm$ bounded by its rim, round, and apply [F6]; the side not containing the exterior of $B_\pm$ is the required ball. Their collars give compatible markings. Let $S_1,S_2$ be the disks on $S$ bounded by $C$, labelled by the two sides of $P$, and put $r_i=|L\cap S_i|$. Then $r_1+r_2=2b$. In each original bridge ball exactly one bridge arc crosses $P_\pm$: it is the arc carrying its unique puncture. Its two endpoints on $S$ lie on opposite sides of $C$, because the bridge crosses that separating disk once. Every other bridge arc is wholly on one side. Consequently $r_i$ is odd.

Cap each of the two cut ball-arcs of $L$ by a boundary arc on $P$ running from the upper puncture to the lower puncture and crossing $C$ once, chosen as the two type-I traces joined by an arc of $C$ between their distinct foot endpoints, then rounded slightly in the collar of $C$ so that it crosses $C$ transversely just once. Push the two caps into their respective boundary collars. On each side this cap is a trivial ball-arc meeting the capped bridge sphere $S_i\cup$(cap disk) once. Its upper and lower portions extend the severed bridge arcs. Every uncut bridge disk remains in its original region. Each of the two cut bridge disks is cut along its one trace into two disks; on each side join its disk piece to the narrow cap strip. This is a disk attached along one boundary interval, so gives a spanning disk for the extended upper or lower arc. Choose the cap strips in disjoint small quadrant collars of the traces; other disks miss them, and on a given side all disk pieces were originally disjoint. Thus these are simultaneous disjoint spanning-disk systems. The upper and lower ambient pieces are balls: attach the cap half-balls along the displayed windows on $P_\pm$ and use [F6]. We have therefore constructed actual bridge spheres for the two specified oriented factors, not merely diagrams with a proposed number of bridges. Each has $r_i+1$ knot endpoints on its sphere, the extra endpoint being the single crossing of the cap. It follows that their upper arc counts are $n_i=(r_i+1)/2$, and $n_1+n_2=b+1$. Cap orientation is chosen to close the original oriented arc, so [F8] identifies the factors with $K,J$, up to their harmless interchange.

Step 1.1 applied to the two factor bridge spheres gives $b(K)\le n_1$ and $b(J)\le n_2$. Hence $b(K)+b(J)-1\le n_1+n_2-1=b=b(K\#J)$. Together with step 2.1 and the unknot case in step 3.1, this proves the formula for every pair of smooth oriented knots in the Statement. The constructions use finitely many extrema, disks, cuts and collars; their smooth extension and Schoenflies uses are precisely the stated countable-choice suppliers.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the oriented $S^3$ with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism and fix the standard height $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$. Its only critical points are the two poles, and each regular level is a 2-sphere. A **Morse representative** of a smooth oriented knot $K$ is a knot ambient isotopic to $K$ on which $h$ has only nondegenerate critical points. Define the **bridge number** $b(K)$ as the minimum number of local maxima of $h$ on a Morse representative of $K$. The standard unknot is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate 2-plane of $S^3$.

A **regular oriented diagram** is a projection of a smooth oriented knot with finitely many transverse double points, no other multiple points, and an over/under choice at each double point. A **crossing change** switches which branch is over at one chosen double point and leaves the projection and strand orientations unchanged. Define the **unknotting number** $u(K)$ as the minimum number of crossing changes needed to turn some regular diagram of a representative of $K$ into a diagram of the standard unknot. Both minima are taken in subsets of $\mathbb N$. The Morse-representative set is nonempty by the first well-definedness result below; under countable choice the regular-diagram existence result and the descending-diagram theorem below make the unknotting set nonempty. The bridge-number definition and the least-element argument in $\mathbb N$ require no choice; countable choice is used only to invoke the stated regular-projection supplier for $u(K)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. Let $A\subset M$ be a connected properly embedded incompressible annulus with $\partial A\subset\partial M$. If $A$ is boundary-compressible, then $A$ is boundary-parallel.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

For $n=2,3$, a given smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ into a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold is isotopic through embeddings to a small coordinate round ball, and that embedding isotopy extends ambiently with compact support. For a parametrized smooth $n$-ball $B$ and a parametrized smooth boundary $(n-1)$-disk $W$, the pair $(B,W)$ is diffeomorphic to the standard ball with a hemispherical window. The diffeomorphism can retain the specified window parameter, using stereographic parameters on the standard hemisphere and allowing the necessary orientation of that parameter. No choice axiom is assumed.

Consequently, attaching a parametrized smooth $n$-ball to a smooth $n$-manifold along such a window does not change its diffeomorphism type, provided an attaching collar and corner rounding are supplied. The resulting diffeomorphism is supported in the added ball and an arbitrarily small receiving collar. The inverse assertion holds for removing a ball that meets the boundary in exactly one such window with the supplied collar charts. In dimension two the windows are intervals.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smoothly embedded sphere transverse to $K$ in exactly two points. Cutting along $S$ gives two properly embedded arcs; cap each arc by an orientation-compatible simple arc on $S$, pushed slightly into the corresponding boundary collar to obtain oriented knots $K_1$ and $K_2$. Then the oriented isotopy class of $K$ is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the bridge-number definition. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in the standard $S^3$, $b(K)=1$ if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the fixed oriented coordinate circle used as the standard unknot.

derivations.claim: We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$.
Choose bridge representatives realizing $b(K)$ and $b(J)$, which is possible by [F1] and step 1.1. Each comes with its bridge sphere and disjoint upper and lower bridge-spanning disks.

Choose one point of each knot on its bridge sphere where an upper bridge arc and a lower bridge arc meet. Take product-coordinate balls around the two points so each ball meets the sphere in a disk, the knot in one short arc crossing that disk once, and each of the two incident bridge-spanning disks in a half-disk. Remove the ball interiors and glue the punctured spheres by the connected-sum map from [F2]. The two selected upper bridge arcs join into one proper upper arc, and the two selected lower bridge arcs join into one proper lower arc. The new upper spanning disk is the union of the two punctured upper disks and the gluing rectangle; two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk. The same construction gives the lower spanning disk. Every unselected bridge arc and disk remains unchanged and disjoint from these disks. Thus the connected-sum position has $b(K)+b(J)-1$ upper arcs, so $b(K\#J)\le b(K)+b(J)-1$.

If either factor is the unknot, [F8] gives equality immediately. Suppose therefore both are nontrivial. Choose a bridge sphere $S$ of $L=K\#J$ with $b=b(L)$ upper arcs, by step 1.1. Transport the connected-sum construction's two-puncture sphere through the representative isotopy; this gives a smooth sphere $P$ cutting $L$ into the specified factors. Choose a sufficiently small product tube adapted to its two transverse punctures and form $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$. The annulus core is a positive or negative meridian in the tube: both its boundary components bound the normal disks $P\cap N(L)$ and its core is homotopic within $A$ to either boundary. By [F4], composing $\pi_1(A)=\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(E_L)$ with abelianization sends its generator to $\pm1\in\mathbb Z$. The inclusion is therefore injective.

There is no boundary compression of $A$. If there were, [F5] would give a parallelism to one of the two annuli $A_0$ on the boundary torus between its meridional boundaries. This implies that one factor is the unknot, as can be checked with the markings: write the tube over the corresponding subinterval of the core knot as $D^2\times I$, with side $A_0=\partial D^2\times I$ and end disks the two disks $P\cap N(L)$. Attach the annulus parallelism to this side, retaining its rim collars. It merely enlarges the radial disk coordinate in each $I$-fiber, so the result is a ball with boundary the original $P$ after rounding. Its knot arc is the core $\{0\}\times I$, and it cobounds with an arc on that ball's boundary a disk given by a fixed radial interval times $I$, rounded at its ends. Capping this arc on $P$ produces an unknot. The same construction works for either complementary annulus of the torus; it uses its actual product parameter, not just a homological slope. By [F8] the resulting unknot is one of the given factors, contradicting nontriviality. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold for this particular $P$, and we may apply its isotopy and disk changes without changing $(L,S)$ or the specified factors.

In the resulting normal form $P\cap S=C$ is one circle disjoint from $L$. The two disks $P_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$ each contain one puncture. Indeed the two disk-intersection arcs of [F3] have their puncture endpoints one on each side, as in that lemma's final normalization. Each $P_\pm$ is a proper disk cutting its bridge ball into two balls: cap it by either of the two disks on $\partial B_\pm$ bounded by its rim, round, and apply [F6]; the side not containing the exterior of $B_\pm$ is the required ball. Their collars give compatible markings. Let $S_1,S_2$ be the disks on $S$ bounded by $C$, labelled by the two sides of $P$, and put $r_i=|L\cap S_i|$. Then $r_1+r_2=2b$. In each original bridge ball exactly one bridge arc crosses $P_\pm$: it is the arc carrying its unique puncture. Its two endpoints on $S$ lie on opposite sides of $C$, because the bridge crosses that separating disk once. Every other bridge arc is wholly on one side. Consequently $r_i$ is odd.

Cap each of the two cut ball-arcs of $L$ by a boundary arc on $P$ running from the upper puncture to the lower puncture and crossing $C$ once, chosen as the two type-I traces joined by an arc of $C$ between their distinct foot endpoints, then rounded slightly in the collar of $C$ so that it crosses $C$ transversely just once. Push the two caps into their respective boundary collars. On each side this cap is a trivial ball-arc meeting the capped bridge sphere $S_i\cup$(cap disk) once. Its upper and lower portions extend the severed bridge arcs. Every uncut bridge disk remains in its original region. Each of the two cut bridge disks is cut along its one trace into two disks; on each side join its disk piece to the narrow cap strip. This is a disk attached along one boundary interval, so gives a spanning disk for the extended upper or lower arc. Choose the cap strips in disjoint small quadrant collars of the traces; other disks miss them, and on a given side all disk pieces were originally disjoint. Thus these are simultaneous disjoint spanning-disk systems. The upper and lower ambient pieces are balls: attach the cap half-balls along the displayed windows on $P_\pm$ and use [F6]. We have therefore constructed actual bridge spheres for the two specified oriented factors, not merely diagrams with a proposed number of bridges. Each has $r_i+1$ knot endpoints on its sphere, the extra endpoint being the single crossing of the cap. It follows that their upper arc counts are $n_i=(r_i+1)/2$, and $n_1+n_2=b+1$. Cap orientation is chosen to close the original oriented arc, so [F8] identifies the factors with $K,J$, up to their harmless interchange.

Step 1.1 applied to the two factor bridge spheres gives $b(K)\le n_1$ and $b(J)\le n_2$. Hence $b(K)+b(J)-1\le n_1+n_2-1=b=b(K\#J)$. Together with step 3.1 and the unknot case in step 2.2, this proves the formula for every pair of smooth oriented knots in the Statement. The constructions use finitely many extrema, disks, cuts and collars; their smooth extension and Schoenflies uses are precisely the stated countable-choice suppliers.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For every smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1	o S^3$, let $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$ be the quotient normal bundle. Orient its two-dimensional fibres so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a positive basis of the normal fibre gives the fixed orientation of $S^3$. Then $
u_K$ admits a smooth orientation-preserving bundle isomorphism $
u_K\cong K	imes\mathbb R^2$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. Thus $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $M$.

Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedding, and suppose its normal bundle
$\nu(S)$ ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]) has
been equipped with its standard smooth-vector-bundle structure. Under
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ the existence of this structure is supplied by
[[prop-normal-and-conormal-bundles-are-smooth-vector-bundles]].

**Choose a tube adapted to $F$.** The smooth boundary collar of $F$ gives $c:K\times[0,\delta)\to F$ with $c(s,0)=s$; in local ambient charts extend it smoothly a small distance to negative collar parameter, shrinking it so its image stays in the domain of a tubular chart $\Phi_0$ from [F1]. $$\Psi:K\times(-\delta,\delta)\to K\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Psi(s,r)=(\pi(c(s,r)),r)$$

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$D_L(u)=\det(u^{-1}V-uV^T)$$
is independent of the surface and integral basis, belongs to $\mathbb Z[u-u^{-1}]$, equals $1$ for the unknot, and satisfies
$$D_{L_+}(u)-D_{L_-}(u)=(u-u^{-1})D_{L_0}(u)$$
for every oriented skein triple. Thus $D_L(u)=
abla_L(u-u^{-1})$ for the unique Conway polynomial normalized by $
abla_U=1$ and $
abla_+-
abla_-=z
abla_0$.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented three-sphere, and let $F$ be a connected compact oriented smooth embedded surface with oriented boundary $K$. Fix the standard round metric on $S^3$. A normal field along $K$ assigns to every point $p\in K$ a nonzero vector in the plane orthogonal to $T_pK$; two such fields represent the same framing class when they are homotopic through nonzero normal fields. The inward unit vector tangent to $F$ along $K$, together with the positive quarter-turn in each oriented normal plane, gives a reference frame. In this frame the relative normal field is a map $K\cong S^1\to S^1$, and its degree gives a bijection from framing classes to $\mathbb Z$. Adding $n$ positive full twists changes this integer by $n$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot
$K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, its normal bundle is
$\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, oriented so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a
positive basis of a normal fibre gives the ambient orientation. A **framing**
of $K$ is a homotopy class through smooth nowhere-zero sections of $\nu K$.
The normal bundle is made a smooth vector bundle under this axiom; a framed
knot includes the section class as data, not a choice made afterwards. For the
relative integer use the round metric transferred from the unit sphere in
$\mathbb R^4$ by the explicit diffeomorphism
$$x\longmapsto\left(\frac{2x}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2},\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2-1}{1+\lVert x\rVert^2}\right),\qquad\infty\longmapsto(0,0,0,1).$$

For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, set $J_0=c(K,\delta)$. It is embedded, lies in $\operatorname{int}F$, and is disjoint from $K$. No prescribed collar velocity is assumed: since $c$ is an embedding onto a boundary neighbourhood, $\partial_t c(p,0)$ is inward transverse to $K$ in $F$. Its normal quotient is therefore $a(p)s(p)$ for a smooth function $a(p)>0$; a tangential component is allowed.

Taylor expansion in finitely many bundle charts gives, uniformly on $K$, $w_t(x)=t a(x)s(x)+O(t^2)$. Uniformly these vectors have norm $O(\delta)$; a common disk bundle about the compact zero section lies in the tubular domain, so all interpolating graphs lie in that domain when $\delta$ is small. Each graph projects identically to $K$, hence is an embedded circle, and $\Phi$ carries it to an embedded circle disjoint from $K$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For every group extension
$$1\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow 1,$$
the maps induced by inclusion, quotient, and transgression form an exact sequence
$$H_2(G;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_2(Q;\mathbb Z) \longrightarrow N/[G,N]\longrightarrow H_1(G;\mathbb Z) \longrightarrow H_1(Q;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow 0.$$
Here $[G,N]$ is the normal subgroup generated by the commutators
$gng^{-1}n^{-1}$ with $g\in G$ and $n\in N$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume DC and the supplied projective-resolution convention for derived group homology. For every left $G$-module $M$, $H_n(G;M)$ is naturally the homology of $C_n(G;M)=(\overline B_n(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)_G$, with diagonal left action and alternating vertex-deletion differential. Equivalently it is computed by $\overline B^{\rm right}(G)\otimes_{\mathbb ZG}M$, where $b\cdot g=g^{-1}b$.

By [A1] and [L1], the DC condition of the bar-homology supplier in [F2]
holds. The case $n=1$ is the map between two trivial quotients. For $n=2$, the
induced map $A/\Gamma_2A\to B/\Gamma_2B$ is exactly the assumed isomorphism on
$H_1$ by [F2]. These are the base cases.

Fix $n\ge2$ and assume $A/\Gamma_nA\to B/\Gamma_nB$ is an isomorphism.
Apply [F1] to the extensions
$1\to\Gamma_nA\to A\to A/\Gamma_nA\to1$ and
$1\to\Gamma_nB\to B\to B/\Gamma_nB\to1$. Since
$\Gamma_nX\subseteq[X,X]$ for $n\ge2$, the maps
$H_1(X)\to H_1(X/\Gamma_nX)$ are isomorphisms. Exactness therefore makes the
transgression $H_2(X/\Gamma_nX)\to\Gamma_nX/[X,\Gamma_nX]$ onto, with kernel
the image of $H_2(X)$. By definition $[X,\Gamma_nX]=\Gamma_{n+1}X$.

Naturality of [F1] makes the map
$H_2(A/\Gamma_nA)\to H_2(B/\Gamma_nB)$ compatible with the two transgressions.
It is an isomorphism because the quotient-group map is an isomorphism by the
induction hypothesis. The epimorphism $H_2(A)\to H_2(B)$ makes the image of
$H_2(A)$ in $H_2(A/\Gamma_nA)$ map onto the image of $H_2(B)$ in
$H_2(B/\Gamma_nB)$. The induced map on the two cokernels is consequently an
isomorphism. By step 1.2 and exactness, those cokernels are
$\Gamma_nA/\Gamma_{n+1}A$ and $\Gamma_nB/\Gamma_{n+1}B$.

The inclusions and quotient maps give exact central extensions
$$1\to\Gamma_nX/\Gamma_{n+1}X\to X/\Gamma_{n+1}X\to X/\Gamma_nX\to1, \qquad X=A,B,$$
because $[X,\Gamma_nX]=\Gamma_{n+1}X$. The maps on the kernel and quotient
terms are isomorphisms by step 1.3 and the induction hypothesis. The middle
map is injective: an element in its kernel projects to the identity in the
quotient, hence lies in the kernel term, where injectivity holds. It is
surjective: for a target element, lift its quotient class through the quotient
isomorphism and then correct the chosen middle lift by a kernel element using
the kernel isomorphism. Thus $A/\Gamma_{n+1}A\to B/\Gamma_{n+1}B$ is an
isomorphism.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove by induction the isomorphism for every finite
$n$. Apart from the inherited AC used to obtain the homology sequence [F1],
the induction uses only exactness and a single element lift at a time; no
additional choice principle is used.

For every left $G$-module $M$, $H_n(G;M)$ is naturally the homology of $C_n(G;M)=(\overline B_n(G)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M)_G$, with diagonal left action and alternating vertex-deletion differential. derivations.claim: By [A1] and [L1], the DC condition of the bar-homology supplier in [F2] holds. The case $n=1$ is the map between two trivial quotients. For $n=2$, the induced map $A/\Gamma_2A\to B/\Gamma_2B$ is exactly the assumed isomorphism on $H_1$ by [F2]. These are the base cases.

citations.quote: Assume full AC and fix a smooth based knot $K\subset S^3$ with the earring and admissible singular bundle data of the preceding definitions. For regular perturbation data, the perturbed Chern–Simons critical points and finite-energy singular anti-self-dual trajectories define a finite free cochain complex $C^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$ with differential $d$ satisfying $d^2=0$. Its homology is independent of the chosen regular metric and perturbation up to the declared overall sign and is invariant under isotopy of the based knot data.

Assume full AC. For the smooth based unknot $U\subset S^3$, the integral singular earring instanton group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, and its rationalization has dimension one. There are regular choices with one critical generator and zero differential. Its generator is specified only up to the usual orientation sign; no distinguished sign-independent canonical class or sutured-excision identification is asserted.

derivations.claim: In the chosen closure, the standard marked circle meets $\bar R$ once, so $c_1(w)$ evaluates oddly on $\bar R$. The ordinary admissible theory in [F3] therefore applies. The torus has genus one, so the extreme-surface identity in [F3] gives $\ker(\mu(y)-2)\cap\ker\mu(\bar R)^N=\ker(\mu(y)-2)\cap\ker\mu(\bar R)$ for every $N\ge1$. Taking the union over $N$ therefore identifies the Definition's generalized surface-$0$/ordinary point-$+2$ subspace with the source's ordinary simultaneous $(0,2)$ eigenspace $I_*(\bar Y\mid\bar R)_w$. This is the exact torus convention in [F4], rather than an assumption of semisimplicity. It is finite-dimensional, and [F4] identifies the allowed closures up to isomorphism. This proves well-definedness of the rational group used here, without choosing a canonical basis or confusing it with the doubled full ordinary group.

Apply [F6] with the same based earring, connecting arc and determinant normalization. It gives the required rational isomorphism $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Q)\cong KHI(K;\mathbb Q)$. The local complex in [F1] is exactly its source.

For the unknot $U$, combine [F2] with step 1.2 to obtain $\dim_{\mathbb Q}KHI(U;\mathbb Q)=1$. This retains the local integral unknot calculation; the external input is the excision bridge, not a replacement for that calculation.

For a nontrivial smooth classical knot, the published genus/rank consequence in [F5] gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q}KHI(K;\mathbb Q)>1$. This is the established nonvanishing/decomposition input, explicitly imported rather than deduced from the already resolved singular complex or integral cube.

The unknot and nontrivial cases exhaust the knots in the statement. Steps 2.1–2.2 show that the finite-dimensional group always has dimension at least one and has dimension one exactly for the unknot. Step 1.2 supplies the additional isomorphism claimed in the statement.
